body:
`persistedCount` returns a bare int, and a key nobody wrote and a key written as `0` both come back `0`. No caller downstream can tell which it was, or decide what the person meant, because the information needed to decide it is gone before the call returns.

That is safe where it is used today and nothing said so. All four callers feed `ctxbudget.Limits`, where `0` means use the default, and each row's `read` returns the resolver rather than the stored value. So a person who types `0` into `context fill` watches the default appear in the row. The loss is visible to the person who caused it.

This adds the law to the doc comment, in the file's own voice for a stated law: what it destroys, why that is safe here, and that a caller who needs to tell unset from zero uses `persistedInt` and decides at the call site.

Comment only. No behaviour changes.

Found while sweeping shipped settings for values whose meaning is decided somewhere other than where the setting is declared. `persistedCount` is the one reader in that family that makes the question undecidable downstream rather than answering it wrongly.

## What a person can do now that they could not

- Put a skill in front of the conversation by hand. `/skill` opens a picker over
  every skill it found, and the attached ones ride as a tray chip.
- Have the right skill chosen by the words of the message, without attaching

in place, not copied.

The tmux suite drove the real binary against a real model, in a project with one
skill on the shelf:

- the turn's row names it while the turn runs

After the turn settles, the skills row is folded away with the rest of the
machinery and expanding the chip does not bring it back. #1363 has the mechanism
and two ways to fix it. The obvious flag was tried here and reverted: a told note

body:
Two entries in `.github/workflows/ci.yml`'s branch lists.

## Why

I was asked to make sure `santos/dev2` was green before merging, went looking
for its checks, and found it has none.

- `PR gate` (`ci.yml`) triggers on `pull_request`/`push` for **`dev`** only.
- `Full check` (`ci-full.yml`) triggers for **`staging`** and **`main`**, plus a
  09:00 UTC cron that runs against the default branch.
- So a pull request based on `santos/dev2` is answered by `license/cla` and
  nothing else, and a push onto that line runs nothing at all.

Four of my own open pull requests show exactly one check each, which is what
sent me looking.

`santos/dev2` is where feature work merges many times a day. Whether it compiles,
is formatted, passes vet, holds the laws, carries a change entry, keeps the
manual honest, or passes the full suite of every package it touched has been a
question only a person with a cluster could answer. #1361 records what the answer
was when somebody finally asked: the one suite that drives the real binary
against a real model is **7 of 18 subtests red** on that line.

The comment sits beside the existing note about #372, because it is the same
failure one level up. #372 was a test filter nobody remembered; this is a branch
nobody listed.

## What this does not do

It does not add the tagged tmux e2e suite to any workflow. That suite needs a
provider key and costs money per run, so its cadence is a budget decision rather
than a line to add, and #1361 asks for it separately.

## Verification

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` parses (`yaml.safe_load`). No test reads this
workflow's triggers: `internal/release/workflow_test.go`'s branch assertion is
on `release.yml`'s push list (`dev`, `staging`, `main`, unchanged), and
`internal/ci/testtooling_test.go` reads this file's light-job **step list**, not
its `on:` block.

The change proves itself: if it is right, this pull request gets a `check` run
it did not have before, and so does every pull request into this line after it.

body:
Unblocks #1355. Two subtests of `TestTUIE2E` failed on `belt/bash-default-restored` — the run worked, the row a person sees did not.

## The cause

`internal/session/task_run_belt.go`'s `startKnownTaskRun` seeds a plan store, names the store's task with the number the person is answered with, and publishes a row under that number (`publishRunRow`, task_run_belt.go:307 for a joined hand-off and :354 for the root). It never calls `graph.admit`, so **the graph holds no node for that row**.

`internal/tui3/taskplan.go`'s `planRowShown` deduped the store's row against the conversation's node rows **by title** — its own comment said "THIS SURFACE CANNOT SEE THE STORE ID" — dropped the plan row, and the place drew the node half. That row wore `working` (`session.taskRunningStatus`'s default, the reading of a node nobody is driving) where the store said `running`, and `enter` over it opened a room the engine holds no node for, so the page with the worker's trajectory was unreachable from the screen.

**The second half of the cause only the drive could find.** `PlanTaskRow.ID` is `planStoreID(task.ID)` — `t-41` — while the store's own id is the bare `41`. The first fix published the bare id, the identity joined nothing, and the real screen still drew the node half. The door publishes `planStoreID(storeID)` now: one spelling of a store id crossing the seam.

## The fix, and why not the alternatives

`session.TaskNotice.PlanTask` says **which task of the store this row is** — set by the door that mints both halves in one breath, in `planStoreID`'s spelling (the one `PlanTaskRow.ID` carries and `PlanTaskPage` is asked for), carried forward by the one function every publisher goes through, and written into the checkpoint. `internal/tui3` carries it onto the row and `readTasks` drops node rows whose named store task the plan read holds, so the store's own row is drawn: its state word, and the page `enter` opens.

The title dedupe stays for the **node road**, where `plandb_plan.go` seeds a store from the graph's own nodes: there the node is real and is the half with a room behind it, and its store ids (`root`, a random base36 word) are never the row's number, so title is all that road has.

- *Keep the plan row whenever both exist* was rejected: without an identity the only discriminator is still the title, which cannot tell the two roads apart, and it would invert the node road's dedupe.
- *Stop publishing the run's row* was rejected: that row is what `stoprun.go` resolves `task:N` through, what `ContinueRun` picks a run back up from, what the work tree ages, and the only row there is before the plan read lands. A capability that cannot work is absent, not broken — the row that opened nothing is gone, not the run.

One source of truth: the store id crosses the seam in one spelling, and the identity is stated by the publisher rather than guessed from prose.

## Three things the suite was not reading

Each of these is pre-existing and each made the lane lie, so they are fixed here rather than described:

1. **`enter` was pressed with the cursor on the conversation group**, whose door is the conversation and always was. The press read the chat; one of the two waits passed anyway, because the mark it looks for is drawn on the conversation too.
2. **The row search took the first line carrying the work's name** — at this width that is the record pane's heading, which leads with the selected row's title and wears no state. A screen whose row said `done · 4 steps · $0.03` was reported bare.
3. **The mid-run live step and the worker's own `plandb done` are a moment and a model's choice**, not facts about the surface: a brief this small finishes before the page opens, and the run writes the ending itself when the worker does not (`internal/run/worker.go`). Both are observed and logged. What is asserted in their place is that the press opened the **store's** page — `planNoteBoxWord` and `planStepsSpend`, two words no room draws. The `→` is waited out through the two words the foot gives for a shut and an open group, rather than slept through.

## Not a regression

The defect is **pre-existing on `santos/dev2`**, where `CODEAF_TASK_BELT=bash` reaches the same door; the restore only promotes it from opt-in to default.

```
# origin/santos/dev2 @ 99f301b08, its own copy of the scenario, its own binary
--- FAIL: TestTUIE2E (65.64s)
    --- FAIL: TestTUIE2E/TaskOnTheRunEngine (65.64s)
      tui_e2e_test.go:2178: the run's row does not wear "done" …
      tui_e2e_test.go:2210: Enter over the run's row never opened the store's plan page …
```

## Proof

Both real drives on this branch, on Spark:

```
--- PASS: TestTUIE2E/TaskOnTheRunEngine (37.70s)
--- PASS: TestTUIE2E/TaskOnTheDefaultBelt (37.73s)
```

`make test-quick` is green. Unit cover: `internal/session/planrow_identity_test.go` asks the real door for a row and the real plan read for its rows and fails unless one id is in both — which is the half that was wrong the first time; `internal/tui3/planrow_identity_test.go` walks the notice through `taskUpdate`, `taskSheetMine` and the place's reading, holds the node road's dedupe, and holds a row whose store task the plan read does not answer for. With `planStoreDraws` disabled the run-road test fails with the defect's own shape and the two guard tests still pass.

The touched-package suites were not run: the box was carrying a `make check` and another real-model baseline.

## Manual

`internal/manual/chat/worker-harness.md` already says "**`enter` opens the task's page** … built from the store's own read", and lists the state words a run's row wears off `planStateWord`. The manual was right and the code was wrong; no page changed.

body:
Follow-up to #1343, which bought four attempts and then delivered them as fast as the endpoint could fail.

## Two things

**A defect in #1343.** The turn loop computed the retry wait behind `if verdict.Retries() && !isCut`. That guard was written when no cut could ask for a backoff, and stayed after #1343 gave one to a cut against a single machine — so the verdict carried a wait the loop silently dropped. The verdict's own figure is honoured now whatever shape produced it.

**And the bound is removed where a bound has nothing to buy.** Every limit in the failure policy exists because the time could be spent on something else: another endpoint when routing has a pool, another model when a chain is configured, an ending the person can act on. A person talking to their own server has none of those. Giving up returns them to a prompt whose only sensible use is to ask the same question again, so the ending is not a move, it is the harness making them retry by hand.

`waitsForEver` is four facts, all load-bearing:

- **a cut**, because a refusal is an endpoint saying no and a cut is one saying nothing yet
- **one machine**, because with a pool the next ask is already somewhere else and has its own short allowance
- **no chain**, because a person who configured a next model asked for the hop
- **watched** (`Config.Interactive`), because the same loop with nobody in front of it is a hang that spends a worker's whole wall clock on a server that may never answer. A task node keeps its count.

It is the only verdict the caller's deadline does not end.

## The schedule is a ramp to a ceiling, not a doubling

Backing further and further away is a manner towards a shared service under strain, and none of that describes a machine on the same desk: asking is free, there is no rate limit, and what is being waited for finishes at a moment nobody can predict and everybody wants noticed at once. A schedule that had reached four minutes between asks would turn a server that came back in ninety seconds into four more minutes of watching a spinner. So it doubles while doubling is cheap and holds at `OneMachineCutCeiling`, ten seconds.

## And the waiting is said out loud

An unbounded retry is the one with no denominator to count towards, and a status reading `retrying` for ten minutes is indistinguishable from a wedged program. The line carries what a person would ask and the one thing they can do:

```
no answer 7 times in 2m · still asking · esc stops
```

## `Verdict.Unbounded` is a field and not an inference

The first cut of this read `Attempts == 0` as "unbounded". Zero already meant something older: an ordinary failure keeps no count here and is bounded by the deadline instead. Reading the two as one stopped the deadline ending any failing request, which `TestAFailingStepMovesToThePersonsPickAndNotTheLadder` and `TestFourMalformedRefusalsAreTransportAndTheTierNeverMoves` both caught. A test now pins the two apart.

## Evidence

Fresh clone on the test box at `3aad0781b`:

```
BUILD_RC 0 · WINBUILD_RC 0 · VET_RC 0 · gofmt list empty
CHANGES_RC 0
ok internal/taxonomy 1.670s
ok internal/provider 72.940s
ok internal/session 15.152s
LAWS_RC 0
```

body:
Change 2 of `docs/design/chat-coordination/DESIGN.md` — *The chat sees the plan
when the person speaks*.

**Stacks on #1356** (change 1). It is branched from `chat/notes-are-a-channel`,
so this PR's diff against `santos/dev2` contains #1356's commits too; land #1356
first. The digest reads the newest note on each row, which is #1356's data.

## The problem

A person says "actually, skip the migration". One of the run's tasks is doing
the migration at that moment. Nothing tells the chat that, so it answers the
person and the task carries on spending. Asking would not fix it: the `tasks`
tool has been able to answer this since the first run, and the turn where
somebody changes direction is exactly the turn where nothing in what they said
suggests looking. The information has to be pushed.

## What moved

- **`internal/session/plandigest.go`** (new) — while a run is live, each of the
  person's messages opens with a bounded digest of the plan: one line per task,
  the number the person sees, title, state, and its newest note. `planDigest()`
  is the same read `tasks` makes (`runPlanTasks`), narrowed to a row.
- **Bounded, and the bound is a constant with a test** — `planDigestRows = 8`,
  plus `planDigestLineChars` and `planDigestNoteChars` on the two strings a run's
  own models wrote. What the bound leaves out is counted and named, never
  silently dropped.
- **No results, no steps, no transcripts.**
  `TestTheDigestCarriesNoResultNoStepAndNoTranscript` asserts that against a
  store that holds all three.
- **Off when nothing is open**, and absent on the node road
  (`Config.oneTaskRoad`) — the same predicate the hand-off facts branch on.
- **The person never sees it.** `planDigested` is `standingMarked`'s shape: the
  model reads the digest and their sentence, the journal keeps their sentence
  alone.
- **`internal/session/beltfacts.go`** — one paragraph, on the plan road's
  `oneRoad` fragment alone: if what they just said makes a running task wrong,
  steer or stop THAT task before answering, and leave the rest alone.
- **Manual** — a section on `worker-harness.md` in the words of somebody who has
  just changed their mind with work in flight, and four probes.

## Acceptance

Scenarios 2 and 5 of the design, driven on the real binary on Spark. Quoted
lines follow in a comment.

## A finding about the design

The design's channel table says a task's brief is revised through
`revise_assignment`, and change 2's prompt sentence says the chat should "steer
or stop" a task. `revise_assignment` is **a worker's verb, not the chat's** —
`Config.mayRevise()` is `InTask && tasker != nil && taskID != 0`, and the tool's
own comment says "A conversation has no assignment to revise". What the chat
actually holds over a live run today is `tasks {"id": N, "stop": true}`, which
`stopBeltRow`/`stopJoinedRow` resolve to the run's own row or to one hand-off
that joined it, plus (with #1356) a note on any row. It has no door onto an
internal split part like `#1.2`. So the prompt sentence's "steer" is `stop`
today; the revise half is change 4's `plan` tool.

body:
Change 1 of `docs/design/chat-coordination/DESIGN.md` — *Notes are a channel, not a log*.

A note addressed to a task now reaches that task's running worker, between its
steps, on the road the belt already uses for its own sentences. Before this, the
channel was written to by three hands and read by nobody but the screen: a
worker that found a sibling's premise wrong wrote what it knew onto that task's
page, and the page was the end of it.

## What moved

- **`internal/run/bashworker.go`** — at each step boundary the loop reads its
  task's unread notes and steers them into the turn that is running
  (`Agent.Steer`, the same road `sameStepSpoken` takes). A turn that ends in the
  moment before the steer lands is owed them instead, so nothing is lost to that
  race. `owed` replaces the single `noteOwed` string because two sentences can
  fall in the same gap. The bound is `notesPerDelivery = 5`, and it bounds the
  *words*, not the channel: what it leaves behind is still unread and comes at
  the next boundary.
- **The mark is the worker's alone** — an in-memory set of note ids for the life
  of the loop. The design's "two readers of unread notes" hazard cannot arise:
  the screen touches nothing, so a note the person opened is never a note the
  worker missed.
- **`internal/session/prompts/bashworker.md`** — one paragraph each way: write a
  note onto a sibling's task when you find its premise wrong, and read a note on
  your own as a colleague's word, never an order, with your work order
  unchanged.
- **`internal/session/tools_tasks.go`** — the chat's `tasks` listing carries each
  row's newest note (`· note: …`), and a task's page carries its notes in full
  under `notes`, bounded by `runAskNotesPerTask`. A `note` field on the same door
  lets the conversation write one, **offered only where a plan store exists**
  (`Config.oneTaskRoad`), so the node road's request bytes are byte-for-byte
  unchanged.
- **`internal/plandb`** — `NoteAgentChat`, so a note the conversation left is
  drawn apart from the person's. The chat does not get to write in the person's
  voice; that is `relayToTask`'s law applied to the same hazard.
- **Manual** — two new sections on `worker-harness.md` and seven probes, plus
  the correction of a claim that was already there and already false: the page
  and two doc comments said a note reached the worker "in its next frame", and
  nothing read notes at all.

## Acceptance

Driven on the real binary on Spark, hosted, against a real model, under tmux.
Quoted lines and the capture files follow in a comment on this PR.

## Not in this change

Changes 2, 3 and 4 of the design.

body:
Restores the #1335 end state that #1340 reverted, and removes the worker bound the run engine was quietly applying.

## The default

Unset `CODEAF_TASK_BELT` is the worker harness again. `node`, `legacy` and `off` reach the older engine; anything else, including an empty value, is the harness. Every test file that #1340 touched goes back to its #1335 spelling, including the one-line `CODEAF_TASK_BELT=node` pin in `internal/session`'s and `cmd/codeaf`'s `TestMain` that names the older engine's suite once instead of a hundred and forty times, and `bashbelt_default_test.go` asserts the default in a truth table.

#1340 moved the default back on an eleven-run-per-arm comparison whose cells were launched in two unequal waves (four, then sixteen; load 2.5 then 38), so its wall times measured the launch schedule and its quality gap was one task. The comparison that replaces it is a 32-cell shuffled single batch on Spark (2026-09-21), eight DeepSWE tasks, two replicates, both arms interleaved so they saw the same load, `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` on every seat, each cell graded by its fixture's own suite with the official test patch applied:

| arm | scored | passed | median cost | median wall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| harness (bash) | 14 | 3 (21%) | $0.239 | 1010 s |
| node | 13 | 2 (15%) | $0.384 | 2924 s |

Pooled over every batch run this week (61 scored cells): harness 22% at $0.310 median, node 23% at $0.376. The harness is cheaper and roughly three times faster at the same quality; the wall gap is the node belt running its parts one after another. Crew arms with a separate plan seat and the flat single-worker arm were run beside these and were dominated on cost at equal or lower quality.

## The bound

`internal/config`'s `task.parallel` is 0 out of the box and its own hint says 0 is no limit. The chat door hands that 0 to the run engine, and `run.NewSupervisor` read it as 1, so every task a conversation put on the harness ran one part at a time. `codeaf do` did not read the setting at all; it carried a constant of four. This PR:

- makes a slot count below one no bound in the supervisor, with `full()` as the one place the bound is read;
- has `codeaf do` resolve its slot count from `task.parallel` like the chat door, with `--slots <n>` to name one for a run (`0` is no limit; blank is the setting), documented in `--help`, the `codeaf do` flag table and *How many tasks run at once*;
- has `drain` read the returns before waiting on the goroutines, because an unbounded run can have more workers out than the return channel is deep and a worker blocked on handing in its return never reaches `Done`.

Tests: `TestSupervisorLaunchesEveryReadyLeafAtOnceWithNoSlotBound` (six leaves on the seat together), `TestAnUnboundedRunEndedEarlyStillDrainsEveryWorker` (forty in flight, cost limit crossed by two, Run must come back under its own wall), `TestCodeafDoRunsAsManyWorkersAsTaskParallelSays`, `TestTheSlotsFlagTellsBlankFromZeroAndRefusesTheRest`.

## The tmux suite names its belt

`start()` launches every scenario with `CODEAF_TASK_BELT=node`, the road each was written for, and `startWithEnv` runs the child under `env -u CODEAF_TASK_BELT …` so a word exported in the runner's shell cannot choose the road; an assignment in a scenario's own env follows the `-u` and still wins. `TaskOnTheDefaultBelt` is new: it launches with the variable absent and reads the run road off the tasks place, the plan page and the thread, which is the only test of the default in the tree. The comment over `testTaskOnTheRunEngine` and the words table say what is true now. The tagged package compiles (`go vet -tags e2e ./internal/e2e/`); it has not been driven against a model on this branch.

## Proof

All on Spark, worktree `~/af-bash-restore` at `84e7d25f4` (this branch's tip), `BASE=origin/santos/dev2` (`8a83f4132`). Nothing ran on the laptop.

- `make pr-ready BASE=origin/santos/dev2` at `84e7d25f4`, pid 2148478, log `/tmp/bash-restore-prready3.log`: the whole quick gate green (build, vet, fmt, packed manual, change entries, manual gates, 31 law packages ok); `test-touched` refused the box lock because another session's `go test ./...` held it.
- `make test-touched BASE=origin/santos/dev2` at `84e7d25f4` once the lock freed, pid 2229868, log `/tmp/bash-restore-touched3.log`: `cmd/codeaf` 91.1s ok, `internal/config` 5.3s ok, `internal/e2e` 0.4s ok, `internal/run` 23.5s ok, `internal/session` 242.7s ok. All `-count=1`, through the known-red ledger.
- The same two steps had already passed at `6d6cb15e7` (before the e2e commit): `/tmp/bash-restore-prready2.log`, `/tmp/bash-restore-touched.log`; `internal/session` 247.8s ok there.
- Negative control: the two new `internal/run` tests copied onto a clean `8a83f4132` worktree both fail with `peak concurrency = 1`, so they test the defect and not the fixture.
- An earlier attempt at `86c2f94d6` failed two laws on `codeaf --help` reaching 111 lines against its 110-line cap (`TestUsageNamesEveryDispatchedDoorAndKeepsTheLineCap`, `TestTheHelpPageIsGroupedCommandsAndExamplesAndNotTheEnvironmentTable`); `--slots` is on `codeaf do --help` alone now, beside `--check-model`, which the summary already leaves there.

Not run: the tmux e2e suite against a real model, and any real-binary drive. Owner's call before merge.

body:
Two documents under `docs/design/chat-coordination/`. No code.

## BELT-DOE.md — why the default moves back to bash

The record of the measurement. Three batches, 66 cells, one binary
(`619860cc6`), one model (`z-ai/glm-5.3-flash`) on every seat, so no arm
could win by having a stronger model.

The 32-cell shuffled batch is the only one whose wall figures are valid
(both arms interleaved into one launch, so every cell met the same
contention):

| arm | scored | passes | rate | mean $ | mean wall |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **bash** | 14 | 3 | 21% | **$0.239** | **1010s** |
| node | 13 | 2 | 15% | $0.384 | 2924s |

Pooled over all three batches the quality is a tie (five passes each) and
bash is about a third cheaper. Node's slowness is structural, not the
auditor: `defaultRunSlots = 4` against a node road with one
`sync.WaitGroup` and no pool. 37 samples from one node cell's log all read
`N tasks pending, 1 running`.

The document also records what it does NOT establish (n is small, one
model, DeepSWE fixtures only, and `Slots` is about to change), and the
instrument fault that nearly invalidated the whole grid: both
`bench/bashloop` and the DeepSWE rig ran their control arm with
`CODEAF_TASK_BELT` unset, so the moment unset meant bash they would have
compared bash to bash and reported a difference of zero as a measurement.

## DESIGN.md — the chat as manager

The chat and the plan store are joined in one direction: the chat puts
work in and is woken when work lands. Four things a person notices are
each a missing reader on a channel that is already written to:

1. **Notes are a channel, not a log.** A note addressed to a task reaches
   its running worker on the road the engine already uses for its own
   sentences (`sameStepNote`, carried by `noteOwed`), and the chat's
   `tasks` output prints notes it currently drops.
2. **The chat sees the plan when the person speaks.** A bounded digest
   opens each turn while a run is live, so the chat can steer or stop a
   task the person just made wrong.
3. **Consent is the run's budget.** The first card names a dollar cap;
   inside a live run under its cap the chat may add, steer, note or stop
   without a card. Explicitly NOT a consent flag the model sets: that
   asks the person exactly when the model is unsure and not when it is
   confident, which is the wrong way round.
4. **One door for the chat, light doors for workers.** `propose_task`'s
   five required fields stay at the chat's door; a worker's `plandb add`
   stays title-plus-description, because checks were 69% of one measured
   run's spend and forcing one on every subtask multiplies that.

A section records what is deliberately not built and why: no sentinel
(miniplan's was advisory-only and showed no accuracy effect), no manager
seat, no more planning machinery (the arm that planned hardest produced
25-29 tasks per run for one pass in four at double the cost).

**Acceptance is end-to-end first.** Every change is accepted only on a
person-shaped drive of `bin/codeaf` against a real model in tmux on the
cluster, with the drawn words quoted from the capture. Five scenarios are
written out, including one that asserts the node road is unchanged. Unit
tests prove the seams and are not the bar.

body:
A custom provider that answers 200 and streams nothing ended the turn after two immediate asks, about ten seconds apart, with no wait between them and no way to configure one.

## What was happening

1. The guard cuts a stream that produced nothing — `CutSilent`.
2. `noteCutProvider` asks whether striking that endpoint moved anything. With no router behind the build the request names no machine and none names itself, so `pace()` returns false and `StreamCut.Rerouted` is false on **every** cut such a build will ever take.
3. `transportBudget` reads `!Rerouted` as `BlindCutAttempts = 2`, documented as "the next attempt lands in the same place by the same rules, so the extra asks buy nothing".
4. `waitFor` returns 0 for a cut, documented as "what mends it is being served by somebody else, which costs no time at all".

Both sentences are about a POOL. `Rerouted` false had two documented causes — routing switched off, and a stream that died before naming its server — and both leave a pool the next draw comes from. There is a third, and it wants the opposite answer: a build with one machine struck nothing because there was nothing to strike. Asking again is the only move there is, and time is the only thing that mends a server which just answered nothing.

## The change

- `StreamCut.OneMachine`, set in `stampCut` where the adapter already knows it: the request expressed no preference and no chunk named a server.
- `Evidence.OneMachine`, carried through the session's transport ladder. It is ANDed across a step's cuts, so one cut that did have a pool means the step had one and keeps the narrow allowance.
- `OneMachineCutAttempts = 4`, and the cut takes the same doubling wait a refusal gets in front of each ask.

Nothing else moves. A rerouted silence still spends three with no wait, degeneration still spends two, and a configured model chain is still reached the same way when the allowance runs out.

## Evidence

Fresh clone on the test box at `37d0847ad`:

```
BUILD_RC 0 · WINBUILD_RC 0 · VET_RC 0 · gofmt list empty
CHANGES_RC 0
ok internal/taxonomy 1.770s
ok internal/provider 72.297s
ok internal/session 15.232s   (-run 'Cut|Transport|Ladder|Retry|Empty')
LAWS_RC 0
```

New tests pin both directions: a one-machine cut asks four times with a doubling wait and ends in the same hop-or-stop, and a cut that had a pool keeps its short allowance and its zero wait.

body:
A replay arriving onto a surface that is already drawing the conversation put
the whole record above itself: every answer twice, and two seams.

## The law this breaks is written down three times

`session.EarlierHistory`'s own doc says what the file holds and what a surface
may do with it:

> the same conversation is in the file twice: once as it happened, above the
> marker, and once with its tool results stubbed and its long runs of work
> folded, below. Drawing both would show the session to itself twice.

`internal/tui3/replay.go` says it twice more, on `roomRecord` and on
`backfill`: the region is drawn and the copy is never a row.

## What replayList was doing

It keeps everything already on screen, and that is right for what it was written
for, in its own words:

> The record this is built from is fetched off the loop and the box is live the
> whole time it is in flight, so a person who switched conversation and typed
> straight away had their message appended to and then buried by the history
> that arrived behind it.

BUT IT KEPT ALL OF IT. Rows a PREVIOUS replay drew from this same record are not
something said afterwards. They are the record, and keeping them puts the record
on top of itself.

## The fix

`app.recordRows` is how many blocks at the front of the drawn conversation came
from the record: the opening replay, every helping `app.backfill` handed up, and
the seam rows drawn between them. `app.prepend` adds to it in the same walk that
draws the rows, and `replayList` keeps only what is past it.

IT IS COUNTED RATHER THAN RECOGNISED. Two rows of one conversation are equal in
every field a comparison could reach, so there is nothing to match on afterwards
and no heuristic to get wrong. The count is dropped wherever the rows it counts
are dropped, which is `rebuildTranscript` and `clearConversation`.

## The production road to a second replay is UNPROVEN

This is stated plainly because it is not established and the body should not
imply otherwise.

Every caller of `app.attachConversation` calls `detachConversation` first, which
clears the drawn conversation: `welcome.go`, `takeover.go`, `app.go`, and both
keeper roads including `leaveFront`, whose attach has no detach on the line
above it but makes one earlier in the same function. The off-loop read is
guarded too: `takeUp` bumps `frontGen`, `offLoop` captures it, and a read for a
conversation the person has left folds with `here=false`.

So what is fixed here is a PROPERTY `replayList` owes whatever calls it, not a
traced sequence. It is worth pinning on its own terms: the function keeps rows
it cannot distinguish from the ones it is about to draw, and the law it would
break is the one the engine states three times over.

## Acceptance

`internal/tui3/replay_once_test.go`.

`TestAReplayOntoADrawnConversationDrawsItOnce` counts each line of the
conversation on the screen, and counts the seam. It asserts the conversation is
told once BEFORE the second replay as well, so the count afterwards is a
statement about the replay rather than about the fixture.

On `fb67f070f` as it stands, every line of it:

```
replay_once_test.go:68: "old answer 0" is on the screen 2 times, want once
replay_once_test.go:68: "kept answer 0" is on the screen 2 times, want once
...
replay_once_test.go:68: the seam is drawn 2 times, want once
```

`TestASentenceTypedWhileTheRecordWasComingSurvivesTheReplay` is the control, and
it is the one that matters most here: a fix that simply dropped what was on
screen would pass the first test and lose the exact thing `inTheGap` exists to
protect. It pins that the sentence is still there and that the conversation is
still drawn once.

## Checks

Written against `fb67f070f`, and the red above was established on that head.

```
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/tui3	327.990s
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/session	247.581s
```

body:
A compaction pass that found nothing to do announced itself exactly as one that
had rewritten the transcript, and the surface believed it. The place a person
was reading was dropped to the compaction floor, the conversation between the
two was declared already drawn, and the marker promising more above went out.

## One value, two meanings, and the failing one was silent

`EventCompacted` is sent on both paths, and that is right: `EventCompacting`
opens a row and it has to be possible to settle it whether the pass found
anything or not. Its own doc says so.

> EventCompacted always follows it, success or failure: a surface opens a row on
> this one and settles it on that one, and a pass that found nothing to do says
> so rather than leaving the row open.

It said so in `Hint` and nowhere a reader could act on. `app.rebase` took every
one of them as a replacement and handed the scrollback over:

- `replayFrom` was set to `earlierFloor`, so every entry between the reader's
  place and the floor was recorded as already drawn.
- `earlierFrom` was set from an index into the live transcript and used as an
  index into the region.
- `earlierSeam` was set true, so the seam was recorded as drawn and then never
  drawn.

## What it cost, measured

A resumed session compacted once, forty turns said since it, a reader who had
not crossed the seam. One refused pass, then scroll to the top:

```
18 of 40 answers never drawn, seam drawn = false, moreHistory = false
```

The surface says the conversation is complete with that much of it unreachable.

ON A SESSION THAT WAS NEVER COMPACTED AT ALL the same call sets `replayFrom` to
0 and the marker goes out with half the conversation undrawn. That is the
ordinary path, not the compacted one.

## The fix

`session.Event.Unchanged` is the disjoint range, set only by the refused arm of
`Agent.compact`, and the surface rebases only when a pass actually happened.

THE ZERO VALUE IS "A PASS HAPPENED", deliberately. The field rides the wire
behind a json tag of its own, so a peer built before it existed does not send
it, reads false, and behaves exactly as it always did. The other polarity would
have made every older peer stop rebasing.

## Acceptance

Two tests in two packages, because the fix is in two halves and either half
alone leaves the defect standing.

`internal/session/compaction_refused_event_test.go` pins the session half: a
refused pass sets the field, and a pass that really edited the transcript does
not. The second is the control, without which a build that marked every pass
unchanged would pass the first.

`internal/tui3/compact_refused_test.go` pins what a surface does with it: the
reader's place is not moved, every one of the forty answers is still reachable
by scrolling, the conversation's first message is still reachable, and the seam
is drawn rather than marked drawn. Its control is that a pass that DID happen
still hands the bookkeeping over, without which a build that simply stopped
rebasing would pass.

The tui3 test builds its event by hand, so it passes on the surface half alone.
That is exactly why the session test is written as well, and the three states
were run rather than reasoned about:

| tree | internal/session | internal/tui3 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| the field alone, nothing sets it, nothing reads it | FAIL | FAIL |
| the session sets it | ok | FAIL |
| the surface reads it | ok | ok |

The tui3 failure in the first two states is the defect in its own words:

```
compact_refused_test.go:39: a pass that compacted nothing moved the place a
person was reading, from 52 to 12
```

## Checks

Written against `fb67f070f`. The three states above were RUN on that head, not
carried over: `internal/tui3/app.go` differs between `dev` and `santos/dev2`,
which is one of the two files this changes, so the red was re-established rather
than assumed.

```
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/session	248.161s
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/tui3	328.173s
```

One run, both packages, under the box's one heavy-suite lock, with `-count=1`.
`internal/tui3` is in it because that is where the bookkeeping lives, and
`internal/session` because that is where the field is set.

`bash scripts/laws.sh` exits 0. `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` prints nothing.
title: session, chat: a pass that compacted nothing stops taking the conversation away

body:
#1335 moved the default on an instruction rather than a measurement, and its own change entry said so. The measurement has now been made and it does not support the move, so the default goes back.

### What was measured

Two engines, **one binary**, DeepSWE fixtures, `z-ai/glm-5.3-flash` on every seat, graded by each fixture's own suite with the official test patch applied on top. Eleven runs per arm across two replicates and seven tasks, of which **five actually scored**.

| arm | passes | tests missed | total $ | **$ per pass** |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **node belt** | **3** | **7** | **$4.04** | **$1.35** |
| bash belt | 2 | 14 | $4.14 | $2.23 |

Wall time was **not** compared. The cells shared a box and the load moved from 2.5 to 38 between launches, so their times measure the launch schedule rather than the arms.

Two caveats stated rather than buried: this is a **one-task difference** in outcome, so the quality gap is suggestive and not settled; the cost gap is the firmer half. And bash's test-miss count is quoted as 14 rather than 80 because one cell broke a suite wholesale — it still counts as a non-pass, but one pathological run should not decide a comparison.

The earlier eighteen-task comparison in `docs/design/bash-task-loop/REPORT.md` (17/18 node, 13/18 bash) points the same way. Nothing measured has ever favoured the harness.

### The harness is not withdrawn

`CODEAF_TASK_BELT=bash` reaches it exactly as before #1335. Every byte is still in the binary; the run engine, the plan store and the crew seats are untouched. What moves is which belt a person who has said nothing gets.

### Two things from #1335 are kept rather than reverted with it

**The bench names a belt on both arms.** `bench/bashloop` ran arm A with the variable unset, which is correct only while unset means the node belt. The moment a default moves, an arm relying on absence becomes a copy of the arm it is compared against and the driver reports a difference of zero as a measurement. Both arms name a word now. **This is true whichever belt is default**, which is why it does not travel with the revert.

**The default is asserted.** It had never been written down anywhere — it was carried only by the absence of a value in other tests, so it could move, and did, without one test in the tree saying a word. `bashbelt_default_test.go` spells the whole answer out, including that the match is exact (`BASH` and `bashx` do not reach the harness) and that a blank value reads as unset.

### Proof, on Spark

| step | result |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal ./bench` | clean (list captured, not the exit code) |
| `go build ./...` / `GOOS=windows go build ./...` | 0 / 0 |
| `go vet ./...` | 0 |
| `scripts/laws.sh` | exit 0, **0 FAIL lines** |
| `session`, `cmd/codeaf`, `run`, `plandb`, `bashloop` | 5/5 exit 0, 0 failures |
| new default tests, `-v` | 10 PASS, 0 FAIL (8 rows + 2 parents) |

Santosh's ask (Slack, 2026-09-21): the browser sign-in OpenRouter already has, for Codex too, and a terminal door for signing in.

## What changes

- **Codex is a model service.** `/connect` has a `Codex` row that says `browser`; enter opens the sign-in the Codex CLI uses (S256 PKCE, the fixed loopback callback on 1455 then 1457), the waiting card keeps the address to copy, and a finished sign-in moves the conversation to `codex/gpt-5.5`. The models are the account's own list; ids are `codex/<slug>` everywhere.
- **The wire.** The provider client keeps speaking chat completions. A translating transport on `provider.Config.HTTPClient` turns each turn into a Responses-API request on the ChatGPT backend and its stream back into the chunks the client already decodes: text, reasoning summaries, tool calls, usage. Encrypted reasoning rides the `reasoning_details` field the session already round-trips. Tokens live in an owner-only `codex.json` in the profile, registered for redaction, refreshed single-flight with the file re-read first.
- **`codeaf connect [service] [--no-browser] [--region intl|cn]` and `codeaf disconnect <service>`.** `openrouter` and `codex` sign in in the browser (or print the address, with the `ssh -L` line for a machine without one); the key services take a key on stdin or ask without echo; no argument lists what this profile knows. Under Housekeeping on `codeaf --help`.
- **No price is ever shown for a codex call.** Tokens are counted. A spent plan window ends the turn with `codex reached your chatgpt plan's usage limit · it resets on its own`; an expired sign-in with `codex sign-in has expired · /connect or codeaf connect codex signs in again`.
- **The manual, README and GUIDE** say all of the above, including that this signs in the way the Codex CLI does and OpenAI's terms for a ChatGPT plan apply.

Out of scope, and said so in the pages: first run (unchanged, OpenRouter only), the device-code road, OpenAI API keys (the custom-service row), Codex's own base instructions, websockets.

## How it was verified

- Every contract item in the spec has a named test; the wire is proven through a real `provider.Client`, the real config chain and a real `session.Agent` against `httptest` issuer and backend servers. No real host is contacted by any test.
- A fixture drive of the built binary (a fake issuer that redirects like a browser that clicked yes, and a fake backend): the printed authorize address carries exactly the Codex CLI's parameters; the callback lands `codex connected · <email> · pro plan`; the token file is mode 0600; the code exchange happens and no API-key exchange does; `codeaf connect` lists the row as connected; a `--once` turn reaches the backend with the bearer, `chatgpt-account-id`, `originator`, `OpenAI-Beta`, `store:false`, `stream:true`, non-empty instructions and no OpenRouter attribution; no dollar figure is printed; no token appears in any output; `codeaf disconnect codex` removes the file.
- Constants were read from the installed Codex CLI binary and Codex's own source, and the backend's models listing was called once with the owner's own Codex sign-in to ground the vendored fallback list.

- **The default road.** Every step of the first drive used `--no-host`, the in-process door, and the owner found on the real screen that a plain `codeaf chat` answered the Codex row with `codex did not connect · codex browser sign-in is unavailable here`: the ordinary launch takes the engine road, whose screen is assembled by the `--host` builder plus `localDoors`, and the Codex seam had been handed to the in-process door alone (the same family as #906). `localDoors` now hands it over, the doors test asserts both sides, and the drive has a phase that runs bare `codeaf` in a pristine home, goes through `/connect` → `Codex` with a stub browser on `PATH`, lands `codex connected · <email> · pro plan` on the card, answers `say hi` through the daemon, then runs `--once` without `--no-host`. Against the build before the fix that phase fails with the owner's exact sentence; on this head every check passes.
- **The real backend.** Two turns on the real ChatGPT backend from a throwaway profile seeded with the owner's Codex CLI access token (a placeholder refresh token, so the CLI's own sign-in was never rotated): a plain reply, and a tool call round trip. No token bytes in any output.

What only the owner can verify: a real click-through on `auth.openai.com` with a real ChatGPT plan.

Found on the way and filed, not in this PR: #1383 — a Codex model keeps the previous model's context window because the listing's `context_window` (272k) is dropped.

## What the adversarial review found, and what the fix round closed

A read-only review of the first seven commits refuted eight claims, all now fixed with a test that would fail on regression:

- **Refresh across processes.** Two codeaf processes near expiry could invalidate each other's rotated refresh token. The refresh now holds the repository's file lock across load, refresh and save, and re-reads first, so whichever process refreshed wins (proven with two re-executed test processes sharing one token file against an issuer that invalidates a refresh token after one use).
- **Only the issuer signs you out.** A 429, a 5xx or a network error during refresh no longer clears the token file; only the issuer's own 400/401 marks the sign-in expired.
- **The expiry sentence reaches the person**, headless or in the chat, and a token file deleted underneath a running conversation is the same condition. The dispatcher does not spend its retry walk on a dead credential.
- **A failed or cut reply is an error, not a success.** `response.failed` and `error` events become a classifiable 402 or 502 on both the streaming and whole-response roads; an incomplete reply carries `length` only for `max_output_tokens`.
- **The transport's tokens never leave it.** Every body, status and error it returns is scrubbed; provider's error ingress and the call log scrub as a second boundary; a fake backend that echoes the bearer in a 400 leaves no token bytes in the turn's error, the transcript, the call log or the debug record.
- **The last catalog road.** The media resolver built a catalog without the codex client; every connected-service catalog now comes from one constructor, and a `go/ast` law refuses any other literal.
- **A headless plan refusal keeps its own words.** A `--once` run used to end every 401/402/403-class refusal with `your key was not accepted for this model`, for Z.ai as much as for Codex; both roads now end it the way the chat already did: the service, that the account cannot pay, and what the vendor said.
- Also: absent usage stays absent; a browser that would not start says so and the terminal keeps waiting; the listener test pins 1455 then 1457; first run is rendered and asserted to offer no Codex.

A second read-only review of the fixed branch closed those and added a refresh that could wait forever behind another process sitting in an issuer round trip with no deadline. Now the issuer exchange has a thirty-second deadline, both locks are taken without blocking and given up when the turn is cancelled or after a minute with one plain sentence, and the lock file is owner-only. From the same round: provider's error ingress removes only the credentials this process registered and leaves every other byte alone; an expired sign-in is accounted once through the taxonomy like any terminal failure instead of short-circuiting the loop; the transcript journal and the error event scrub assembled text at write time (the journal only for registered credentials, so a key a person pasted into their own message replays on resume exactly as written); and the catalog law refuses an assignment to `Source` as well as a literal.

Evidence, the fixture, and both review ledgers are in the handoff folder on the owner's machine; the fixture drive of the final binary passes all thirteen checks. One unrelated load-sensitive session test surfaced in the local gate and is filed as #1339.

`CODEAF_TASK_BELT` kept its name, its one reader and the sense of every caller. What moved is the answer it gives when nobody has spoken: `bashBeltAsked` was a match against `bash` and is now a lookup in a closed list of the words that mean the older road — `node`, `legacy`, `off`. Both engines are still in one binary, and `/task` and `codeaf do` both take the run road with nothing set.

The list is closed on purpose. An unrecognised value leaves a person on the harness rather than moving them off it: a typo in an environment variable must not be able to change which engine does the work, and the failure it would cause is silent — the run simply comes out on a road nobody chose. An exported but blank value reads as unset, which is the default, which is bash.

### What else had to move

**The bench was the one place this could have been wrong without saying so.** `bench/bashloop` ran arm A with the variable unset. After the flip both arms would have ridden the bash belt and the driver would have reported a difference of zero as a measurement. Both arms now name a word, and the branch that handled an absent one is deleted rather than left dead.

**141 tests** in `internal/session` and `cmd/codeaf` were written against the node engine and said so by saying nothing. They did not become wrong when the default moved; they became silent about which road they meant. Each package's `TestMain` names that road once instead of each test naming it. A test that means the harness sets `bash` for itself and wins — every harness test in those packages already did.

That pin has a cost: with it in place nothing in those packages would notice if the default went back. So `bashbelt_default_test.go` asserts the truth table directly — unset is bash, the three words turn it off, case and surrounding space do not matter, an unknown word moves nobody — and a second test asserts the pin itself.

The manual pages that told a person the harness was not the default now tell them it is and name the three words that turn it off (`worker-harness.md`, `how-tasks-run.md`, `tasks.md`).

### Proof, on Spark

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal ./bench` | clean (list captured, not the exit code) |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `GOOS=windows go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet ./...` | exit 0 |
| `scripts/laws.sh` | exit 0, 0 FAIL lines |
| `session, cmd/codeaf, run, plandb, enginehost, bashloop, config, manual` | 8/8 exit 0, 0 failures |
| new test, `-v` | 12 PASS, 0 FAIL (10 rows + 2 parents, enumeration matches) |

**Negative control:** the predicate was reverted to `== "bash"` in place and `TestTheBeltIsBashUnlessOneOfThreeWordsSaysOtherwise` went red on 5 rows naming the exact values. The test can fail.

### The evidence this lands against

It does not argue for the change on its own, and that is recorded in the change entry rather than left out. `docs/design/bash-task-loop/REPORT.md` measured one binary over eighteen tasks and put the older belt at 17 and the bash belt at 13. That comparison predates every wave of the worker harness that followed it and does not describe the road this switch now chooses, but no run since has replaced it. **The default moved on the owner's instruction, not on a measurement**, and the measurement that would settle it has not been made.

body:
## Why

Santosh asked for internal dev usage — downloads and everything around them —
to be separated from the main install. Today a dev build can be installed, but
only *over* `~/.codeaf/bin/codeaf`: its launch check is silent, `/update` with no
word installs **stable** over it, and the curl line it offers reinstalls stable.
So a dev daily driver was three surprises away from being a stable binary again.

This makes a dev build a thing you can keep: it installs beside codeaf under its
own file name, it follows the dev channel, and every road it offers back leads to
the file you are actually running.

## What changes

The product is still **codeaf**. `devaf` is only a *file name* — every sentence
the program prints still says codeaf, and `devaf version` prints
`codeaf dev-… · go… linux/amd64`. Nothing is renamed: not the state root, not the
socket names, not one identifier.

- **The installer takes a name.** `--name WORD` and `CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME`, checked
  against `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$` before anything is written (anything else
  is a usage error, exit 2, naming the rule). The binary, the temporary file, the
  printed line and the closing `version` run all use that name. `INSTALL_NAME` sits
  on one unindented line directly under the `CHANNEL` line so the website proxy can
  rewrite it exactly the way it already rewrites the channel.
- **A channel build follows its channel.** A `dev-*` or `staging-*` build asks *its*
  channel at launch and gets the same one dim line when that channel has something
  newer; `/update` and `codeaf update` with no channel word select it. An explicit
  word or tag still wins — `/update stable` on a devaf installs stable over that same
  file, because the person asked. Stable and rc behave exactly as before; a source
  build is still silent and still refused.
- **Two tags of one channel are ordered** by publish moment first, then by the
  `YYYYMMDD` in the tag, and a same-day tie with a moment missing goes to the release
  the API named. The running build's own moment comes out of the release list the
  check already fetches, so there is no extra request and no build-moment stamp. A
  build ahead of the newest is never silently downgraded.
- **The cache is one file per channel.** `update-check.dev.json` and
  `update-check.staging.json`, cached for **one hour** because dev publishes several
  times a day and a devaf beside a codeaf must not thrash one file. Stable and rc keep
  `update-check.json` and 24 hours, byte-for-byte as before.
- **The curl line names this file.** `update.CurlLine(executable, channel)` replaces
  the one constant everywhere a road back is offered: a file named `devaf` is told to
  reinstall from `/get/devaf`, a `codeaf` on a channel from `/get/codeaf/<channel>`,
  and any other name carries `CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME=<name>`. A source build's refusal
  still prints the `CurlCommand` constant.
- **Shared state.** devaf and codeaf share `~/.codeaf` — keys, conversations, one
  engine host per workspace — under the existing retire-or-attach law. Nothing here
  changes it.
- **Dev release notes** carry `curl -fsSL https://agentfield.ai/get/devaf | bash` and
  one sentence saying what it installs. Only the dev channel gets the block.

## Validation contract, and how each line is proven

| | Behaviour | Proof |
| --- | --- | --- |
| V1 | `--name devaf --dev` writes `<dir>/devaf`, prints the real file, ends with that file's version line, leaves a sibling `codeaf` byte-identical; the variable does the same; the flag wins; `../x`, `-x`, `""`, a bad variable and a bare `--name` all exit 2 and write nothing | `internal/release` · `TestV1InstallerName` |
| V2 | `INSTALL_NAME="${CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME:-codeaf}"` is one unindented line, exactly once, directly under `CHANNEL`; `--help` names both spellings | `internal/release` · `TestV2InstallerNameSeamAndHelp`, `TestInstallerKeepsTheWebsiteChannelSeam` |
| V3 | a dev build one build behind gets exactly one notice and a devaf gets the devaf road; the newest gets none; staging asks the staging list; stable's request and notice are unchanged; source makes no request; one call to `releases?per_page=100` | `internal/update` · `TestV3LaunchNoticeForChannelBuilds`, `TestSourceLaunchesNeverReachTheNetwork` |
| V4 | the ordering law, both directions, including the cases it left open and the pairs it cannot rank at all | `internal/update` · `TestV4ChannelOrdering`, `TestV4UnrankablePairsAreNeitherNewerNorAhead` |
| V5 | a dev build writes and reads only `update-check.dev.json`; one hour there, 24 hours on stable; alternating launches in one profile make one request each | `internal/update` · `TestV5ChannelCacheFilesAndLifetimes` |
| V6 | `/update` and `codeaf update` with no word follow the running build; every explicit override wins; a check across two channels says only what it can order | `internal/tui3` · `TestV6UpdateChoiceFollowsTheRunningBuildUnlessOverridden`; `cmd/codeaf` · `TestV6TerminalUpdateDefaultsToTheRunningDevChannel`, `TestV6CrossChannelChecksSayOnlyWhatTheyCanOrder` |
| V7 | an ahead dev build is refused in both doors with the documented sentence and installs nothing; `--check` exits 0 with the newest/running line; naming the tag installs it; a publish moment beats the tag's date through the whole door | `cmd/codeaf` · `TestV7TerminalUpdateRefusesAnAheadDevUnlessTheTagIsNamed`, `TestV7APublishMomentOutranksTheDateInTheTag`; `internal/tui3` · `TestV7ChatUpdateRefusesAnAheadChannelBuildUnlessTheTagIsNamed` |
| V8 | the twelve-row curl table, and the line reaching the launch notice, `/update`'s failure, the source refusal and a failed replace | `internal/update` · `TestV8CurlLineTable`, `TestV8InstallFailureCarriesTheCallersCurlLine`; `cmd/codeaf` · `TestV8TerminalFailureUsesTheRunningFilesCurlLine`; `internal/tui3` · `TestV8UpdateNotesUseTheRightCurlLine` |
| V9 | "what is devaf", "devaf", "can I run two versions of codeaf side by side", "how do I keep my dev build up to date" and "how do I install the latest dev build beside my codeaf" all reach the terminal page | `internal/manual` · `TestV9DevafQuestionsReachTheTerminalManual` and the probe table |
| V10 | the dev notes block spells `agentfield.ai/get/devaf` and no other channel enters it | `internal/release` · `TestV10DevReleaseNotesNameTheDevafInstaller` |

## Verified by hand

- `scripts/install.sh --name '../x' | '-x' | ''` each prints
  `codeaf: --name / CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME must match ^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]*$`
  and writes nothing; `--name devaf` against the real release service really does
  write `<dir>/devaf`.
- `codeaf version` does **not** create the state root, so moving the installer's
  closing version run after the install-marker block (which is what "the last action
  runs that file's version" asks for) changes no marker behaviour — only the order in
  which the version line and the telemetry notice print.
- Gates run in the worktree: `go build ./... && go vet ./...` clean, `gofmt -l cmd internal`
  silent, `bash test/installer-telemetry.sh` → `35 passed, 0 failed`, the four touched
  packages green, and `make pr-ready` green.
- An adversarial read-only review round against the contract; its one real finding
  (the manual overclaiming what `--check` does across two channels) is fixed in the
  last commit, with two tests that pin the corrected sentences.

## Not verified here

- **Windows.** `CurlLine` strips `.exe` and the installer appends its existing
  extension, both covered by tests, but no native Windows shell run was made.
- **The live proxy.** `agentfield.ai/get/devaf` is the other half of this change and
  ships as a separate website2.0 pull request. That route rewrites two lines of this
  installer — the channel and the name — and **fails closed with a 502** until this
  pull request reaches the `dev` branch, because the line it must rewrite does not
  exist there yet. Land this first.

## Added after the first review pass

- **A release candidate follows stable, so it is offered the stable road.** The first
  draft took the curl line from the tag's own channel, which handed an rc build
  `…/get/codeaf/rc` while the notice beside it named the stable release — it would have
  reinstalled a channel that build's own `/update` never selects. `update.FollowedChannel`
  is now the single answer to "which channel is this build on" (dev and staging follow
  themselves, everything else follows stable), and the launch check, the surface and the
  terminal door all take the curl line from it. The two places that spelled the same rule
  out longhand to pick a default channel ask it too. Proven by
  `TestTheChannelABuildFollowsIsStableUnlessItIsDevOrStaging`,
  `TestAReleaseCandidateNoticeOffersTheStableRoad` and
  `TestAFailedReleaseCandidateUpdateOffersTheStableRoad`; all three were checked to fail
  against the old behaviour before the fix, and a real stamped `v0.3.0-rc.1` binary was
  driven by hand to confirm it.
- **`CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME` is registered as operator plumbing.** `CurlLine` spells the
  word into the road it offers a binary installed under another name, and the settings
  registry law counts every `CODEAF_*` word in the tree. It is the installer's pin and
  codeaf never reads it, so it lands on the allowlist rather than becoming a row a person
  could set and this binary could not act on.
- **The keys page answers "how do I exit codeaf" again.** Two new sections landed in one
  release — this branch's shell-update section and #1108's headless exit-code section on
  dev, both genuinely about exit CODES — and between them they pushed the page that
  answers the question out of the results. Neither branch is red alone; the pair is. The
  quitting section was written almost entirely in *quit*, *leave* and *close*, so it now
  opens with the sentence a person actually types and says *exit* where it said *leaves*.
  Fixing the page rather than the probe is the rule this corpus is held to.

## Verified against the real binary, by an independent lane

Head `1b9eb958d` was built six ways (stamped `dev-20260917-a0cc22169334` as `devaf` and as
`codeaf`, `dev-20260921-ffffffffffff`, `dev-20260918-9258f7052379`, `v0.2.1`, unstamped) and
driven under tmux against a local mirror of the real release list and one real dev asset,
never GitHub. Eleven ledger rows, all passing: the launch line for a behind dev build ends
with the devaf road and only the codeaf-named file gets `/get/codeaf/dev`; `/update` on a
devaf downloads, checks, installs at the devaf path and restarts the same transcript
(`/status` names the new build, `/proc/<pid>/exe` is the devaf file, sha matches the
asset); an ahead dev build gets no line and both doors refuse the implicit downgrade with
the quoted sentences, `--version` installs it; an equal build says it is newest; the
stable road is unchanged and writes `update-check.json` while dev writes
`update-check.dev.json`; a source build makes no request; the installer with `--name devaf
--dev` writes `devaf` beside an untouched `codeaf`, the variable form does the same, and the
three bad names exit 2 writing nothing; three alternating launches of a dev and a stable
build in one profile made two requests. Extras driven: a staging build follows staging, a
file named `winner` prints the `CODEAF_INSTALL_NAME=winner` form, `/update stable` on a
devaf takes the override and a failed download ends with the devaf line. The rc road was
driven at both heads: wrong at `1b9eb958d` (`/get/codeaf/rc` beside a notice naming
`v0.3.0`), right at `806be7745`.

The four manual gaps that drive surfaced — the third curl form and the chat's source-build
refusal unquoted, a wrong clause about cross-channel `--check`, and "how do I keep my dev
build up to date" ranking behind the dev-server page — are closed in `a6d98c596`, by heading

## What was true

The `touched packages` job, the required half of the `check` gate into `dev`, derived its test set as every directory holding a changed `.go` file and handed that list to `go test` without asking which module the directory belongs to. The Makefile's `test-touched` target carried a second copy of the same walk.

## What is true now

A directory under its own `go.mod` is another module, not a package of this one. Both derivations now walk up from each changed directory to the first `go.mod` and keep the directory only when that `go.mod` is the root's. `ci.yml` and `test-touched` print the same list again, so `make pr-ready` predicts the gate.

## Why now

#1108 adds bench fixtures under `bench/bashloop/fixtures/`, each a small program with a `go.mod` of its own so a worker can build and test it in place. At its head the job fed the seven fixture directories to `go test`, which answered `main module (github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf) does not contain package …` and failed the job as a setup error (Actions run 35557647066) while every real package passed, `internal/session` and `internal/tui3` included. The Makefile half of this fix is byte-identical to the one already on that branch; the workflow half is what was missing.

## Verified

- The patched `ci.yml` block, extracted verbatim and run against the #1108 diff with `BASE=9258f7052`: 43 directories to 36, the seven dropped are exactly `bench/bashloop/fixtures/*`, and the Makefile derivation prints the same 36.
- `make test-quick` rc 0 on this branch; `go test ./internal/ci/` ok; the YAML parses.
- `ci-full.yml` does not need it: it shards `go list ./...`, which lists root-module packages only.

body:
A task that ended `failed` with its work still held wore `your call` and counted
toward `needs you` for the rest of the session. Nothing was waiting on any of
those answers.

Closes #1328.

## The engine already says this, in two places the reading disagreed with

`internal/session/task_landing_question.go` raises a landing question for
`TaskUnverified` and retires it for every other state. A failed node therefore
has no question object and never had one: no turn is parked on it, and no
conversation is holding it.

`Agent.handToModelOnAuto` writes a decider only for `TaskUnverified`, and its
comment says why in terms that settle this one:

> AND IT IS ONLY EVER ABOUT THE ONE STATE THAT HAS A DECISION IN IT. A node that
> landed done, incomplete or stopped is not waiting on anybody's word, and
> writing an owner onto it would invent a question nobody is asking.

`taskLifecycleStatus` gave that same node `TaskPresenceNeedsLook`, which becomes
`Attention`, which is a demand. Two readers of one state, and the fix is to make
the reading agree with the law already written rather than to add a third
opinion.

THE ROW STOPS ASSERTING A WAITER THAT DOES NOT EXIST.

## What changed, and what deliberately did not

`taskStatusDemand` now takes the facts, and one predicate turns `Attention` off
for a failed held landing a person did not stop.

The card is untouched, and that is the point. The tier, the word, the reason and
both answers all stay: the branch is on disk, taking it anyway is a real thing
to do, and a person who goes looking at the row is owed the offer. What goes is
only `TaskStatus.Attention`, which is what files a row under `needs you`.

It is the same separation, for the same reason, that `internal/tui3`'s
`taskstatus.go` already makes for a question somebody else is holding: "The
tier, the word and the question are untouched: the row still wears the `?` and
still reads its reason, because a person watching it is owed both."

No new field, no owner written, no clock, no count, no graph walk, no disk read.

## It does not delete the demand

It moves it back to whoever has one. If something in a conversation ever does
need this answer to carry on, it ASKS, and an ask raises the mark through its
own lane in `Agent.waitingOnPerson` with no help from this row. A held landing
will not wear the mark as the engine stands, because nothing ever waits on one
today; wire a real park onto that answer and it marks again, through the ask
lane, with no further change here.

## Three candidate signals that were rejected, with the reason

The issue asks what "moved past it" should be measured against. None of the
three it names can answer it.

A LATER NODE THAT LANDED THE SAME BRANCH cannot happen. A branch is
`task/<slug>-<shortID>` and `shortID` is three bytes of `crypto/rand`, so no two
nodes ever share a branch name. A predicate on it could never be true and a test
for it could never fail.

A CONTINUATION LEAVES NO SECOND NODE. `task_continue.go` re-arms the node in
place: same id, same spec, same tree. A new proposal is explicitly a different
piece of work, with no recorded link. There is no supersession edge to read.

A BRANCH THAT NO LONGER EXISTS needs a disk probe on the road that draws every
card, which is exactly a claim the notice does not carry.

A static `dependsOn` edge was considered and rejected too: it says what COULD
wait, not what IS waiting, so it would still raise a mark at the moment of
failure for any task with a dependent.

## Acceptance

New file `internal/session/task_held_mark_test.go`.

On `e87b147c9` as it stands:

```
--- FAIL: TestAHeldLandingOffersTheAnswerAndDemandsNothing
    a held landing stands in `needs you` with nothing waiting on the answer
```

With the change, `ok`. The red is the base's: `task_status.go` was checked out
to the index to produce it and then restored, rather than the change being
mutated.

THE TEST HAS CONTROLS, because a test that only asserts nothing demands anything
would pass on a reading that stopped demanding everything.
`TestTheRowsSomethingIsWaitingOnStillDemand` pins three rows that still set
`Attention`, each with something genuinely on the other side of the answer: a
conflict, which is two versions of the person's own files and only they can say
which survives; a landing nobody could check; and work nothing is driving. A
third test pins that a person's own stop is OVER and grows no question, since
both settle `failed` and the new predicate must not be what keeps a stopped row
quiet.

The existing held-landing cases in `task_states_test.go` pin the card for
exactly these facts, tier `your call`, `accept anyway` and `not right`, owner
person. They still pass, which is the evidence the card survived rather than an
assertion that it did.

## Checks

Written against `e87b147c9`, and the red above was re-verified on that head
rather than carried over from the earlier base.

```
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/session	252.706s
ok  	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/tui3	331.603s
```

Both under the box's one heavy-suite lock, in one run, with `-count=1`.
`internal/tui3` is in it because that is where `Attention` is read, and a change
to the mark checked only in `internal/session` is checked in the wrong place.

`bash scripts/laws.sh` exits 0. `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` prints nothing.
title: session: a held landing offers its answer and stops demanding one

GitHub renders a co-author as a linked avatar only when the email resolves, and for accounts since mid-2017 that is the numeric id in front of the username. The old trailer used the bare-username noreply form, which is why the co-author line rendered as a dead mailto.

Before:

    Co-Authored-By: codeaf <agentfield-bot@users.noreply.github.com>

After, every commit carries two trailer lines:

    Assisted-by: CodeAF (claude-opus-4-8)
    Co-Authored-By: CodeAF <267109073+agentfield-bot@users.noreply.github.com>

- Co-Authored-By is the GitHub surface: the ID-prefixed address (267109073 is agentfield-bot's verified account id) links the co-author to the CodeAF account with its avatar.
- Assisted-by is the provenance surface: it names the model that wrote the commit, interpolated from the session's Config.Model at the belt render (internal/session/beltfacts.go), and is queryable with git interpret-trailers. It follows the convention Artsy's open RFC argues for, where Co-authored-by reads as a teammate and Assisted-by keeps the human owner.

The fixed arm's prefix waiver rises by the 162 bytes the wider belt fact costs; the lean shape never renders the attribution row. Manual pages and pin tests updated; task-commit author identity, PR/issue/comment footers, and the legacy addresses all stay exactly as they were.

One pre-existing failure noted, not caused by this change: TestLegacyRegisteredWorktreeResumesLandsAndCleansUp fails identically on bare origin/santos/dev (verified by running the single test on a detached checkout of the base commit). Everything else green: go build, go vet, and the internal/exec, internal/session and internal/manual suites.
