body:
The heavy-suite lock is two mechanisms that cannot see each other, so its
exclusivity is a claim the box does not honour (#1307). A checkout at or past
#1264 takes an flock on `/tmp/codeaf-suite-<uid>.lockfile`. A checkout behind it
takes the older directory lock at `/tmp/codeaf-suite-<uid>.lock`. Two heavy
suites run side by side and each believes it has the box to itself.

Dual-checking on the READ side closes one direction only. It stops us starting
beside a stale holder; it cannot stop a stale runner starting beside us, because
never having heard of the flock is precisely what makes it stale, and it will
never be taught to read one. Taking BOTH locks closes the other direction
without changing a single old checkout: a current tree becomes visible to every
stale reader still out there, and the remaining blindness runs in the safe
direction only.

## Three decisions, each of which could have gone the other way

**The directory is CLAIMED first and the refusal is REPORTED last.** The claim
comes first so there is no window in which a current tree holds the flock and is
still invisible to a stale runner. The refusal is deferred until the flock has
had its say because the two collisions are not equally well understood: two
CURRENT trees collide on the flock, and that refusal knows whether the recorded
pid is visible from this pid namespace and what to run when it is not. Reporting
the directory first replaced that diagnosis with a cruder one for the common
case in order to describe a rarer one. The first draft did exactly that and the
existing acceptance arms caught it.

**The directory is freed by whoever holds the flock, which is the HOLDER beside
the suite and not this wrapper.** The flock's lifetime is deliberately the
holder's, and killing the wrapper is explicitly permitted: it must not unlock a
box that is still running a suite. A directory lock released on the wrapper's
schedule would open the box to a stale reader while the flock was still held,
which is the two readers of one state disagreeing, again. The holder inherits
the environment, so it knows the lock by the same name and drops it when the
suite ends.

**The two paths are named independently in the configuration.** Deriving one by
trimming `file` off the other would make two names one fact, and a fact spelled
twice can disagree with itself. It would also follow a test harness driving a
private lock straight to the real one, silently. An empty setting means no
directory lock at all, which is what a platform that never had one wants.

## The test, and the arm that matters

`scripts/one-suite_test.sh` gains two functions and every existing arm is pinned
to a private directory lock, without which the suite would have taken the real
one on whatever box it ran on.

- `run_both_locks`. A held suite is visible to a reader of the DIRECTORY
  mechanism, which is the only road a stale checkout has; it is still visible to
  a reader of the FLOCK, unchanged; and RELEASE DROPS BOTH.
- `run_refused_by_directory`. A stale holder turns a current run away, which is
  the direction that has been costing unattributable reds. It also asserts that
  a refused run leaves the lock exactly where it found it, since it never held
  it.

The release assertion is the one that matters and the one that was awkward to
construct. A half release leaves the box locked to one of the two populations
forever, which is worse than the defect being fixed, because the defect at least
fails open.

### Both new arms were shown to fail, by mutation

Not asserted, run. Each mutation was applied, the arms run against it, and the
code restored:

| mutation | what the arm said |
| --- | --- |
| the holder no longer drops the directory lock | `the directory lock /tmp/.../both.lock.dir outlived the suite that took it` |
| `takeDirLock` reports success without creating anything | `a held suite did not take the directory lock /tmp/.../both.lock.dir` |

Unmutated, the same run prints `one-suite namespace and dual-lock acceptance: ok`.

## One defect found and fixed on the way

The first draft wrote the directory's `pid` file between the suite starting and
the flock being named. The existing arms read the lock file as soon as the suite
reports it is up, so that extra write widened a pre-existing window and they
began reading an empty lock. The pid file is now written after the flock is
named, and the arm that reads it waits for it rather than reading once and
calling an empty file a defect.

## Checks

`bash scripts/one-suite_test.sh` passes, five arms.
`go test ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` all ok.
`go vet ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock` clean, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` empty.
`GOOS=windows go build ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock` builds: that platform has no
holder, so the wrapper keeps the directory lock and frees it itself.

Written against `9b38c2dda`.

Refs #1307.
title: scripts: a heavy suite takes both locks so a stale tree can see it

body:
A landed task whose accept is already in flight kept asking the person to accept
it.

`waitingOnPerson`'s landing arm took `PendingDecisions()[0]` unconditionally and
named it. `PendingDecisions` filters on node state alone, and an accept does not
move the state until the merge finishes, so the entry stays on the list through
the whole settle. The record card already knew better: `question.go` reads the
decision record and says `accepted · still working on it`. Home did not, so the
two readers of one state disagreed, and the person was prodded for a question
they had answered.

## It is a selection, not a guard

The obvious fix is a guard: skip the entry if its answer is in. That is wrong in
a way that passes its own test.

`graph.order` is admission order and the arm took the FIRST entry. With two open
landings, one answered and one not, a guard on `pending[0]` goes quiet in the
all-answered case and still names the ANSWERED landing while the unanswered one
is the reason the row is up. The change takes the first entry that qualifies
instead, and contributes nothing when none do:

```go
for _, pending := range a.PendingDecisions() {
	if strings.TrimSpace(pending.Notice.Settling) != "" {
		continue
	}
	return personAsk{waiting: true, reason: yourCallLine + strings.TrimSpace(pending.Notice.Title)}
}
return personAsk{}
```

`PendingDecisions` itself is untouched. Its membership is state in, state out,
and other callers depend on that, so the skip belongs at the arm that draws the
line.

## The condition is non-empty, not equality

`resolutionInFlightLocked` (`task_run.go`) returns two different strings:
`n.settling`, which a settle claims in plain words such as `your accept`, and
the literal `a merge round` when only the `resolving` flag is set. A test for
the accept spelling would fix half of this, and the missed half is
indistinguishable on screen. Both mean the same thing to the person: the work
proceeds without them.

## The test that matters is the second one

`TestAnAcceptedLandingInFlightDoesNotSayYourCall` is the all-answered case, and
it is the test anybody writes first. A guard on `pending[0]` passes it.

`TestTheYourCallRowNamesTheLandingStillWaiting` is the one that separates the
two shapes. It puts a SECOND landing beside a settling one and asserts which of
them the row names. A fixture with one candidate cannot tell a correct selection
from a lucky one, and a two-candidate fixture that still checks the outcome
rather than the choice is a one-candidate fixture with extra scenery.

Its negative clause is live, which was checked rather than assumed: the settling
node's title really is `Add the guard`, from `unverifiedNode` at
`internal/session/task_resolve_test.go:38`. An assertion that something is
ABSENT passes forever unless the absent thing exists in the fixture.

## The test that should have caught this and did not

The card side of this pair is pinned five times in
`internal/session/questionlifecycle_test.go`, at `:254`, `:297`, `:328`, `:354`
and `:405`. The home side was pinned zero times. Five to nothing, and the two
readers drifted apart while every test stayed green.

## What is deliberately NOT here, and why

There is no three-state test, red on base and red with either half alone. The
brief this came from carried that as a requirement, on the premise that the fix
needed a new field on the Question plus a refresh of the question bank, because
the settled-and-settling fact was believed to be unavailable to any surface.

That premise is wrong, and reading settled it. `PendingDecisions` builds each
entry from `noticeLocked`, and `noticeLocked` sets `Settling` from
`resolutionInFlightLocked`, so the fact is in the arm's hand at the line that
was defective. Nothing needed plumbing. A fix that is not two parts cannot
produce a middle red, so the requirement stopped applying rather than being
skipped.

The bank findings were real and they belong to a DIFFERENT reader: the words
path, `landingQuestion` through `said` into the question bank, which is what
renders a question's own sentence. That is the front tab's problem and is not
touched here.

## Checks

Written against `3d3b7542b` and cherry-picked onto `32b4127bd`. Committed by the
author of the work with the author field corrected to the bot; the change note
is mine.

`gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` is empty. `go test ./internal/session` is running
now through `scripts/one-suite.sh`, under the box's heavy-suite lock, on this
head. Its result is posted to this thread when it reports, and nothing here
rests on it until then.

body:
## What

Closes #1300. Three parts, from the settings review:

**1. One fuzzy matcher for every quick search.** `internal/fuzzy` is a port of fzf's FuzzyMatchV2 with nucleo's documented corrections: a two-matrix optimal DP (query "foo" against "xf foo" finds the correct span, scored 88 where fzf's single-matrix approximation scores 64 on the wrong span), matrix width n-m+1, a pooled slab with no per-item heap churn on the keystroke hot path, an O(n) prefilter, saturating uint16 arithmetic, the camel retune at 5, multi-term AND so a space is part of the query, and per-term smart-case. Twelve surfaces use the one scorer: the settings sheet, the autonomy rows, connections, memory, folder search, the rewind sheet, the command palette, the model picker and the harness picker (lane terms, fold-narrowing and GroupOrder preserved; sort flipped to higher-better), plus the resume roster, the deliverables shelf and the subharness page. The space-key fix rides with it: while a search is live, space types into the query and flips nothing.

**2. Match highlighting.** `internal/fuzzy` now exposes matched positions through DP backtracking (optimal spans, pinned by test), and the settings sheet and model picker rows emphasize exactly the matched characters through the existing token system - no new colors, nothing dimmed, no background fills.

**3. The caret parks where you type.** A `caretRow` hook on the place interface. The audit found three surfaces parking the caret outside the box being typed into - the connections key entry parked it in the resting search box 12 rows below, its choice list left it in the resting box, and the tasks filter parked it in the foot's "type to filter this list" 17 rows up while the letters landed in the control row - plus the task record card blinking a bar at (0,0) on a boxless surface. All fixed through the one mechanism, seven contracts in `internal/tui3/caretpark_test.go`.

Scope decision from the review: chat message contents stay out of the pickers. Pickers are choosing surfaces; content search belongs where results render as snippets, which is the rewind sheet's per-conversation search this PR puts on the new matcher. Cross-conversation search, if wanted, is its own surface and issue.

## Verification

`go build ./...` and `go vet` green, and `go test -count=1` green on `internal/fuzzy`, `internal/registry`, `internal/manual` and the full `internal/tui3` suite on this branch. The manual pages that documented the old three-tier ladder were updated together with their corpus tests.

## Change entries

The three change entries in `docs/changes/unreleased/` (the matcher, the highlight, the caret park) carry this PR's number.

body:
The front tab and the tab beside it answered the same question differently about
the same conversation.

A held tab's mark comes from `behindWatch.signal`, whose cached fact is fed by
`keeper.go`'s `needsPerson`, which calls the engine's `Agent.NeedsPerson`. So a
held tab counts every lane the engine counts.

The front tab's mark comes from `frontSignal`, which re-spells the lane list on
the surface. Two lanes the engine counts were missing from it: standing answers,
and landed tasks saying `your call`. So a conversation could carry the mark
while held and LOSE IT when a person brought it forward, which is the opposite
of what the mark is for.

## Answered from the surface, as the file requires

`frontSignal` answering from the surface rather than the engine is deliberate
and documented: `Agent.NeedsPerson` takes the agent's mutex and allocates a map,
the strip is laid out every frame, and over a remote handle the far side would
be a call per tab per frame. That is unchanged here.

The new reading is `asksStandingOrLanding`, one allocation-free walk over
`a.questions`, the same slice and the same shape as `asksHarness` and
`consentOpen` already use. No lock, no disk, no engine call.

## The exclusion is kept

An automatic proposal carrying a deadline is a countdown, not a question, and
`frontSignal` already excluded it. The new predicate names the two kinds it
counts rather than treating every question as a signal, so the countdown stays
out on both sides, and its doc comment says why.

## The test

`TestTheSameConversationAgreesInFrontAndBehind` puts the SAME conversation in
front and behind and compares the two answers. It carries its control in the
same test: a deadline proposal must also agree, and agree at `tabIdle`, so the
test would fail if the fix had widened the predicate into counting countdowns.

## The test that should have caught this and did not

`tabsignal_test.go` pins `tabNeedsPerson` for held tabs and for front tabs
separately, and `hopsignal_test.go` asserts the hop card and the tab signal
agree. None of them puts one conversation on both sides and compares, which is
the only shape that fails for this defect. This adds that shape.

## Checks

`go test ./internal/tui3`, the whole package, run four times over the work at
330.5s, 332.7s, 334.3s and 335.3s, on the base the work was written against
(`3d3b7542b`), plus focused runs of the new test. This branch is that work
cherry-picked onto the current head, so the gate's run here is the one that
counts.

body:
Two lanes said a person was needed and said nothing about what for.

`personAskLanes` decides THAT a person is needed by OR-ing the lane books.
`waitingOnPerson` then takes the SENTENCE from `presenceAsk().Text`, which walks
the presence desk. Mark and sentence come from two different books, so a lane
counted in the OR that banks no desk row leaves `waiting: true, reason: ""`, and
a surface draws a mark nobody can act on.

Sign-in and the harness lane were both in that state. This routes them through
`presenceAskingWhole`, which is `raiseQuestion` plus the row, and returns one
closure that undoes both.

Three call sites, two conditions: `connect.go` for `connectAsks`, and
`harness.go` plus `harness_build.go`, which write the same `harnessAsks` book,
so the offer and the design card are one condition and one fix.

## What is deliberately NOT converted

Seven call sites raise through `raiseQuestion` and none of them banks a desk
row, so "banks a desk row" is the wrong criterion and would have converted all
seven. THE CRITERION IS WHETHER THE ROW ENDS UP WITH WORDS. One of the seven is
the door inside `presenceAskingWhole` itself and is not a lane. Of the remaining
six, three already get their words from another arm of `waitingOnPerson`: the
sub-harness offer, the fuel gate, and landings. Those three are untouched.

`task_landing_question.go` in particular is left alone: it drops its let-go
deliberately, because settle and answer own that question's retirement, and
banking a row there would leave nobody holding its remover.

## The failure is not always an empty sentence

When no lane has banked a row the reason is empty. When ANOTHER lane has one,
`presenceAsk()` returns that lane's words, so the row says a person is needed
and then describes a different question. Both cases are covered:
`TestWaitingSentenceConnectSignIn`, `TestWaitingSentenceHarnessAsk` and
`TestWaitingSentenceWrongOverlap`, the last being the wrong-sentence case rather
than the empty one.

## The test that should have caught this and did not

`TestNeedsPersonAgreesWithPresence` in `internal/session/attach_test.go` walks
the lanes and pins that `Agent.NeedsPerson()` agrees with the presence file's
boolean. It never asserts the reason is non-empty, so it passes for a lane that
says a person is needed and says nothing about what for. A test that compares
two booleans asserts that the two agree, never that either is right.

## Two comments, and who wrote them

The third commit is mine, not the change's author's. Both converted sites
carried a comment naming `question.go`'s `raiseQuestion` as the door, which
became false at those lines the moment they were converted. They now name
`presenceAskingWhole` and say what it adds. A doc comment that describes the
call above it incorrectly is worse than no comment, because the next reader
trusts it.

## Checks

The change was written against `3d3b7542b` and is cherry-picked here onto
`952e0036a`.

Stated plainly because it bears on how much this body is worth: THE CELL THAT
WROTE THIS DID NOT RUN THE DECLARED CHECK. Its report quotes
`go test ./internal/session -run TestPresenceAskReason` as passing, and no test
of that name exists in the package; a `-run` pattern matching nothing cannot
fail on behaviour. The whole-package check the work was briefed with was never
run. So the verification behind this branch is the diff, read line by line, plus
the gate on this head. Nothing here rests on the cell's own green.


## What would have objected

Naming it, because "the declared check was never run" says a hole existed and
not what closes it. The form that catches this is `run_tests` in `scripts/proof.sh`
on #1308, which runs the named tests and then checks that every name it asked
for actually RAN. Its own failing arm is in `internal/ci/prooflib_test.go`.

Against this branch it would have objected in the same second the step ran, and
it would have named the test that reported nothing. The point is not that
anything lied. `go test` reported its result faithfully: a filter matching
nothing is a run with nothing in it, and `ok` is the honest answer to that. What
the step could ever have caught was compilation and nothing else. A cell can
declare a check, run it, get a true green, and have proved that the package
builds.

Catching it the other way cost a diff read line by line, a name mismatch
noticed, and a grep to confirm.
title: session: a sign-in and a harness ask say what they are waiting for

body:
A watch that stopped because a call needed permission drew a row reading

```
asks: stopped: it needed your ok to run bash
```

Nobody asked anything. `standing.Item.NeedsPerson` carries two different things,
and its own doc says so: a QUESTION a firing put to a person in its own words,
or the line this build writes when a call was refused for want of somebody to
allow it. `switcherStandingNote` put the ask word over both.

The fix asks the one predicate that knows the difference,
`standing.IsPermissionLine`, and says the refusal bare, because it is already a
whole sentence about the item. The ask word stays for the other tenant.

This is the reading three siblings already take and this surface skipped:
`homepanel_needs.go` picks a different door word for a permission line,
`homestanding.go` picks a different destination, and
`standing.ClearNeedsPerson` will only clear the permission tenant. No second
list of spellings is added here; the spellings live in `standing`, in that one
predicate.

It also follows the precedent set a few lines above it in the same function:
`switcherConversationNote` already returns the consent gate's own sentence bare,
for the same reason and with a comment saying so.

## The test, and its failure on base

New: `TestAWatchStoppedForPermissionIsSaidNotAsked` in
`internal/tui3/switcher_test.go`, covering both tenants, so the word is proved
present for a question and absent for a refusal.

On base it fails with the defect in its own words:

```
switcher_test.go:124: the row puts the ask word over a line nobody asked:
got "asks: stopped: it needed your ok to run ..."
```

## The test that should have caught this and did not

There is none for this note in the permission state. The nearest test covers the
switcher's ranking and passes regardless of which tenant the line holds, because
it never reads the note's text in that state. Recorded here rather than left
implicit: this change adds the first assertion about what that row says when
nobody asked.

## Scope

One surface word. The mark, the glyph and the count are deliberately untouched:
whether a stopped-but-nothing-to-answer state should carry its own quieter mark,
and where its door goes, is a separate decision that has not been made. This
change does not prejudge it.

## Checks

`go test ./internal/tui3`, the whole package, ok in 340.670s, run on the base
the work was written against (`3d3b7542b`). This branch is that change
cherry-picked onto the current head (`952e0036a`), so the gate's run on this
head is the one that counts, and I am not quoting the earlier run as if it were
taken here.

body:
Three shapes of proof step were each written more than once in this repo's chains, and each is structurally incapable of reporting the failure it is checking for. They were found in one night, each by a different person, each in a different instrument. This is the one written form of all three, to be sourced.

| The shape | Why it cannot fail |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l ./internal; echo "exit=$?"` | `gofmt -l` prints the files it would reformat and **exits 0 either way**. The list is the signal; the exit code never was. |
| `cmd 2>&1 \| tail -25; echo "exit=$?"` | `$?` is `tail`'s status, and `tail` succeeds at reading a failure. This printed `exit=0` underneath a screen of `--- FAIL`. It does not hide a red, it **manufactures a green directly below the evidence**. |
| `go test -run 'TestA\|TestB\|...'` | A `-run` pattern is a second copy of the list of tests in a file. When they drift, `go test` answers a filter matching nothing with `ok`, because from its side nothing failed. **A named test that did not run is indistinguishable from one that passed.** |

`scripts/proof.sh` gives each one a written form: `fmt_check` reads the list; `step` captures its command's status before anything else can run, keeps output in a file rather than a pipe, and counts failures from that file as a second witness sourced differently from the status; `run_tests` compares the names asked for against the tests that reported, and names every one that reported nothing.

That last point is deliberate. A guard whose satisfaction can only be shown as a tick eventually becomes a tick, so the failure is loud and specific in the same line: both counts, and the names.

## The acceptance is the failing arm

`internal/ci/prooflib_test.go` runs each function **twice**: once where the thing it checks is sound, once where it is broken. Each broken arm also pins what the plain command says about the same situation, because that is the entire argument for the function existing.

| Test | What the plain command says | What the library says |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TestRunTestsCatchesANameThatReportedNothing` | `go test -run '^(TestAlpha\|TestGamma)$'` on a package holding only Alpha and Beta reports **ok, exit 0** | `asked=2  reported=1`, names `TestGamma`, exit 1 |
| `TestFmtCheckFailsOnAFileGofmtWouldRewrite` | `gofmt -l` lists the file and **exits 0** | prints the list, `gofmt=DIRTY`, exit 1 |
| `TestStepReportsTheCommandsOwnStatusAndNotAPipesStatus` | the pipeline reports **`exit=0`** for a command that exited 3 | `probe_exit=3`, `probe_FAIL_lines=1`, exit 3 |

A guard against invisible failure that has only ever been seen passing is the thing it was written to prevent, wearing its own name.

### Those three assertions are the library's expiry date, not belt and braces

Read them again as a set. Each one says *the hazard is still real*.

Most guards never find out when the thing they guard against gets fixed. The upstream tool changes, the hazard goes away, and the guard lives on as cargo that everybody routes around and nobody dares delete, because by every signal available no one can tell what it was for.

This one announces it. If `go test` ever stops reporting `ok` on a filter naming a test that does not exist, if `gofmt -l` ever starts exiting non-zero on a non-empty list, or if a pipeline ever starts carrying the failing command's status, the corresponding test goes red — and **that red means the library's reason for existing has gone**, not that the library is broken. The failure message in each says so in those terms: *this test is no longer about a silent pass*, *this test proves nothing*, *this test is about nothing*.

The same idea runs through the third mutation control. Putting `step`'s command back behind a pipe reproduces the original defect on demand, so the bug that motivated the library is now permanently a test of it.

## Proof

Fresh clone of `436933a6d` on the test box.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l` (the list) | empty |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet ./internal/ci/` | exit 0 |
| the five new tests, verbosely | 5 PASS, 0 FAIL, exit 0 |
| whole `./internal/ci/` | ok, exit 0, 0 FAIL lines |
| `scripts/laws.sh` | exit 0, 0 FAIL lines |

**Three mutation controls on the library itself**, each restored green afterwards. Breaking the library must make its own tests red, or the tests are decoration:

1. `run_tests`' count comparison removed → `TestRunTestsCatchesANameThatReportedNothing` red: *the library agreed with the plain command and reported success*.
2. `fmt_check` made to read the exit code instead of the list → red: *an unformatted tree was reported clean*.
3. `step`'s command put back behind a pipe → red: *step answered 0, not the command's own 3*. That is the original defect, reproduced on demand.

## Scope

**No caller is converted here, and there is none to convert.** A survey for these three shapes across `Makefile`, `scripts/` and `.github/` found zero instances: `make fmt-check` was already written in the correct form, no shipped chain reports a status after a pipe, and no `-run` pattern lists named tests that could drift from a file. Every instance was in an ad-hoc chain script written outside the repository.

That count covers those three shapes in those three directories and claims nothing about any other way a failure can be discarded, and nothing about Go source, which was not looked at. The scope is stated in the entry and in the file header for the same reason everything else here is written twice-proof: a finding whose boundary travels separately from it becomes a claim nobody tested. The survey and what the zero means are in the issue below.

**So these functions may have no caller, and that is not a reason to delete the file.** Its standing value is the test: three assertions about how the tooling behaves that our proof chains depend on, which run on every pull request whether or not a line of it is ever sourced.

Nothing a person using this program can see changes, so no manual page is owed. The test-shaped members of the same family, the review question, and the survey with its scope are in the issue titled "Tests that cannot fail" (#1306).

body:
Fourth cell of the settled close-window design (#1224), on the copy record (#1298). One door, `Agent.ContinueRun(ctx, row)`, that picks up a run nothing is driving.

It adopts the working copy the run recorded when it started and the store already on disk, and hands both to the same engine under the same seats. The supervisor releases claims whose owner is gone and re-reads the ready set on its own next pass, so there is no resume machinery and no second scheduler: carrying on is the ordinary pass, run by a process that was not there for the last one.

## It has no caller, on purpose

Continuing seats workers and spends money. A door that spends money and is reachable before anything means to reach it is not a smaller version of the feature, it is a worse thing than no door. Nothing calls this from any surface, and a person cannot carry a run on today. The card that offers the choice is the next change, and `internal/manual/chat/how-tasks-run.md` says so plainly as of #1304.

## The refusals, and who actually meets them

| In the way | What it says |
| --- | --- |
| a run that never stopped | `<run> is already running`, or `<run> is running, and a conversation drives one run at a time` |
| a number with no run behind it | `there is no run 41 in this conversation` |
| a run that said its last word | `<run> is done, so there is nothing to carry on` |
| a copy never written down | `this run's working copy was not written down when it started, so there is nothing to carry on from` |
| a copy gone from disk | `its working copy is gone from <dir> ... its branch <branch> is still there` |

**The fourth is not a guard against a hypothetical.** The record of a run's copy landed today, so every run already on disk carries none of it. That is the whole existing population, and the first interrupted run most people meet will be one of them. What it says is the permanent answer for those rows, not a message about a version skew that passes.

That refusal is the **same sentence** the row itself shows where the offer would otherwise be, taken from one constant (`errNoRunCopy`, read by `runCannotContinue`). A test compares the door's error text to the row's reason by equality, so a second spelling cannot be written without the build saying so.

## One spec, two roads

`beltRunSpec` is extracted from `startKnownTaskRun`. A continued run is the same run, so it works under the same seats and bounds; a spec built here would drift the day somebody moved a cap on one road.

## Proof

Fresh clone of `df81736f3` on the test box.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `gofmt -l` (the list, not the exit code) | empty |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `GOOS=windows go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet ./internal/session/` | exit 0 |
| the seven new tests | ok, exit 0 |
| #1296 and #1298's tests beside them | ok, exit 0 |
| `scripts/laws.sh` | exit 0, zero FAIL lines |
| `./internal/ci/` (the change entry) | ok, exit 0 |

**Three negative controls, each restored green afterwards:**

1. The door patched to reach for `prepareTaskTree`, the road that **makes** a copy, called exactly as the start road calls it. `TestCarryingOnARunKeepsEveryStepOfTheWorkInItsCopy` goes red naming the deleted file: `the work in the run's copy is gone: .../trees/7/the-work.txt: no such file or directory`. That is the control that matters. The test detects the destruction rather than merely passing.
2. The settled guard deleted. All three subtests go red: `a done run was carried on`, and the same for failed and unverified.
3. The run installed with a cut that ends nothing. `TestAStopReachesARunThatWasCarriedOn` goes red: `timed out waiting for the carried-on run to end`.

Every refusal test asserts twice: that it said no in the person's words, and that **nothing started**. A door that refuses in words and seats workers anyway has spent the money either way.

## Two laws caught this change and both are fixed in it

`scripts/laws.sh` went red on the first run and both reds were mine.

`TestEveryPublisherOfARunningRowIsOneAStopCanReach` named `ContinueRun` as publishing a running row the ledger gave no owner a stop could reach. That is the right demand: a run restarted by a door nothing can end is worse than a run nobody can start. `ContinueRun` is now in `stoppableRowPublishers` under `CancelTask`, and `TestAStopReachesARunThatWasCarriedOn` stops a carried-on run through the ordinary road and checks the workers' context was cut.

`TestNoRoadInTheTaskEngineHasMoreEndingsThanItsLedgerRow` put `taskStatusWords` at 16 decisions against a ceiling of 15, and there is no road to raising the ledger. The interrupted arm is now `taskAskContinuing`, a reader of its own beside `taskAskOf`, which is where it belonged: that one walks the facts of a landing to work out which judgement is owed, and there is no judgement here.

body:
#1296 landed the `interrupted` reading an hour ago and its page says the row "offers two answers: `continue it`, or `leave it`". Both words are real in the reading. Neither is drawn for a run. This removes the promise and states the limit in its place, rather than waiting for the change that makes the answers real to carry it.

## Why the answers are not drawn

There are exactly three readers of `TaskAsk.Yes` and `.No` in the tree, and a run row reaches none of them.

| Reader | Fed by | Why a run row cannot arrive |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `internal/tui3/homepanel_needs.go:424` | `session.TaskIndexEntry` | run rows never reach the task record; `recordTaskIndexEntry` is called only from `orchestrate.go`, and `TaskIndexEntry.StatusFacts` carries no copy |
| `internal/session/question.go:3086` `landingOptions` | `landingQuestion(PendingDecision)` | `PendingDecisions()` walks `graph.nodes` and admits only `state == TaskUnverified`; a run's rows live in the separate `g.runs` map and are never unverified |
| `internal/tui3/taskrecord.go:819` `taskRecordVerbs` | a `questionShown` | needs a question already on screen, and `app.taskRecordLanding` matches only the landing and the conflict |

## What is kept, because it is drawn

The word, the asking mark, and the column that waits for a person all come from `app.taskStatus`, which builds its facts from the surface's own node and so does read a run row. The line `nothing is driving it; everything it did is kept` is `TaskStatus.Reason` and is written by `taskNoteHead`. None of that changed.

In place of the two answers the page now says that nothing picks an interrupted run up yet, and that nothing ever will without being asked. Stating a limit is what somebody asking the manual usually wants.

The answers go back on this page in the change that makes them real, and not before.

## Proof

Fresh clone of `fbbe4d400` on the test box:

| Gate | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `./internal/manual/...` (every probe) | ok, exit 0 |
| `-run Manual ./internal/tui3/` | ok, exit 0 |
| `-run Manual ./internal/session/` | ok, exit 0 |
| `./internal/namelaw/` | ok, exit 0 |
| `./internal/ci/` (the change entry) | ok, exit 0 |

Docs only. No Go source is touched.

body:
**In one sentence:** a run's working copy is written down when the run starts, so carrying it on later adopts the work instead of deleting it.

Third cell of the settled close-window design, #1224, split out ahead of the card on the manager's ruling: the piece where getting it wrong deletes somebody's work gets its own proof and its own gate.

## The hazard this exists to prevent

A run works in a copy of its own. The road that makes that copy carves the directory it is handed and cuts a fresh branch with a random suffix. It is documented as safe to carve, and it is — **exactly once**, because the only thing that can be sitting at a run's path is that run's own wreckage.

Ask it for the same run's copy a second time, which is precisely what a naive "carry on where it left off" would do, and it deletes every step of the work it was meant to resume, cuts a new branch off a new random name, and hands back something that looks perfectly healthy. **Nobody would see it until it was their work.**

## The asymmetry that makes the record necessary

**The directory is derived and the branch is not.** A run's directory is a pure function of the conversation's folder and the run's own number, so any process can work it out again. Its branch carries a random suffix minted at the moment the copy is cut, and nothing wrote it anywhere.

That is the whole reason this record exists. A reader who believes both are reconstructible will delete this change in six months.

## What it does

A run's row now carries its copy: the directory, the branch, the repository it merges into, the ground and how the copy stands on it, the checkout it was cut from and that checkout's commit, and which rung of the ground ladder made the world. Those are the same facts a node of the session's own graph has always carried in its own record, under their own names.

The reader **adopts and never makes**. Nothing in it carves a directory, cuts a branch or derives a path. Every road out is either the copy that was written down or a refusal.

- **A run with no copy recorded is refused, in words naming what is missing.** Every run row on disk today predates this field, so that refusal is the first thing a person will meet. **It is the correct answer forever, not a stopgap.** Such a run's branch was minted at random and recorded nowhere, so no reading of the record, the conversation or the disk can recover it. Anything the reader could do instead is the destructive road wearing a helpful face.
- **A copy that is gone from disk is refused too, and the refusal names the branch,** because the branch is the one thing left that a person can act on.
- **The copy is carried forward in the one function every publisher of a run's row goes through.** **Every publish of a run's row replaces that row outright** — it is not a patch, and that is the fact which makes the carry necessary; it is not visible in the diff. Only the first publish knows where the work is, so any later one that had not thought about the copy would quietly drop the single fact nothing else can recover, and the row would still look complete. Putting the carry in each caller instead would make the record depend on four people remembering, and on the next publisher someone adds knowing to. A notice that names a copy of its own still wins, because it is the more recent reading.

## Not in this cell

Nothing calls the reader yet. This cell makes a continue possible and safe; the card and the key are the next one.

## Tests

Seven, and the first is the one that matters.

**The destruction, shown.** A copy is cut, work is written into it, and the copy is asked for a second time exactly as a resume would ask. The work is gone, and the second branch has a different name from the first while the directory is the same. That is not a bug this change introduces — it is the behaviour of the road a resume would otherwise reuse, pinned so nothing reaches for it again. It skips with an explanation rather than failing if that road ever stops clearing the directory, because then the reason for the record has changed and the test should be rewritten rather than deleted.

The rest: the record is taken from the tree the run is actually working in; it survives the round trip through the store, which is the only trip that matters; a run with no copy is refused; a copy that is gone is refused and names the branch; a copy that is there is adopted whole with the merge still open; and a later publish keeps what the first wrote down.

### Negative controls

One per independent claim.

**Stop the record travelling through the store:**

```
--- FAIL: TestTheCopySurvivesBeingWrittenDownAndReadBack
    the copy did not survive the record, so nothing could be carried on
```

**Stop a later publish carrying it forward:**

```
--- FAIL: TestALaterPublishKeepsTheCopyTheFirstOneWroteDown
    the second publish dropped the copy, so the run became one nobody can carry on
```

The tree was restored and the set reconfirmed green after each.

## Proof

**Re-taken after a rebase onto the current head.** Both negative controls were re-run on the rebased code rather than carried over, because a resolution that dropped half the carry-forward would pass an ordinary suite and fail exactly one of them.

On Spark, under `umask 022`, plain ssh, a detached tree of the exact sha. **Every row ran on head `33640353b`,** stacked on cell b's `ccbfbe692` over santos/dev `c975972c9`.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `GOOS=windows go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet` on session, tui3 | exit 0 |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal`, list tested for emptiness | no files |
| the seven new tests, named | 7 pass, 0 fail |
| negative control, the record stopped travelling through the store | the round-trip test fails, saying the copy did not survive |
| negative control, the carry-forward removed | the publish test fails, saying the second publish dropped the copy |
| `internal/manual`, `internal/namelaw` | ok |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `make changelog-check` | 66 entries, all well formed |
| **`internal/session`, whole suite** | **ok, 241.6s, exit 0** |

The tree was restored and the whole set reconfirmed green after each control. The one-minute load average ranged from about 1.7 to 6.2 across the run, so this is a green under contention rather than on a quiet machine; the range is given rather than a single number because a single number would suggest an idle box.

body:
**In one sentence:** work that was live when the process holding it went away comes back saying `interrupted` — nothing is driving it, everything it did is kept — instead of being stamped failed and stopped.

Second cell of the settled close-window design, #1224. Stacked on #1291.

## What a person saw

A run was mid-flight when codeaf closed. The next morning the conversation reopened and the run's rows were on the column again, stamped **failed** and **stopped**, with the run's own row reading:

```
it ended when codeaf closed; its journal is kept
```

Two untrue things in one line. **Failed** says something went wrong with the work; nothing went wrong, nothing was even found out. **Stopped** says a person ended it; nobody did anything. And `it ended` says the work is over, when every step it took is sitting in its store.

## The word

`interrupted` is the owner's own, settled on 2026-09-20. It means **nothing is driving this, and everything it did is kept**.

It is deliberately neither of the two words it used to be read as. `stopped` stays a person ending the work. `incomplete` stays work that ran and came up short. A closed window, a sleeping machine and an engine that went away are none of those, and collapsing them into either is how work whose only misfortune was a closed window came back looking as though it had gone wrong.

It is also the only landing word that does not mean the work is over.

## Where the word lives

On the reading, which is the one place this program spells a person's words. One rung on the state ladder and one on the presence ladder, and the tier, the mark, the two answers and the sentence beside the word all follow from them. **No surface grew a table of its own.** The only line touched outside that reading is home's mark, so an interrupted row wears the asking mark the rows beside it wear.

- **It sits in the person's tier.** It will not move until somebody answers, which is what that tier means.
- **The two answers are `continue it` and `leave it`,** spelled here so the card in cell c draws words it did not invent.
- **The answer is never the model's,** whatever a settle policy says, because continuing spends money. That is the owner's second answer applied where it bites.
- **Interrupted is settled in the scheduler's sense and not the person's.** No worker holds it and its slot is back, which keeps a restored row off the live work tree; the work itself is still waiting to be picked up.

## A background job is untouched

A job is a process codeaf forked, and a forked process cannot outlive the program that forked it. There is nothing to continue, so `stopped` stays the honest word and the row keeps the path to its log.

## The seam between this cell and the last

**Between #1291 landing and this one landing there is a real window, and it is not an oversight.** #1291 makes a conversation that genuinely ends cut its run. Until this cell lands, reopening still stamps that run failed. So for that interval the product cuts work and then misreports why. The money bleed is what #1291 stops and it is the worse of the two; this cell closes the other half.

## The manual, both directions

- The new word reaches the page that lists the words a task can land with.
- **The page that told a person their run ended when codeaf closed now says what is true.** That page quoted the old sentence verbatim, and a page naming a word while denying the thing around it satisfies every gate and still lies.
- `interrupted` has its own heading, in the words somebody would actually type: what it means, whether they lost their work, whether they can carry on.

**That heading exists because the corpus caught me.** Folding the word into the section that lists the landing words cost another question its page: `why does my task say not done under it` stopped reaching its page and landed on a different one. The section was still well inside the length rule, so this was **dilution rather than size** — a paragraph about a new word spread that section's weight over more ground and it fell behind a competing page. The fix is the page and never the probe.

## Tests

Six new, and two existing ones rewritten rather than deleted. Both of those pinned the old sentence, which is exactly the behaviour this cell changes, so they now assert the new truth.

- The word, and that a closed window is not drawn as a fault.
- The tier, the attention, the ask kind, both answers, the reason, and that the decision is the person's.
- That it is none of stopped, incomplete or done.
- That it holds no slot and is still not over.
- That a row live when the process went away comes back interrupted, unstopped, and invents no sentence about how it ended.
- That a row which had already settled is unchanged by being read back.

### Negative controls

Run twice, once per independent claim.

**Remove the store arm** and three fail, each naming the defect:

```
--- FAIL: TestAResumedConversationRedrawsAMidFlightRunInterrupted
    row 1 came back failed, want it interrupted — nothing is driving it and nothing went wrong
--- FAIL: TestARowThatWasLiveWhenTheProcessWentAwayComesBackInterrupted
    a running row came back failed
--- FAIL: TestAJobStillMovingComesBackStoppedAndKeepsItsLog
    a run's row came back as failed (stopped true), want it interrupted and nobody's stop
```

**Remove the reading arm** and two fail:

```
--- FAIL: TestWorkNothingIsDrivingSaysSoInTheOneWord
    it reads as ""
--- FAIL: TestInterruptedWorkIsThePersonsCallAndSaysWhatTheAnswersAre
    it sits in the "" tier, where nobody would be asked
```

The tree was restored and the whole set reconfirmed green after each.

## Proof

**Re-taken after a rebase, and again after a formatting fix.** This branch was first proven at `68d67632d`, before #1291, #1290 and #1293 landed. Nothing from that run is carried over.

**One row of the earlier proof was not a proof at all.** `gofmt -l` lists unformatted files and exits 0 whichever way, so a step that read its exit code reported green on any tree. An unformatted const block in this change reached a gate because of it. The block is now formatted by the tool rather than by hand, and the check captures the list and fails on non-empty, never consulting the exit code.

body:
A sub-harness run that asks a question blocks inside subharnessEnv.Ask until somebody answers it, and the session went on telling every other window it was working. The question was registered in a.subharnessAsks and readable through OpenQuestions the whole time, but waitingOnPerson never read that lane, so presence never went to waiting, no row appeared on home, no mark was drawn, and the work stopped in silence until somebody happened to open the conversation. The lane's own comment already claimed the row said so.

Two halves, and neither is a fix on its own:

- taskpresence.go: the predicate reads `len(a.subharnessAsks)` alongside the lanes beside it.
- subharness_env.go: the lane raises through `presenceAskingWhole` rather than `raiseQuestion`, so its row is banked at the presence desk and comes down with the question. This matters because the sentence a person reads is taken off the desk (`presenceAsk`), so counting the lane alone would turn the session amber with nothing under it.

ONE TEST, THREE STATES, which is how both halves are shown to be load-bearing rather than asserted. On base it fails with "a session stopped on a sub-harness question says it is working: {waiting:false reason:}". With the predicate alone and no desk row it fails with "the row says a person is needed but not what for". With both it passes at -count=5. It drives the real seam, agent.subharnessEnv and env.Ask on a live agent with consent on, so it would catch this defect in whatever form it came back rather than proving that a predicate reads a map.

THE ROAD WAS SPLIT BECAUSE THE LAW SAID SO. Counting one more lane put waitingOnPerson at sixteen endings against a ceiling of fifteen (complexity_test.go's ratchet), and that ledger only shrinks, so the function is now two jobs along the seam its own comments had already drawn: personAskLanes reads every lane under the agent's lock, waitingOnPerson decides which answer a person reads first. The lock discipline is unchanged and a.mu is still released before PendingDecisions. The road's doc said "It is one function because it is one question", which the split would have made false, so it now says there is one answer given in two steps.

SIBLING LANES ARE DELIBERATELY LEFT. Sign-in, the sub-harness offer and the harness design card raise the same way without banking a desk row, so each already draws a mark with an empty sentence under it. They belong to the desk piece, which needs the owner's word on the state words first, and a change that quietly repaired three lanes while claiming to repair one would be a change nobody could review. A landed task that says `your call` on a page that cannot take the call is the same disease on another lane, also untouched.

The whole-package run whose only failure was TestARecallThatLandsBeforeTheFirstWordIsAskedAgainWithIt, a separately tracked item that fails only under a loaded box and passes alone at -count=10, is being replaced by a clean run on a quiet lock; that head will be posted here.

body:
**In one sentence:** a live run counts as work, so the engine stops retiring the conversation out from under it, and closing that conversation now ends the run instead of leaving it spending against a room nobody can read.

First cell of the settled close-window design, #1224.

## Two halves of one fact

### A run is work

The work tree is the one door every surface and the engine read to ask what is happening. A run's rows are kept beside the task graph rather than in it, so the walk over the graph's own nodes never saw them. A conversation driving a run and nothing else answered that it was working on nothing.

That answer is not cosmetic. The engine asks this same door what idle means before it retires a conversation at thirty minutes. So a run longer than half an hour had its room taken down while its workers were still out.

The run now joins the tree, under the number every other surface already knows it by, so a reader can hand the id straight to the stop road without knowing a run from a task. **Nothing else had to change to keep the engine alive while a run lives**, because the retirement and the host's own quiet both hang off that one reading.

### A run's life is the conversation's

The run drops the proposing turn's cancellation on purpose: it has to outlive the sentence that asked for it. Nothing else could reach it. So its life belonged to neither the turn nor the room but to the process, and a conversation that ended while a run was going left workers spending against a conversation nobody could read or stop.

Closing a conversation now cuts it, in the same place and for the same stated reason as the adaptive runs it already cut. **It writes nothing on the run's own record**: a person's stop puts their reason on the store's root and settles the row in their words, and the room closing is not that. What the run did is in its store, which is where the next launch reads it from.

## Not in this cell

Reading that store back is cell b. This cell does not change what a person sees on reopen, and an unsettled run still reads as stopped there.

## Tests

Five, and a negative control was run on all of them.

- A conversation driving a run is working, with the run's state, title, birth time off the conversation's own clock, and the id every other surface knows it by.
- A conversation driving a run is not idle, which is the reading that keeps the room open.
- A run a person stopped is still work until it settles, and leaves the tree when it leaves the conversation.
- Closing the conversation ends the run.
- Closing the conversation writes no stop on the run's record.

**The negative control.** With the two lines of the fix removed in place, four of the five fail and each names the defect rather than a shape:

```
--- FAIL: TestAConversationDrivingARunIsWorking
    a conversation driving a run says it is working on 0 things, want the run
--- FAIL: TestAConversationDrivingARunIsNotIdle
    a conversation whose only live work is a run reads idle, which is what retires it mid-run
--- FAIL: TestARunAPersonStoppedIsStillWorkUntilItSettles
    a run that is stopping stopped counting as work before its workers were home
--- FAIL: TestClosingTheConversationEndsTheRun
    the conversation closed and the run was left running against a room nobody can read
```

The fifth passes either way by design. It guards the fix against going too far, so it has nothing to say about the defect.

## Proof

On Spark, under `umask 022`, plain ssh, a detached tree of the exact sha. Exit codes read directly. **Every row ran on head `6638d40f2`.** The branch head is `c437c6f36`, which is that commit plus one that corrects the change entry to this pull request's own number. body:
A standing watch fires with nobody there, and until this it was refused its own work. standingRunConfig copied the parent conversation's config, set AskConsent false and InTask true, and never set an approval policy, so a firing carried the conversation's prompt-a-human default while also being told it was inside a task where no person exists. consent.go answers that combination with an in-task refusal: the decision needed a person and there is none. What survived was the read-only lift, which covers git status and nothing else, so a watch could not run one shell command, not even one the person had explicitly allowed. The owner's own watch fired 39 times between 2026-09-16 and today, spent $3.31, and did nothing.

What changes, and it is one line: a firing carries the policy a task node carries, `&approval.Policy{Default: approval.ActionAllow}`, the same value task_run.go sets beside the same AskConsent false and InTask true.

It is not wider than a node. approval's critical table still turns an allow into a prompt for the handful of shapes that destroy a disk or drop the machine, and a prompt with nobody to ask is still a refusal the firing can read and report. The calls that act in the person's name outside this machine stay refused. A bash call whose arguments cannot be read stays refused. No path rule was invented.

THE DECISION IS THE OWNER'S. Santosh chose this shape in his own words on 2026-09-20, "lets go with allow same as task node", after both shapes were put to him with the trade-off. This note is here because the change widens what an unattended firing may do, and a change of that kind should carry who decided it and when.

The test asserts the CALL RUNS rather than reading the policy field: a field assertion would go green the day someone sets the field and breaks the behaviour another way. Failing-first on base it reports "the call never ran: a firing behind its own gate still could not run one command", and it passes with the change. It deliberately pins no refusal wording, so #1288's sentence work is free to change without touching it.

HOW THE GREEN WAS GOT, INCLUDING THE RED. The first whole internal/session run on this branch came back FAIL, and not in code: its tests printed PASS and the package then failed the suite's own repository-churn guard, which saw the checkout's head move from 481ceb8ae to 2dee07970 while it was running. It moved because I amended mid-run. A grep over the added lines found an em dash in a comment where I had quoted the engine's in-task refusal verbatim, and this repository's prose carries no em dashes, quotation included; the comment now says what that line says without reproducing it character for character. The amend changed exactly four comment lines in standing_consent_test.go and no code, tree d5e082dd9 to daabb2f04. The guard fired correctly and the fault was mine, so the run of record is the rerun below, taken on a quiescent tree with nothing touching the checkout.

Verification on Spark: go build ./...; whole internal/session through scripts/one-suite.sh; the standing, consent and needs-line tests focused; go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ./internal/approval; gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal empty; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check.

body:
**In one sentence:** the page a person opens for one task of a run draws that task's brief through the reader the conversation's transcript already uses, so it opens on the work rather than on the scaffold addressed to a worker.

## What a person saw

A run task's page has a `brief` block, folded to three lines. When the task's stored brief was the generated work order a run hands its workers, those three lines were:

```
WHAT THE PERSON ASKED FOR, IN THEIR OWN WORDS
This is the message this work came out of. Treat it as the ask...
```

Two of the three folded lines were machinery, and the third was the rule under the heading. The person's actual ask began below the fold. The page opened on a document addressed to a model.

## What was already there

The surface already owns a reader for exactly this text. The conversation's own transcript draws the same generated work order through it: it recognises the generated opening, relabels the shouted section headings into plain ones, and puts this task's own work first so a child does not open on its parent's whole project.

The transcript had it. The plan page did not, and drew the stored text raw.

## The change

The reader's shared half is lifted out to work over a plain string, and the plan page's brief section calls it. Both surfaces now give one text one reading.

- **A brief that is not the generated document is untouched.** The recognition gate comes first, so a brief a person typed themselves, or wrote by hand, wraps exactly as it always did.
- **The stored text never changes.** Only what is drawn does. The model's input, the payload used for identity and refresh, and the transcript's own caller are all as they were.

### And the fold counts what it draws

`ctrl+o` opens and closes the brief, and it decides whether there is anything to open by counting lines. It was counting the raw wrap while the block drew the reshaped one, so the key and the block could disagree about how much there was. They now count the same function. **This was not in the brief.** It was found while the work was being done, by reading the one other caller of the line counter.

## Tests

- A stored brief that is the generated work order draws with the scaffold heading gone and the task's own work in the first folded line.
- A brief that is not that document draws byte for byte as before.
- The transcript's own drawing of the same text is unchanged.
- The fold key and the block agree on the line count for both shapes of brief.

## How this was written

This change was written by `codeaf do` driving itself, on Spark, from a short brief naming the defect and pointing at the two files. The run planned, edited, tested and committed on its own. What is measured below is the run that produced the commit, read from the usage ledger rather than from the run's own account of itself.

| | |
| --- | --- |
| ending | done, exit 0 |
| wall clock | 8 minutes 52 seconds |
| cost | $0.97 |
| model calls | 73 |
| tokens in | 3,361,876 |
| tokens out | 36,529 |

Two seats: 68 calls on the work seat and 5 on the planning seat. Input dominates output by about ninety to one, which is the shape of a worker that reads a large tree and writes a small patch.

The commit is the run's own, with its own authorship kept. Two commits follow it: the change entry's number, which the run guessed before a pull request existed, and nothing else.

## Proof

On Spark, under `umask 022`, plain ssh, a detached tree of the exact sha. Exit codes read directly. **Every row ran on head `05410eb66`.**

| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |

## What this does not fix

The task page has other regressions and this is not them. The `folder` section was deleted while the manual still promises it, the page carries a fixed block of dead vertical space already logged at high severity, and the harness page has no captions where the room page has them. They are separate and they are still open.

body:
**In one sentence:** a watch that stopped because it needed permission now says what it wanted to run, opens the watch instead of an idle conversation, and can be put down by changing the watch.

## What a person saw

The home screen's `needs you` list carried a row for a watch, marked as needing somebody, whose second line read:

```
refused in a task: default — nobody to ask
```

Four pieces of machinery in the one line that is supposed to tell a person what to do. `enter` on it opened the conversation the watch had been asked for in. That conversation was idle and held nothing to answer. There was nowhere on the screen to act, and the row could not be put down, because only the watch's next firing rewrites that line and this watch had spent its allowance for the day.

## What is true underneath

A firing runs with nobody to ask. A call the person's own approval rules would have put to somebody is therefore refused where it stands, and the worker is told so in the engine's own words, which is right: the worker has to act on them. Those words were then handed straight to the surface.

**This change does not widen what a firing may run.** That is a separate decision and it is open.

## The three halves

- **The line is the person's, and the engine's is still the engine's.** The reader that recognises a refusal now answers with `stopped: it needed your ok to run ` and what the call actually wanted: the command for a shell call, the name of the hand for anything else, `something` when the arguments cannot be read. `needs your ok to run` is the sentence this surface already says when a conversation waits for permission, so the two rows read as one sentence in two tenses rather than two accounts of one fact. The command is read through the same table every other reader of a call uses, so this line and the row the same call would have drawn in a conversation name the same thing.

  **It never says how much was refused.** It is written from the first refused call and knows nothing about the calls that came back fine before it, so it cannot claim that nothing was allowed.

- **The door is the item.** A standing row whose line is about a permission now says `enter on standing`. The thing that stopped is the watch; the conversation holds no question. The watch is where it can be paused, reworded or let go. A row whose line is a QUESTION the firing asked keeps the door it had, because the question was asked in a conversation and that is where it reads.

- **The person can put it down.** Changing the watch clears the line, alongside the next firing which already did. A question is never cleared this way. Opening the item and closing it again does not clear anything either, because nothing moved and the reason is still true.

## One predicate, and what it reads

The line is recognised in one place, asked by the store when a person changes an item, by the surface when it picks a row's door, and by the engine's own reader, so a line cannot be a permission in one place and a question in another.

**It matches what a line says, not how it says it.** Three doors in this build refuse a call that needed a person and had none, and they do not share a sentence:

| Door | What it writes |
| --- | --- |
| the turn inside a task | `refused in a task: <rule> — nobody to ask` |
| the turn with no resolver | `needs approval but no resolver is attached: <rule>` |
| the door that runs this program underneath another one | `<tool>" needs somebody to say yes (<rule>) and nobody is here to ask, so it was refused` |

Holding those as three literals is how the third one came to be unrecognised in the first place, so a shape is a set of parts a line must all carry. The absence of a person is not enough on its own: a QUESTION is model prose and can say "there is nobody on call, who do you want me to ask", so the shape also requires that something was **refused**. Both doors that state the absence say so.

**It knows the old spelling as well as the new one.** Every item stuck on disk today carries the engine's own refusal verbatim, and a watch that has spent its allowance for the day cannot fire again to have it rewritten. A predicate that knew only the new lead would have left every row that provoked this change exactly as it found it.

## Tests

- The line names a synthetic command, carries none of the four machinery words, and claims nothing about calls it did not see.
- A hand that is not a shell call names the hand. Arguments that will not read leave the line saying `something`.
- An ordinary tool failure still raises no line for the person.
- The engine's own refusal is unchanged by the reader that matches on it.
- All three doors' sentences are read as permission stops, and two questions carrying the absence of a person but no refusal are not.
- Changing an item clears the line and moves nothing else about the item; a question the firing asked survives the change; an item needing nobody is untouched.
- A row in the old spelling takes the item's door, and a row carrying a question still opens its conversation.

## Proof

On Spark, under `umask 022`, plain ssh, a detached tree of the exact sha. Exit codes read directly. **Every row below ran on head `078216012`, on santos/dev `cb3f0f356`.**

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `go vet` on session, standing, tui3 | exit 0 |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` | empty |
| `internal/standing`, whole | ok |
| `internal/session`, the standing and refusal tests | ok |
| `internal/tui3`, the needs, standing and home tests | ok |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `internal/manual`, `make changelog-check` | ok, exit 0 |
| **`internal/session`, whole suite** | **ok, 249.5s, exit 0** |
| **`internal/tui3`, whole suite** | **ok, 326.2s, exit 0** |

Both whole suites went through `scripts/one-suite.sh`. Finished 2026-09-20T15:49Z.

### Two reds on the way here, both real

An earlier head was red on `internal/tui3` on one test, and it was this change's own new one: it read the drawn frame for a word that only draws under the cursor. The test was wrong and the code was not; it now reads the row's own cell, which is the claim it makes.

A later head was red on `internal/standing`, and that one was a defect. The predicate held two literals and this build has three doors, so the third door's sentence read as an ordinary tool failure. Matching on what a line says rather than how it says it is the fix above.

body:
FlushUsage waits under a ceiling and returns the same way whether every row reached the disk or the deadline fired first, so the caller cannot tell a join from a timeout. That is how an eighth test joined the late-home-write class tonight: internal/session TestRecordingUsageNeverWaitsOnTheDisk failed with `TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat .../001: directory not empty`, and the leftover named itself, a regular usage.jsonl of 7446 bytes where the test had made a fifo. The test read a flush that had run out of time as a flush that was finished, returned, and its temp home was removed while rows were still queued; the writer's next append recreated the directory (openUsageLedger does MkdirAll, then opens with O_CREATE|O_APPEND) and wrote a regular file into it.

What changes:

- FlushUsage returns true when everything in front of it reached the disk and false when the ceiling fired. The wait itself is unchanged and deliberate: a stalled ledger must not hold a terminal open.
- StopUsageWriter(path) ends one path's writer and waits for it, the single-path form of the close the process already performs (#1259's CloseUsage), sharing its rule that the queue is closed under the writers lock so a concurrent RecordUsage can never send on a closing queue.
- usageFlushLimit becomes a var so a test can shrink the deadline in one line rather than putting load on the box to provoke it.
- The shipped test defers the stop and fails if the flush reports a deadline rather than a drain.

WHAT THE JOIN IS WORTH, PLAINLY. StopUsageWriter is bounded by usageFlushLimit, the same ceiling FlushUsage and CloseUsage accept, and it answers whether the writer really finished. Where it returns true, no row can land afterwards, which is the shipped test's case because its pipe is fully drained before the stop. Where it returns false the writer is parked inside its open or its write, and detaching closes the queue while run() ranges that queue to completion, so the rows ALREADY queued still land when it unblocks. Stopping prevents new rows and tells the truth; it does not cancel a backlog. Closing that gap would mean a writer that drops a backlog it can no longer write, which is a separate decision about a person's ledger and not this change.

So this rests on the reading above plus two seam tests, not on watching the original red turn green: a parked writer's flush reports false rather than claiming a drain, and a stopped path leaves the registry so no later row can queue for a home that is going away.

body:
The locked descriptor was handed to the heavy suite itself. An advisory lock lives on the open file description, and an inherited descriptor is not close-on-exec, so every process the suite left behind kept the whole box locked. That is not hypothetical: on 2026-09-19 an orphaned test shell, with its working directory already deleted, held this lock for eight minutes after a green run, and the next gate waited on a process that was running no suite at all.

What changes:

- The suite is started with no lock descriptor. The locked descriptor goes to a holder started beside it, in its own session, which execs nothing and so can pass the lock to nobody. The holder watches the suite's pid and exits when it is gone. Watching a pid is honest here in a way reading one from a file is not: the holder was started beside the suite, by the wrapper that started it, in the same pid namespace. The recorded start time from the kernel guards the one remaining misreading, a pid reused after the suite exits.
- The wrapper drops its own copy once the holder has it, so the lock is the suite's rather than the wrapper's: a wrapper killed mid-run still does not unlock a box that is running a suite, which is what #1270 set out to fix and this keeps.
- The lock file now records the suite's pid, when it started, and the holder's pid.
- After the suite ends, the wrapper checks the lock and, if it is still held after two seconds, says so and names `lsof`. It ends nothing: the one thing worse than a locked box is a process killed by someone who has not identified it.

If the holder itself is killed, the lock frees while the suite may still be running. That is the failure this chooses, and it is worth stating plainly. The holder waits and does nothing else, so it dies only to a deliberate kill, an out-of-memory sweep, or the box going down; it lives in its own session, so a signal aimed at the suite or at the wrapper misses it; the lock file names both pids, so a free lock under a running suite can still be read back to whoever dropped it; and a lock that nothing can release stops the box, where a lock freed early costs one concurrent suite and a red nobody caused. The kernel makes the same trade when a lock holder dies.

Two shipped tests changed, and both are consequences rather than tidying:

- `TestRefusalNamesADeadHolderWhenAGrandchildKeepsTheLock` described a situation that can no longer arise, since a grandchild never receives the lock. It is now `TestRefusalNamesAPidItCannotSeeWithoutCallingItGone`, which proves the same refusal wording on the case that wording is really for, a holder in another pid namespace, and asserts the output never calls a holder it cannot see gone.
- The release is asynchronous now, within the holder's 50ms poll, so the killed-wrapper regression waits a bounded two seconds for the lock instead of asking once.

Failing-first: the new `TestTheLockIsFreeWhenTheSuiteEndsThoughItLeftAProcessBehind` fails on base with the incident in miniature, the contender refused by a suite that has already exited, and passes with the holder.

Verification on Spark, tree 7a4691643 unchanged before and after: `go test ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock` at `-count=10` ok; `make build-cross` green on all six targets; `bash scripts/one-suite_test.sh` ok, including both namespace orders and the host-B case, with the script taught to read the lock file's fields rather than split the line in two; `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` empty; `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check` ok; `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` ok.

body:
**In one sentence:** a command cancelled in the same instant it started could keep running after its call answered `Command aborted`; the call now ends it itself.

## What was wrong

A foreground bash call waits on three things: the command's exit, the cancellation, and a handover to a background job. The cancellation arm returned at once and its comment said a second goroutine, the cancel watcher, had already sent the kill by then. Nothing ordered that. Returning closes the watcher's own stop channel, and a watcher that had not reached its wait yet then finds two reasons to wake, is handed one at random, and on the wrong one sends nothing.

The window is a cancel that coincides with a start: a run whose dollar limit is reached by the very call that issued the command, a time limit that fires as a command begins, a context already done. The command is started as the leader of a session of its own, so it lived on under no parent, in a folder that was then removed.

Seen once on the real binary: a hosted run ended `incomplete` on its dollar limit, and its command's shell was still running three minutes later under no parent. It ended by itself; nothing was signalled.

## The law

**THE ARM THAT ENDS THE WAIT ENDS THE COMMAND.** The cancellation arm sends the group kill itself. Two exceptions, both stated beside it:

- A call that was handed on as a background job is not killed and answers with its handover, whichever of two ready cases the wait was given.
- A process already reaped is not signalled, because its pid is free to be somebody else's.

The watcher stays for the stretch before the wait is reached. A second kill to a group that is gone changes nothing.

## Tests

Both find the command's own process through the promoter's door and assert the process is gone, not only that the call came back.

- `TestACommandStartedUnderAContextAlreadyDoneIsEnded`: 200 rounds. **Red at round 1 without the fix**, with the command still running; green 600 rounds with it.
- `TestACommandCancelledWhileItRunsIsEnded`: the ordinary stop, mid-command.

## What this does not claim

Shells that tests of a time limit left looping on a shared box have the same shape. They were not reproduced: 100 quiet runs of that test at trunk left nothing, and eight hosted dollar-limit drives, four on trunk and four on this change, left nothing either. The change entry says the same.

An engine ended by a signal in the middle of a command leaves that command running too. That is a separate fact and a product decision, not part of this change.

A run's dollar limit was the conversation's spend limit, whole, however much the conversation had already spent. A conversation that had spent four of its five dollars could start a run allowed five more. `--max-cost` did not bound a run at all, and the manual said so.

**In one sentence:** what a task spends now counts toward the conversation's own total while it is still spending it, so your spend limit, `--max-cost`, `/cost` and the status line no longer leave task runs out.

## What was wrong

A task run under the bash belt spent money the conversation never counted. Its workers are agents of their own. Each banked its paid calls on its own account and wrote them to the usage ledger on disk, and the road that drives a run to its landing added nothing home, on any ending. A conversation with a five dollar limit could start any number of five dollar runs, one after another. The two older roads, a task node and an adaptive run, always folded theirs.

Found while reviewing the dollar-remainder cell, which had taken the saved recipe's spend test for this road.

## The law

**A RUN IS THE PERSON'S MONEY AND IT REACHES THE CONVERSATION'S OWN TOTAL, EXACTLY ONCE, WHATEVER WAY THE RUN ENDED.** What the conversation counts as spent never goes down, and a limit on the conversation counts what a run still working has spent so far.

- The run hands its owner its reconciled cumulative total whenever it rises, through one callback on the run's spec. It listens to its workers' live figures whether or not the run itself was handed a dollar limit.
- The session keeps one rising figure per run and adds only the difference each time. The run's own final total closes any gap, before the road splits for a person's stop, so done, incomplete, a limit, a person's stop and an error all count.
- It goes through the fold door that writes no usage ledger line, because each worker already wrote its own calls there. The day's figure on disk is unchanged.

## Tests

- Through the real door, `StartTask` under the bash belt: a finished run, an incomplete run and a run a person stopped each leave their dollars in the conversation's total once. Each was written first and seen red at zero.
