**In one sentence:** a task a limit ended now says which limit it was, `a time limit you set stopped it` or `a dollar limit you set stopped it`, and no longer calls it a fault.

## What was wrong

A run its elapsed-time limit or its dollar limit ended drew its reason as `a fault: a limit you set stopped it`. A limit a person set is not a fault, and a person who set both could not tell which one fired.

## What changed

- **The run records which limit ended it**, where it decides it, beside its one outcome word. The outcome word is unchanged: such a run still reads `incomplete`. The fact crosses the engine seam one for one.
- **The reason line names the limit** and carries no `a fault:` in front. Every other ending keeps its reading.
- **A joined row the run's ending took down mid-flight** drew a fault of its own. It now draws the run's ending.
- **The limit named is the first one reached.** A worker the time limit cut can come home with a receipt past the dollar limit; that return no longer renames the ending.

The cell counted a part a person stopped alone as cut by a limit that ended the run later. A limit writes no store row, so a cancelled row under a standing root is a person's stop. **In one sentence:** a test of the turn the chat wakes by itself stopped failing about once in forty runs on a busy machine; nothing a person sees changes.

## What was wrong

`TestAWokenTurnPastTheCeilingMovesToAFreshContext` was red about once in forty runs on a loaded machine and never on a quiet one. Cell c351 ran it under deliberate load and gave the verdict: the test's fault, not the product's.

The checkpoint fixtures pin the order of a reading and an answer through the turn's context. A submitted turn inherits that context from its caller. A turn the agent wakes by itself has no caller and started under the plain background, so the fixture could reach every turn but that one, and a late reading raced the answer.

## The change

One unexported field on the agent, `wokenTurnBase`. A fixture sets it so a woken turn starts under the watched context. It is nil in the running product, which starts a woken turn under the background exactly as before, and its comment says so.

**Why a seam and not a lifetime context.** Closing a session already ends a woken turn the way it ends any turn: every turn gets its own cancel when it starts, and `Close` takes that cancel and waits for the turn. The agent has no lifetime context; its memory pass, its naming errand, its wall reader and its turn each have a stop of their own. Deriving woken turns from a new lifetime context would be a larger change than this fix deserves. The manager accepted the one-field seam on that reading.

- `TestAWokenTurnHandsOverHoweverLateItsReadingLands`: a completer that lands the sketch reading 50 ms late. With the fixture's line removed it fails after 60 s; with it, it passes.

**In one sentence:** a run can no longer report `done` while a finished piece of its work has not been checked, whatever order its workers came home in.

## What was wrong

A worker writes its own done to the plan store and comes home a moment later. Its return is what adds its check. The run read the store row as the landing, so anything that happened in that moment went ahead on work nobody had reviewed:

- **A root that finishes while its child's worker is still out.** The store admits the root's done, because every child it has reads done. The child's check then had to go beneath a done root, the store refused it, and the run dropped the refusal without a word and answered `done`.
- **A root woken off the child's row.** The same moment, the other way round.
- **A return already waiting in the run's channel** when a pass looked at the root's ending.
- **A root that returned an error after storing its own done** was not reviewed at all.

None of this happens on a quiet machine. The parked-root order, the one #1271 closed in the store, was measured in five loaded runs of four hundred; the others are the same moment reached by other roads.

## The law

**NO RUN ANSWERS DONE WHILE A FINISHED PIECE OF WORK HAS HAD NO REVIEW ROUND, WHATEVER THE ORDER OF RETURNS. A LANDING IS A RETURN THE RUN HAS ABSORBED, NOT A STORE ROW.**

- The root's completion, a parent's wake and the run's own answer all wait for the worker of a done task to come home. A failed or cancelled row has no review to seat and counts as landed at once.
- **The wait is bounded by the worker.** It reads its own row when the command it is in ends, so the run waits at most the belt's ceiling on one command, 600 seconds. Before, the run ended over that worker and its review was silently lost. The pass does NOT cancel such a worker: `endCancelledWorkers` carries the shipped law FAILED AND CANCELLED, NEVER DONE for exactly this reason.
- `Store.AddReviewCheck` seats a check beneath its parent whatever the parent wrote about itself meanwhile, and moves every done task above it back to waiting on it, each keeping the result it earned. It was `AddRootCheck`, for a childless done root only. Nothing but a check comes in that way; `AddMany` refuses every other child of a terminal task as before.
- A root reopened like this finished over a landing it was never given, so once the check lands it is owed the wake any parent is owed.
- A review the store will not seat ends the run `incomplete`. It is never skipped.
- A pass absorbs the returns already waiting before it looks at the root, and reads the root's row after that, never before.

## From the cells, and what review found

Cells c348 (queued returns), c349 (the root that returns an error over its own done) and c358 (the landing rule and the store seam). c358 was green on its own white-box tests and NOT against the order it was written for:

- Two tests force the loaded orders through the run's own loop with channels and no sleeps, in `internal/run/review_order_test.go`. With c358 alone the running root still answered `done` with its check sitting `ready`, 13 runs in 50: the pass read the root's row, THEN absorbed the return that reopened it, then judged the stale row. Fixed by reading after.
- c358 edited the landed entry of #1233. Restored; this change has its own.
- The store seam kept a name that was no longer true and had no store test. `internal/plandb/review_check_test.go` holds it: both done ancestors reopen with their words kept, a child that is not a check and a check with no parent are refused, the task between closes by itself when the check lands, the root is the run's to complete.
- My own drain test from #1268 forced the drain with a done worker that lingers until cancelled. Under the landing rule that state no longer exists, so it now drains by the caller's ending. The shipped `TestStartWaitsForAWorkerTheCompletedTreeLeftBehind` has its leaf come home by itself for the same reason, and drain keeps a direct test.

catalog: the lazy warm is owned, cancelled and joined at close, so it cannot write under a later home

## What changed

catalog.LoadLazy started its warm as a bare guard.Go on the caller's context, and every production caller
passed context.Background(). Nothing cancelled it and nothing joined it, so after a process closed the warm
could still finish its fetch and call writeCache(cachePath(...)), which resolves home.Dir() at WRITE time
when Options.Dir is empty. That is the late-home writer behind the intermittent "TempDir RemoveAll:
directory not empty" reds: the write lands in whichever CODEAF_HOME the NEXT test has set.

#1179 had already joined the WAITER (warmV3Models gating on models.Warmed(ctx)), which is why the class
looked closed; it never touched the catalog package's own write inside LoadLazy's goroutine.

- internal/catalog/catalog.go: a lazy Catalog now owns a derived cancelable context and a warmDone channel.
  LoadLazy derives the warm context from the caller's and closes warmDone when the warm exits. Catalog.Close
  cancels and then synchronously joins. load() checks ctx.Err() AFTER a successful fetch and BEFORE
  writeCache, so a transport that succeeds LATE, after the close, does not write; the join is what makes it

**In one sentence:** a check command that carries a backslash inside double quotes, such as a search pattern written `"a\|b"`, is now accepted as the one command it is, and both readers of "is this one command" share one quote scanner.

## What was wrong

`approval.FirstCompositionOutsideQuotes` refused every backslash inside double quotes, whatever it stood before. A declared check of one command, measured on 2026-09-19, was turned away naming the backslash. Its sibling `FirstBarOutsideQuotes`, which finds where a line's first stage ends, had no escape rule at all and read `"a\" | b"` as a quotation that closed at the escaped quote. Two quote loops were a safety argument with two versions.

## The rule, by the shell's quoting property

One scanner, `scanShellQuotes`, under both readers. A reader differs from the other only in which characters it calls live.

- Inside single quotes every character is text, a backslash included.
- Inside double quotes a dollar and a backtick stay live, because the shell still expands them. A backslash there makes the character after it text, whichever character that is, so the pair is stepped over whole. That is what keeps an escaped quote from closing the quotation and a doubled backslash from hiding the quote that does close it.
- **Conservative by construction.** A shape the scanner cannot prove is one whole command is uncertain, and both readers treat uncertain as refused: a quotation left open, a backslash with nothing after it, a backslash before a newline, and every backslash outside quotes, which was always refused and still is.
- The bar reader answers no bar when the shape ahead of any bar is uncertain. The line is then left whole, the uncertainty still in it, and the composition reader refuses it at the door. A cut there would hand the door a shorter command than the one written.

## The table, `internal/approval/composition_test.go`

The first row is a synthetic line of the shape and length that was turned away: one ordinary program and one double-quoted pattern holding escaped bars and an escaped quote, 203 bytes. Admitted: that row, `"a\" ; b"` as one word, `"a\\b"`, a single-quoted `'a\|$()'`, `"a\$b"`, an escaped backtick. Still refused, each naming its character: `"a\\" ; b` (the semicolon), `$(...)` and a backtick inside double quotes, a trailing backslash, a backslash before a newline inside and outside double quotes, `'a\' ; b`, both unclosed quotes, and a backslash outside quotes. The bar reader has the mirror rows.

## Every caller, through its real function

That 203 byte line goes through `auditableDeclaredCheck` in the plan store, `preparedAuditCommand`, `firstStage` and `wholeClause`. `commandLike`, the declared-check list and the audit door built from it stand behind a length law, so they are fed the same shape at 45 bytes.

**A 203 byte check is still refused at those three, for length, and a following change owns that.** This change carries the safety reader and nothing else.

**The shell is the witness.** `TestACheckWithAQuotedBarIsAdmittedRunAndItsExitCodeRecorded` runs checks through the checker's real gate in a real shell and asserts a marker file no second command may create. Its row `grep "a\"; touch RAN; \"" walls.md` sat in the must-refuse list under the old rule. It is one command, so it is now admitted, RUN by that shell, and the marker is asserted absent. `grep "a\\" ; touch RAN`, which is two commands, took its place on the refused side. The same row moved the same way in the plan store's test and in the session's shape test.

## What I did not take from cell c353

- It rewrote the shipped refusal sentence and the checks schema description. Both shipped sentences still name a form that passes, and its schema sentence ran past the 200 byte description law. Both are byte for byte as shipped.
- It raised the declared-check length limit from 200 to 256. That is a different law with a different reason and is out of this change.
- It dropped the reader's law comment. It is back, over the scanner.

The manual changes one sentence, the one that became false: what a backslash inside double quotes does.

enginehost: a readiness gate proves a real accept, and two raw-Dial callers retry the stale-socket window

## What changed

The host readiness gate treated "the socket file exists and the lock is held" as ready. A host's own startup
order (internal/enginehost/host.go) takes the lock, then removes the old socket, then net.Listen. So there is
a window where the lock is held and a stale socket file is present while nothing is listening yet, and a
caller that dialed in that window was refused.

- internal/enginehost/stale_test.go: waitForHostQuietly now confirms a REAL accept by calling
  Ask(workspace, remote.WhoIs{}), so it returns only after Dial plus the remote whois handshake, not on a
  socket pathname plus a held lock. The forced-window regression preserves a closed Unix socket, holds the
  lock, proves readiness stays blocked, then starts a real host and proves it completes. Host startup order
  is unchanged. Failing-first: the pre-fix file+lock gate fails at stale_test.go with "stale socket plus
  held lock was accepted as ready".
- Product callers: both raw enginehost.Dial callers were traced and found exposed to the same
  remove-to-listen window with no preceding Attach to that host:
  - cmd/codeaf/chatv3_local.go (codeaf chat --once road probe): the former raw Dial had no preceding Attach
    and could race the window, silently choosing the in-process road. It now retries only on ECONNREFUSED,
    tolerates ENOENT during the replacement interval, and leaves unrelated errors and initially missing
    sockets unchanged. Regression: chatv3_local_test.go.
  - cmd/codeaf/chatv3_taskowner.go (cross-workspace task-owner open): the launch Attach is to the launch
    workspace only; a task-owner click can target another restarting host with no preceding Attach. It now
    uses the same narrowly bounded retry. Regression: chatv3_taskowner_test.go. Same-workspace launch stays
    protected by its earlier Attach.
  The retry is bounded: at most 26 attempts over ~250 ms, each Dial keeping enginehost's own 2s ceiling.

## Acceptance (Spark, on the PR head, rebased on 761cdab1e; authors are the bot; tree unchanged before/after)

- scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./internal/enginehost: ok 14.3s; scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./cmd/codeaf:
  ok 113.3s.
- Race nets: go test ./internal/enginehost -run TestWaitForHostQuietlyRequiresAListeningHost -count=50 ok;
  go test ./cmd/codeaf -run (the two window regressions) -count=20 ok. Failing-first for each recorded above.

  ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok. No em dashes in the added lines.


One known window, named so nobody rediscovers it: the readiness probe takes the host lock for an instant, so a host calling takeLock in that same instant would read it busy. The window is microseconds and it only opens after a dial has already failed, so a launch loses at worst one retry pause.

body:
**In one sentence:** a task that is waiting on other work can no longer be marked finished by a late step of its own worker, which under load used to close a run before its work was checked.

## What was wrong

A worker that parks its task with `plandb wait` could still finish it. A round the worker had already started still ends its tool, and when that tool was the task's own `plandb done` the plan store admitted it: the claim a park releases was never what the store checked for the run's own task.

On the run's own task that closed a run over work nobody had reviewed. The root parked on its child, the child wrote its own done, the root's late finish landed, and the run answered `done` while the child's worker was still out. Five loaded runs in four hundred did this and no quiet run did. Every one left a task that was done and still flagged waiting.

## What changes

One function in `internal/plandb/store.go`, `refuseParked`, called by the three roads that write an ending: a worker's done, a worker's fail, and the run's own completion of its root. A parked task hears `task "<id>" is waiting and can only be finished after it is woken`. `Store.Wake` stays the only place the flag clears. Nothing else changes: `StopRoot` and `Cancel` are untouched, so a person's stop still ends a parked task.

Done together with waiting is now a pair no road in the store can write.

## What the run does with the refusal

Read from `internal/run/run.go`, which this change does not touch. `completeTree` calls `CompleteRoot` and drops its error, as it always has. When the root is parked the call is now refused, the root stays open and parked, and the run does not hang on it: the same pass goes on to `launchWaits`, which wakes a parked task as soon as everything it waited on has ended, clears the flag through `Store.Wake`, and launches its worker again. That worker's finish is an ordinary one. A park cannot repeat forever, because `plandb wait` refuses a wait with nothing open, and the run's own limits bound the rest. The forced test below goes through this road end to end.

## What this does not claim

The store rule alone does not give "no run answers done while a finished piece of work has had no review round". With the late finish refused, the run still wakes the root off the child's store row while the child's worker is out. That is the run's own law about what counts as a landing. It is fixed on `fix/no-run-answers-done-before-a-review`, stacked on this branch, and its forced tests are red against this head. A store that refuses the fingerprint is good by itself.

## Proof

On Spark, under `umask 022`, tree `~/src/trees/parked-c0925b8eb`, head c0925b8eb on santos/dev da3368d46, finished 2026-09-19T21:07Z.

| Step | Result |

| `go build ./...`, `go vet` | exit 0 |
| `internal/session`, whole, under the box lock | ok, 245 s |
| `internal/run`, `internal/plandb`, `internal/manual`, `internal/guard`, `internal/namelaw` | ok |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` | empty |
| `make changelog-check`, `make build-cross` | exit 0 |

Failing first: `TestAParkedRootsLateFinishIsRefusedAndTheRunCarriesOn` against trunk's store answers `the parked root's late finish answered ""`, the late finish admitted. The test forces the loaded order with channels and no sleeps: the child's done lands in the store, then the late finish arrives, and only then does the child's worker come home.

`internal/plandb/parked_finish_test.go` holds the store's side: done, fail and the root's completion each refused while parked and each admitted after a wake.

scripts: the heavy-suite lock follows the suite, not the wrapper

## What changed

#1264 made the heavy-suite lock a kernel file lock held on the wrapper's descriptor, released when the
WRAPPER exits. If the wrapper is killed while the go test child keeps running as an orphan, the lock RELEASES
while a heavy suite is still executing, so a second heavy suite starts concurrently, the load defect #1264
set out to end.

- cmd/codeaf-suite-lock/lock_unix.go (//go:build unix): appends the already-locked *os.File to
  exec.Cmd.ExtraFiles, so the child inherits a descriptor for the SAME open file description. The advisory
  lock is held until every fd on that description is closed, so it survives the wrapper's death and stays
  held until the suite exits.
- cmd/codeaf-suite-lock/lock_windows.go (//go:build windows): the build-tagged no-op counterpart, so the
  package still compiles on both Windows targets in build-cross.
- cmd/codeaf-suite-lock/main.go: inheritance is installed before Start, and cmd.Process.Pid is written after
  Start, so an ordinary refusal names the live suite, not the dead wrapper.

## The cost of an inherited descriptor, and an honest refusal

The inherited descriptor is not close-on-exec, so everything the suite starts inherits it: the test binaries,
and any daemon THEY start and leak. Our tests start engine hosts, which close no inherited descriptors on the
way up (internal/enginehost/detach_unix.go only sets SysProcAttr{Setsid: true}), so a leaked host keeps the
lock. This is not theoretical: the learning crew's queue daemon wedged its own restart the same way today,
its flock descriptor inherited by every cell it launched, the cells outliving it and keeping the lock. Their
fix was closing the descriptor in launched children, which this helper cannot do for go test's children.

So the refusal is made honest rather than clever. The pid in the lock file is meaningful only in the HOLDER's
pid namespace: read from another namespace it may be a live suite, a pid that maps to nothing, or an
unrelated process. The refusal therefore NEVER says the holder is gone. When the recorded pid is not visible
from here (pidVisibleHere: kill(pid,0) on unix, a no-op returning true on Windows where the descriptor is not
inherited) it says exactly that and gives BOTH readings, another process namespace or a holder that exited and
left the lock to a process it started, then names lsof on the lock file and that it must be run where every
process is visible. A visible holder still gets the ordinary wait message. The first line is byte for byte
unchanged, so a gate keying on it still matches.

## Acceptance (Spark, rebased on santos/dev da3368d46; tree unchanged before and after)

- Failing-first: the test commit fails on base at main_test.go:63 (metadata named the wrapper pid); with the
  fix, -count=20 passes.
- TestRefusalNamesADeadHolderWhenAGrandchildKeepsTheLock backgrounds a grandchild that inherits the locked
  descriptor and outlives the suite, and asserts the not-visible line and the lsof hint; it is red on the
  prior code, which said only "Wait for it".
- scripts/one-suite_test.sh: one-suite namespace acceptance ok, now also asserting that a contender in a
  fresh pid namespace, which cannot see a host holder's pid, is told the pid is not visible from here rather
  than that a live suite is gone.
- make build-cross: all six targets, exit 0. go test ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock -count=10 ok. gofmt -l ./cmd
  ./internal empty; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check ok; go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok.
  No em dashes in the added lines.

Stacked on #1262. The diff against that branch is this change alone.

## What was wrong

A run's dollar limit was read only when a worker came home. A worker's spend reached the run's count in its report, so one long worker could pass the limit many times over before anything counted it. #1262's body named this hole; this closes it.

## What changes

- **A worker says what it has spent as each model call is paid for.** The worker reads the agent's running total as each event comes by and tells the run whenever it has risen. The figure is cumulative, so the run adds only what is new and a dollar is counted once.
- **The run adds it while the worker is still working.** When the sum reaches the limit the run launches nothing new, ends the work in flight, absorbs every ending, and answers `a limit you set stopped it`. That is the time limit's road from #1262. Nothing is dropped.
- **A worker never waits on the run to report.** It writes its figure under a lock and leaves a token the loop may miss. A missed token loses nothing, because the next read takes the whole figure.
- **A return still reconciles.** The report is the receipt. A report smaller than what was already counted takes nothing back, because the money was spent.
- A run with no dollar limit counts as it always did, at each return.

The call that reaches the limit is already paid for, so a run can end a little over its figure. The manual says so.

## Two faults the review found in the first version, and the tests that hold them

The first version came from a work cell. Both faults passed its own tests, which used stand-in workers only.

1. **A freeze.** Spend figures travelled over the returns channel with a blocking send. The drain waits for workers and reads nothing, so a worker that reported while the run drained blocked for good and the run never answered. `TestAWorkerReportingSpendWhileTheRunDrainsDoesNotHoldTheRunOpen` finishes the tree while one worker is still out, then has that worker report 64 times after its context ends. On the first version it fails with "the run never answered" after 3 of 64 reports, which is the channel's depth. It passes here.
2. **The real worker never reported.** The report was wired where the turn's usage arrives, which is the turn's end, and a worker's turn is its whole working life. `TestBashWorkerReportsItsSpendWhileItIsStillWorking` drives the real worker through a scripted seat. On the first version it saw one report for three paid calls. It passes here, one rising figure per paid call, the last equal to the report.

The cell's four supervisor tests are kept: one worker alone crossing the limit, two workers crossing it together, a run with no limit, and a worker that returns under the limit counted once.

## A run's spend never goes down

A worker whose task the store cancelled under it used to hand back no spend the run counted. Those were paid dollars missing from the run's figure and from a person's limit. The rule now: what a run counts as spent never goes down, and it includes every paid call whatever way its task ended. The cancelled worker's words and steps are still dropped. `TestSpendOfAWorkerWhoseTaskTheStoreCancelledStaysInTheRunsCount` holds it with a limit and without one. The shipped test that pinned the old figure now expects the cancelled leaf's dollars and none of its steps, and is renamed to say so.

The same rule reaches a worker the run outlives. When the tree finishes while a worker is still out, the drain ends it and used to drop its return whole. The drain now waits for it as before, then reads the returns left in the channel without waiting and settles only their dollars. The shipped cancelled-leaf test takes this road, because there the run ends before the leaf comes home.

## Proof

Head ca32515e4, stacked on #1262's d57b3c955 on trunk 137bb8cd1, Spark, 2026-09-19, under `umask 022`. Exit codes read directly.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `go build ./...` and `go vet` | exit 0 |
| `make test` of `internal/run`, `internal/plandb`, `internal/manual`, `internal/guard`, `internal/namelaw`, `cmd/codeaf` | exit 0 |
| the new and changed run tests, 20 times over | ok |
| the same tests under `-race` | ok |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` | empty |
| `make changelog-check` | exit 0 |
| `make build-cross` | exit 0 |

Failing-first, each on the head before its fix: the drain test on the cell's own supervisor fails with "the run never answered" after 3 of 64 reports; the real-worker test sees one report for three paid calls; the cancelled-spend test reads a run spend of 0. The shipped cancelled-leaf test is what showed that the drain, and not only the absorb, was where a cancelled worker's dollars went missing: there the run ends before the leaf comes home.

The change touches `internal/run` and one manual paragraph, and draws no new word, so no whole `internal/session` or `internal/tui3` run was owed. The ending a person sees is #1262's, whose hosted frame is in that PR.

chatv3: stop and join the pool judge sweep at close, and inventory process goroutines with a class law

## What changed

Every openV3Launch started guard.Go("pool/judge-sweep", ...) as a bare goroutine, not registered on the
profile errand tracker, so closeAll (which joins only the tracked pool errands) did not wait for it. The
sweep writes under config.ProfilePath(profileDir, "pool"), which resolves at write time to home.Join("pool")
when the profile dir is empty, and home.Join reads CODEAF_HOME at call time. So a sweep that outlived Close
could resolve an empty profile path against a LATER CODEAF_HOME and write pool files into another launch's
home, the late-home-writer class behind the intermittent "TempDir RemoveAll: directory not empty" gate reds,
including in tests that open no process of their own.

- cmd/codeaf/chatv3.go, cmd/codeaf/poolrecord.go: the judge sweep is now owned by the profile pool errand
  set (registered through the errand tracker with a context), so stopPoolErrands in closeAll cancels and
  JOINS it before Close returns. The join is outside the enqueue lock. Per-launch semantics are kept and a
  second launch/process in the same binary starts its own sweep.
- cmd/codeaf/pooljudge_close_test.go: a real-close-path test proving no pool file is created after Close
  returns (fails on base with the bare goroutine), the cross-test variant (a survivor sweep from one
  CODEAF_HOME does not recreate a pool under a second launch's home), and that two processes each sweep.
- cmd/codeaf/chatv3_guard_class_test.go: a class law that inventories every guard.Go a v3 process starts
  and requires each long-lived one to name what stops it and where closeAll joins it. chatv3/models,
  engine/models and chatv3/sweep-home are recorded as KNOWN-OPEN with the cells that own them (catalog warm
  and place-sweep walk), so the law lands green now and shrinks as those land.

## Cancel does not burn a landing (review fix)

poolJudgeLandingContext wrote judgeLast and markJudged whenever no judge scored, INCLUDING the case where a
close cancelled the parent context mid-judge and every candidate failed on that cancellation, not on the run.
That permanently burned the landing so no later start rejudged it. It now returns without writeJudgeLast and
without markJudged when the parent context is done and no score came back, leaving the landing for the next
start. sweepClaimContext no longer counts such a landing (judged++ ran after the call) and leaves the claim
in place, so the next sweep recovers it instead of a completed sweep removing it. The shadowed per-candidate
context inside the loop is out of scope at the check; ctx there is the parent.

Failing-first: TestJudgeLandingLeftUnjudgedWhenCancelledMidJudge cancels the context before the ask, so every
candidate returns the cancel error and no score; on base the landing is markJudged (alreadyJudged true) and
the test fails at pooljudge_close_test.go:189, with the fix it is left unjudged and the test passes.

## What a close waits for, at most

closeAll cancels the sweep's context and joins the errand. The join waits at most for one in-flight judge ask
to observe the cancel and return; each ask is bounded by its per-candidate context, and the folder scan
between candidates is not waited on. So Close returns promptly rather than blocking on a full judge pass.

## Acceptance (Spark, on the PR head 74f26ae3c, rebased on santos/dev 137bb8cd1; tree unchanged before/after)

- scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./cmd/codeaf: ok 99.7s (whole package, via the new kernel-file-lock one-suite
  from #1264, on the landed head).
- go test ./cmd/codeaf -run TestJudgeLandingLeftUnjudgedWhenCancelledMidJudge -count=5: ok; failing-first
  proven by stashing only poolrecord.go (test red at :189), then restoring (green).
- gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal empty; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check ok (40 entries well formed); go test
  ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok. No em dashes in the added lines.

body:
**In one sentence:** a task whose worker keeps running the same command and getting the same answer is told once what the run saw and what it can do, and is ended three identical steps later instead of burning to the 200 step cap.

## What was true

A run worker's loop ends on a store finish, a store park, four replies in a row with no action, the step cap, the wall, or an errored turn. A reply that carried a tool call resets the no-action count, so a worker that alternates ONE action and ONE text reply never reaches that ending. Only the step cap, 200 finished calls, stopped it. A real pair of workers did about 820 model calls in 30 minutes in exactly that alternation.

## What is true now

**THE SAME COMMAND COMING BACK WITH THE SAME ANSWER, WITH NOTHING MOVING UNDER THE WORKER'S OWN TASK BETWEEN THE LOOKS, IS A WORKER THAT HAS STOPPED MAKING PROGRESS. BEFORE ITS TASK ENDS, THE RUN SAYS SO ONCE.**

- After 3 identical finished steps the run speaks once, in its own voice, inside the turn that is still running. It says what it saw and the three things a worker can do: try something else, wait for a thing outside the plan in one longer action, or park with `plandb wait` when the plan names what it waits on.
- The note states how long one action may run, 600 seconds, read from the belt's own constant and never retyped, so it cannot recommend a wait the belt would cut short.
- 3 more identical steps after the note end the task, `incomplete`, with `the same command came back with the same answer 6 times in a row: the work was not moving`.
- A different action after the note resets everything, the note included. The note records no step and draws no row.
- The property is read from what the run already records about a step: the tool, the command as spelled, the head of the answer, and the store's own record of movement. No word of any command or any error is read, so it holds whatever the tool and whatever the cause.
- The count runs over finished steps, not model calls, so the words a worker says between its actions change nothing.
- Three things reset it: a different command, a different answer, or a move in the worker's own part of the store.
- A worker the store says is blocked on another task is not ended. It is parked through the belt's own wait and wakes when that wait is over.
- The two bounds are two constants, interpolated into every sentence that states them.

## By hand, after the manager's review

- **Movement is read under the worker's own task, not over the whole store.** The cell read the whole store, which kept a broken worker alive for as long as its siblings went on working. It now counts the worker's own row and any row under it, at any depth. What a sibling does is not this worker's progress.
- **A call aborted by the law's own ending is not a step.** A model that answers at once had its next action begun and aborted after the law fired, and the record carried a fifth step under an ending that says four. The new busy-run test found it. The cell's own seat alternated a call and a reply, so its turn had always ended first.

## Cases it does not catch, all bounded by the step cap as before

An A, B, A, B alternation with static answers. A worker that moves its own part of the store on every look. A look that differs only beyond the recorded 2 KiB head.

## The note, from cell c357, with my corrections

A worker waiting on something outside the plan (a build, a remote job) looks with the same command and gets the same answer. That is the most common honest loop there is, and the first version ended it on a bound the worker had never been told about. The note goes in through the session's own steer door, mid turn. A turn that ended between the step and the steer is owed the note at the next round's opening, the road the no-action note already rides, so the sentence is said exactly once either way.

By hand: the manual said a person could "steer a note into" the task; it now uses the steering section's own word, `note`, and says that a note on the task counts as something changing, which the movement reading makes true. Its section lost the asker's word in my first trim and the probe `why did my task stop on its own` reached another page; the word is back and the probe passes.

## Tests, all through the real worker with a scripted seat, no sleeps

- A worker that changes its action after the note is not ended, and the note is in the messages its seat was sent exactly once.
- A worker that ignores the note ends at 6 steps under a cap of 60, with the plain reason, and the note was sent once.
- The note draws no step of its own in the record.
- The alternating shape, the parked road, the growing answer, the own-task movement, the busy sibling and the movement reading itself all still hold, with only the asserted number moved.

The manual's "Why did my task stop on its own?" says what the worker is told and when, and what a person can do, with four probes.

## What was true

A step's row leaves out the change into the run's copy and any part addressed to the run's record. Under the row, one dim line drew the head of what came back. That head is cut from the ONE observation the record holds for the whole line. When a left-out part printed first, the dim line showed that part's words under a row that no longer showed the part.

## What is true now

**THE HEAD OF WHAT CAME BACK IS DRAWN UNDER A ROW ONLY WHEN EVERY PART LEFT OUT OF THE ROW CANNOT HAVE WRITTEN TO IT AND STOPS EVERYTHING AFTER IT IF IT FAILS.**

- A left-out part addressed to the run's record withholds the dim line.
- A left-out change into the run's copy keeps it only when it is joined so that its failure ends the line. Joined any other way, what follows runs after a failed change and the head may be that failure's.
- A row with nothing left out keeps it.

The engine establishes the fact with the other display facts and it crosses the wire as a field. The surface never reads the words that came back. The field is the negative on purpose (`ObservationHeadWithheld`), so a step from an engine built before it draws its head as it did.

Nothing can do better from the record as it is. The belt runs the whole line as one shell with its output interleaved, and no part's output has a boundary (diagnosis cell c340).

## How much of a real page this takes away

Counted with the engine's own facts over 25 real recorded task records on Spark, 309 steps, from today's hosted drives and two cells' runs:

| | Steps |
| --- | --- |
| no row at all, as before | 29 |
| rows drawn | 280 |
| rows that keep their dim line | 242 |
| rows that lose it | 38 |

Every one of the 38 lost it to a left-out record part. None lost it to the way a copy change was joined. On the hosted drive for #1260, all 7 rows keep theirs. So about six rows in seven keep their output, and the page has not lost it. Running record parts as their own step in the engine is not needed for this.

## The shipped head assertions: one decision, three places

Three shipped assertions ask for a head under a row. They are one decision with one reason: the head is the first line of the whole answer, so it belongs to the first part that PRINTED, not the first part SHOWN. Where a left-out part can print, the engine cannot say the head is the work's, and it withholds it.

| Test | Row | Head asserted | Now |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `TestTaskPageOmitsOwnRecordIDsAndRunCopyPath` | `ls` beside a left-out record command | `files` | moved to the never list; the step carries the engine's fact |
| `TestHostedPlanPartsCrossTheWireAndFilterThePage` | `printf` beside a left-out record command, over the wire | `recorded-output` | moved to the never list; the test also asserts the fact crossed the wire |
| `TestTaskPageOmitsOwnRecordIDsAndRunCopyPath` | work after a lone leading change into the run copy joined by `&&` | `ok` | unchanged and still passes: that part cannot print and its failure stops the rest |

Each changed test says the reason in its own comment. The hosted one was found by the whole tui3 suite on Spark, not by reading.

## Tests

New drawn-page cases beside it: a record part before the work, after it, and as the head of a pipeline that stands in a sequence, each with an observation that is that part's own print, which appears nowhere on the page. Only the copy change left out keeps the head. Nothing left out keeps it. The engine's fact is pinned over the shipped table of command shapes, with one added: the copy change joined by `;` withholds.

The manual gets its own section, "Why is there no output under a step", with a probe.

body:
## What changed

scripts/one-suite.sh serialized heavy suites with a per-uid lock directory whose liveness was a pid check
(kill -0 plus a cmdline match). Cells run their test worker in a separate pid namespace over a shared
/tmp, so the pid a cell writes is a namespace-local pid that a host reads as a different process or none,
and the lock is judged stale and taken. Measured on Spark: three heavy suites at once, and, once a cell
rewrote the lock with its namespace-local pid between two host runs, host-versus-host double-took too.
Concurrent heavy suites drove box load into the 20s and manufactured the load-sensitive test reds that
cost gate runs.

The lock is now an advisory file lock held on an open descriptor, so its liveness does not depend on any
process seeing another's pid, and it is released when the holder dies (a suite killed mid-run leaves the
box unlocked, no stale pid bookkeeping):

- cmd/codeaf-suite-lock: a small helper that takes the lock through internal/filelock (the cross-platform
  lock #1248 already ships, unix.Flock on unix and LockFileEx on Windows), holds it on its fd for the
  child's lifetime, writes its pid and start time into the lock file only so a refused contender can name
  the holder, and forwards ordinary stops to the child. Exit status is propagated with the cross-platform
  ExitCode, so the helper compiles and ships on every release target including both Windows builds now in
  the full check's build-cross.
- scripts/one-suite.sh: builds and execs the helper instead of the pid-staleness dance; same refusal
  wording naming the holder, same package scope taking the lock.
- scripts/one-suite_test.sh: drives the real one-suite.sh and asserts refusal in both orders (a namespace
  starter against a host holder and the reverse), and the three-party case, a host holder, a cell starter
  refused, and a host arriving AFTER the cell's attempt STILL refused and still naming the original
  holder, which is the host-versus-host double-take the old lock allowed.

The lock dying with its holder's descriptor is the design point: there is no pid to go stale across a
namespace boundary at all.

## Acceptance (Spark, on the PR head; tree unchanged before and after)

- make build-cross: darwin, linux, windows for amd64 and arm64, all built, 73s, exit 0 (the raw unix.Flock
  helper could not build the Windows targets; internal/filelock does).
- go test ./cmd/codeaf-suite-lock (TestContentionNamesHolderAndDeathUnlocks): ok, the lock file names the
  holder pid, the refusal is exact, and a SIGKILLed holder leaves the next acquirer succeeding.
- bash scripts/one-suite_test.sh: one-suite namespace acceptance: ok (both orders and the host-after-cell
  case, driving the real scripts/one-suite.sh).
- scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./internal/guard via the new helper: ok, a normal run takes and releases.
- gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal empty; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check ok; go test ./internal/guard
  ./internal/namelaw ok. No em dashes in the added lines.

body:
## What changed

TestANewDirectionArrivesWithTheClaimUnspent (internal/session/completion_stale_test.go) queued the
forced revision through the fixture-only helper queueDirection, which appends straight to agent.steering
and, unlike a person's real direction, has no "start a fresh turn if the agent is not running" recovery.
That is why the test intermittently journaled only one ending under load (about 1 in 40 in a gate run at
load ~9): the lifted revision could be dropped at turn teardown instead of earning its own ending.

The test now submits the revision through the real path, agent.Submit(ctx, revision), and collects that
turn's own event stream. Submit either splices the direction into the running turn with a live stream or
starts a new turn when the agent is not running, so the queued revision always gets a turn and an ending,
exactly as a person's direction does in production. The existing assertions are unchanged (queued==true,
admitted==0, at least two journaled ceilings, all dropped:nothing-left).

## Why this is a test fix, not a product defect (settled from the code)

The earlier note that this was "a genuine lost second ending" and this "test-only fix" are reconciled by
reading the teardown, not by -count (which proves nothing here: the old test also passed -count=3000 on an
idle box, the loss was about 1 in 40 only under an artificial a.mu perturbation).

A queued direction earns its second ending at turn teardown, and both paths that could start it are gated
on completed==true:
- agent.go:1759 lifts a spliced direction to the follow-up queue (liftSteersLocked), and it is started
  only if nextFollowUpLocked(completed) returns one at agent.go:1784; nextFollowUpLocked drops every
  follow-up when !completed (agent.go:1909-1910).
- the drained-but-unanswered wake (agent.go:1791) is likewise gated on completed.

completed is runTurn's return (agent.go:1836), and runTurn returns false ONLY on a stopped or errored
turn: ctx interrupt or deadline (loop.go:846, loop.go:943), a permanent mid-stream failure (loop.go:982),
or an abandoned turn (loop.go:1270). A normal checkpoint "nothing left" completion returns true
(loop.go:856). So a person's direction is dropped only when the turn was interrupted, errored, or
abandoned, which is the documented drain law: "a drain must never resurrect a stopped turn"
(nextFollowUpLocked). On a normal completion the queued direction always gets its own turn and ending.

And the person is told when a direction is not taken up on an abnormal end: a spliced steer gets an
explicit EventSteerFellThrough on their stream (steer.go:875) and a journaled appendSteerFellThrough line
(steer.go:882), both from liftSteersLocked (steer.go:856), before the follow-up is dropped, and a plain
direction is drained into the transcript in the person's own words by drainSteeringLocked (agent.go:1760)
regardless of completed. Only the automatic
re-ask is withheld, which is the drain law. So the drop is not silent.

submitUser while the turn is running appends to a.steering (agent.go:971) exactly as queueDirection does,
so it is the SAME teardown that governs both; the difference is only that Submit also subscribes a live
stream (agent.go:976). The old test therefore used a non-production injection (queueDirection) and needed
a perturbation to force the abnormal (completed==false) end that alone loses the ending. Routing the test
through Submit and collecting the revision's own stream makes it ask for exactly what the product promises
(a direction submitted during a normal turn gets an ending), and the >=2-ceilings assertion still fails if
that promise is ever broken. No product code changes; the product question is not left open, because the
only loss path is an interrupted/errored/abandoned turn, which is intended.

## Acceptance (Spark)

- Focused determinism: go test ./internal/session -run '^TestANewDirectionArrivesWithTheClaimUnspent$'
  -count=200 passed (2.0s), no lost ending.
- one-suite full acceptance on 1c213967b: `scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./internal/session ./internal/guard
  ./internal/namelaw` exit 0 (internal/session 247.4s, guard 0.7s, namelaw 3.9s).

Cherry-picked from the diagnosis run's commit onto trunk 7cefdf1f4; one file changed, 7 insertions,
1 deletion. gofmt -l empty, no em dashes, go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check exit 0.

## What was true

A session's elapsed-time limit never reached a run that `/task` started. The flag becomes `session.Budget.Wall`, the interactive check reads it before a new turn, and nothing handed it to the run engine. A run carried a dollar limit and no time limit, so it ran past the hours its person set.

## What is true now

- `RunSpec.Elapsed` carries what is left of the session's wall when the run starts, on the same clock the interactive check uses. `run.Limits.Elapsed` ends the run on it.
- The ending is the cost limit's own: nothing new is launched, the outcome is `a limit you set stopped it`, and what finished lands the ordinary way. A session with no time limit puts none on its runs.
- The one difference is the work in flight. A cost limit lets it finish. A time limit ends it and absorbs each ending, the way the caller's wall already does, so a cut task reads `incomplete` and what it spent is in the run's account.
- A run that ended on a limit with no result of its own says the limit's sentence on its row. It said nothing there before.

## The dollar limit, for comparison

The dollar limit does not lose a worker. It lets in-flight workers finish and absorbs every one, so each is counted. Its hole is a different one: spend is added only when a worker RETURNS, so the ceiling is checked at returns and never during a worker's run. A long worker can carry the run past its ceiling by up to that worker's whole spend, and with several slots by several workers' worth. This change does not touch that. The first version of the time limit here did drop workers: it drained them and set the in-flight count to zero by hand, which left their tasks claimed on a run that was over. That is what the failing assertion on the run's spend and its held workers now pins.

## From the cell, and what I changed by hand

Built from cell c330's commits. By hand: the in-flight endings are absorbed instead of dropped, with a test that fails on the dropped version. I removed the cell's commit that detached the run from its caller's context, because what a closed window or a quit does to a live run is the owner's open call and not this change's. The manual section moved out of the flags section it had split, says which limit is which, and a redundant file-reading test went in favour of the probe.

## Proof, on Spark

Head d57b3c955 on trunk 137bb8cd1, one tree on Spark, 19:40Z to 19:48Z on 2026-09-19, under `umask 022`. Exit codes read directly.

| Check | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `go build ./...` and `go vet` of run, session, tui3, manual | exit 0 |
| whole `internal/session` under the suite lock | ok, 260.5 s |
| `internal/run`, `internal/plandb`, `internal/manual`, `internal/guard`, `internal/namelaw` | ok |
| `cmd/codeaf` | ok, 96.5 s |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` | empty |
| `make changelog-check` | exit 0 |
| `make build-cross` | exit 0 |

Seen once at an earlier head and attributed: `TestAWokenTurnPastTheCeilingMovesWorkToATask` timed out in its 60 s wait inside a whole session run while the box also carried three cells, eight busy shells and a second suite. Alone on the same tree it passed 20 of 20 in 1.5 s. It is a test of the old task road, which this change does not touch, and it passed in the run above. A separate cell is reading what that wait depends on.

## Hosted frame, real binary, on Spark

One drive per binary, hosted, in a throwaway home: `codeaf chat --yolo --max-hours 0.03` (108 s), then one `/task` whose worker writes a file and sits in a single `sleep 400`. The screen was read every five seconds for 260 s.

| Arm | Binary | What the screen did |
| --- | --- | --- |
| branch | built from d57b3c955 | the run ended at 105 s. Drawn: `◆ Write the word started into a new file · incomplete · 1m42s · 1 file · merged` and under it `a fault: a limit you set stopped it · ctrl+o output`. Record: 1 step, ending `the run's wall stopped it`. |
| trunk | 761cdab1e | still `working` at 261 s, more than twice the limit, no ending drawn and none in the record. |

My first try drew only the product's own refusal, because `--max-hours` is refused without `--yolo`. The second try is the one above. The trunk arm's `sleep 400` outlived its engine by about two minutes and ended by itself; nothing was signalled.

## What a worker owes this road

The time limit cancels every worker in flight and then waits on the returns channel for each of them, the same shape as the caller's wall. A worker that ignored its context would therefore hold the run's ending. The one shipped worker observes it: its turn runs under that context and the command it is running is cut with it. The branch arm above is that road on the real binary.

## What reaches a run now, and what does not

- `--max-hours` reaches a run, as what is left of the conversation's wall when the run starts.
- `--max-cost` does NOT reach a run. A run's dollar limit is the conversation's spend ceiling alone, and `--max-cost` is still read only before a new interactive turn. A person who types `--max-cost 2` and starts a run has not bounded that run. That is a following change, together with handing a run what is LEFT of a dollar limit instead of the whole figure.
- #1268, stacked on this, makes the dollar limit hold while a worker is still working.

`--max-cost` still does not reach a run: a run's dollar limit is the conversation's spend ceiling. The manual now says so.

## What was true

A worker that answered one turn with several tool calls had none of them run, and each was answered by the belt with its own correction. Every one was recorded as a step, and a run's task page drew them as steps: a command a person reads as having run, with the belt's sentence to the worker in dim under it. On the real binary that was rows 2, 3 and 4 of a page, each reading `[not run] no action executed: return exactly one bash tool call per response`.

## What is true now

A step records whether its call ran, and if it did not, which of two things it was. Both facts are set where the event is known and cross the wire as fields. The page reads the fields and never the words of the answer.

- **A correction about the form of a reply has no row.** Several calls in one answer, a call that could not be read, a tool that is not on the belt, a held process rule. Nothing was attempted on the world. It stays in the record and in the head's step count.
- **An action the worker tried and was refused is drawn, as one dim line in the step's place.** `refused`, the word the permissions page already uses, then the command as typed, cut the way every step's command is. It carries no number, because a number on that page is a step that ran. The rows around it keep their recorded numbers. The answer written for the worker is not drawn.

## Where the separating fact is established

`HarnessMade` could not tell the two apart. The new fact is `Event.Refused`: a door refused an action the model attempted. It is set at the one place every pre-action veto passes through, from the veto's own author, so a door added later cannot forget it. The run engine records it on the step beside `NotRun`, and `PlanStep` carries it. A record written before the fields draws as it did.

One reading I made: "not counted as a step that ran" is kept by the line having no number. The head's count stays the record's count, which is also what the step cap counts, so the figures a person reads and the cap agree.

## Tests, failing first

- The drawn page, through the hosted fixture with the real remote client and server: a refused action draws exactly one line, `refused · <command>`, with no number and without the worker's answer. A correction in the same record draws nothing. Rows 1 and 4 keep their numbers and the head reads `4 steps`.
- The event, through the real turn loop on the belt: a two-call response is harness-made and not refused, a push the remote guard refuses is both, a call that ran is neither.
- The record: the run engine writes both facts, and no exit for either.

The manual said a batch had its first call run. It does not. The section is corrected, and a new section in the asker's words answers "a line under steps says refused", with its probe.

## What changed

A v3 process starts a background usage writer per ledger path (internal/session/usage_ledger.go); it
drained its queue on its own and nothing joined it at Close, so a usage row could still be written after
closeAll returned. This adds CloseUsage, which stops each writer and waits for its run loop to exit, and
calls it from closeAll after the usage flush. RecordUsage, FlushUsage and CloseUsage all resolve, enqueue
to, and close a writer's queue under the one writers lock, so a close cannot race a concurrent record or
flush.

- internal/session/usage_ledger.go: usageWriter gains a stopped channel; usageWriterForLocked and
  CloseUsage; RecordUsage enqueues under usageWritersMu.
- cmd/codeaf/chatv3_process.go: closeAll calls session.CloseUsage() after the usage flush.
- doc.go, engine.go (runRemoteEngine + runEngineHost), exec.go, image.go, chatv3.go: call CloseUsage on
  the paths that record usage outside a v3 process.

## Hold fixes (manager review)

Two defects found in review, both fixed in this branch with failing-first tests
(internal/session/usage_close_ceiling_test.go):

1. CloseUsage kept FlushUsage's bargain. FlushUsage waits under one usageFlushLimit deadline because a
   writer parked inside openUsageLedger on a stalled mount never drains, and an unbounded wait at
   v3Process.closeAll is a hung ~/.codeaf holding the exit open ("a spending record is worth less than the
   exit"). CloseUsage now takes the same single ceiling for the whole call and leaves a still-stuck writer
   behind at that accepted cost. Test TestCloseUsageReturnsUnderTheCeilingWhenAWriterStalls fails on the
   unbounded wait (12s, "the wait has no ceiling") and passes with the ceiling;
   TestCloseUsageJoinsAndLeavesTheLastRowOnDisk keeps the normal case (writer joined, last row on disk).

2. FlushUsage no longer sends on a closed queue. It copied writers under the lock and sent on their queues
   outside it, while CloseUsage closes those queues under the lock, so a flush across a close panicked
   (send on closed channel). FlushUsage now enqueues its markers under usageWritersMu (non-blocking, the
   same door RecordUsage uses) and waits on the accepted markers outside the lock under the ceiling. Test
   TestFlushUsageAndCloseUsageDoNotRace fires flush and close at the same writers 200 times under -race:
   it panics/-races on the old code (panic at usage_ledger.go send site) and is clean with the fix.

The two locked sections that must not hold the lock across a wait (CloseUsage, FlushUsage) are extracted
into detachUsageWriters and enqueueUsageFlush, each with a deferred Unlock, so every usageWritersMu.Lock
is immediately followed by defer Unlock. Lock-defer guard law
(internal/guard TestEveryLockInTheGuardedTreeUnlocksFromADefer, TestLockAllowlistIsStillReal) passes with
no allowlist entry.

FlushUsage callers after this PR: only v3Process.closeAll (immediately before CloseUsage, on the same
goroutine, so the two cannot run against each other) and the exit doors in doc.go/engine.go/exec.go/
image.go/chatv3.go (each a process on its way out; none on a turn path). None can race a concurrent Close
of the same registry, and both now enqueue under the lock regardless.

## Why the usage writer is not part of the CODEAF_HOME re-resolution class

The usage writer HOLDS its path: usageWriterFor(path) captures the path when the writer is created, and
the only caller that resolves the path (RecordUsage via UsageLedgerPath) runs synchronously on a turn,
never on the background goroutine. It does not call home.Join/home.Dir at write time, so unlike the pool
judge sweep (poolrecord.go) and the catalog warm (catalog.go), a surviving usage writer cannot land a row
in a later test's CODEAF_HOME. The defect here is only the missing join; no cross-test leak. Recorded so
this writer is not re-investigated with that class.

## Tests

- internal/session/usage_close_ceiling_test.go: TestCloseUsageReturnsUnderTheCeilingWhenAWriterStalls,
  TestCloseUsageJoinsAndLeavesTheLastRowOnDisk, TestFlushUsageAndCloseUsageDoNotRace.
- cmd/codeaf/usage_close_test.go: TestProcessCloseJoinsTheUsageWriter.
- internal/guard/usagewriter_test.go and internal/session/retiredpin_wire_test.go.

## Acceptance (Spark, one-suite)

Failing-first proof (internal/session, focused -race): the ceiling test fails 12s ("the wait has no
ceiling") on the unbounded wait; the flush/close test panics "send on closed channel" at the send site
under -race. Both green after the fix (3.8s).

`scripts/one-suite.sh go test ./cmd/codeaf ./internal/session ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` on
trunk 7cefdf1f4 with the fix:
- cmd/codeaf ok 112.445s
- internal/session ok 246.493s
- internal/guard ok 0.664s (lock-defer law green)
- internal/namelaw ok 3.734s
- exit 0

Head 7083af1a3, tree 8c82cb52f144de1d4d73155c6836c9b837508c22. go build ./... clean, gofmt -l empty,
go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check exit 0, no em dashes in the added lines.

## What a person saw

A run a person stopped read `stopped` on the side list and `incomplete` on its own page and in the tasks place, at the same moment. The side list draws the row the session publishes. The run's page reads the plan store, where a stopped task is cancelled, and the surface spelled failed and cancelled alike as `incomplete`.

## What changes

- A task whose ending is a person's stop reads `stopped` wherever its state word is drawn: the side list, the tasks place, the task's page, and the list of parts on a parent's page.
- Every part that stop ended with it reads `stopped` too. The store ends everything under a cancelled task in the same write and at the same instant, so a part counts when it was cancelled in the very instant an ancestor of it was stopped.
- A part that had already failed, or that the run cancelled for its own reasons at another moment, keeps `incomplete`.
- A stopped task has ended: it is offered no verb and no next step, and it is not read as work that can still move.

## How

- The fact is established where it is known. The session reads it from the store and sends it over the wire as a field of the row. The surface never finds it by reading a sentence.
- The word is decided in one place. The three functions that answer a row's word, its reading and whether it has ended now take the row instead of the store's status string, and every caller goes through them.
- The glyph follows the word the way an ordinary stopped task's does.

## Where this came from

The two-arm hosted drive that closed #1253 found the disagreement. A cell built the field, the one-place word and the drawn-word tests, one of them through the real hosted wire. Review by hand found one fault and filled two gaps:

- The question of whether a task has ended still listed only `done` and `incomplete`, so a task a person had just stopped was offered its stop again. Fixed, with a test.
- Parts a stop took down read `incomplete` under a parent that read `stopped`. Answered as above, with a test against a real store.
- The manual's list of a run row's state words said cancelled reads `incomplete`. That sentence is corrected and `stopped` has its own line.

Same drive on both binaries, both built with `make build`: one `/task` that splits into parts, stopped from the conversation 40 seconds in through the stop card, then the run's page opened by a press on its row on the side list.

| `incomplete` on the run's page | 12 | 0 |
| parts under the run | `incomplete · Implement Mul` and so on | `stopped · Add Mul function with tests` and so on |
| landed in the folder | nothing | nothing |

On the final head `d28971eb6`, which sits on #1255, the same drive was run once more: the stopped run's page head reads `stopped · 2 steps · $0.02`, and `incomplete` is nowhere on the page.

Every drive removed its key copy first, ended the engine it started by socket holder and executable equality, and removed its home. No drive folder was left behind.

## What a person saw

Every step a run's worker recorded was drawn on its task page as typed. On a real run most rows began with a change into the run's own copy, and about a third of the rows were the run updating its own record. The work was hard to find among them.

## What changes

- A step row leaves out a leading change into the run's own copy.
- It leaves out any part of the command addressed only to the run's own record, together with whatever that part is piped through.
- A step with nothing else in it has no row. Every other row keeps the number its step ran as, so the numbers can skip and the head's step count stays true.
- Everything kept is drawn exactly as it was typed. A command with nothing left out is drawn whole.
- The recorded command is untouched and is still the record.

## How

- **One reader of command boundaries.** `internal/approval` already owned the reader of where one command ends and the next begins. It now hands out each part with the span it was typed in. The session asks it, and the earlier private splitter is gone.
- **The surface cuts, it never retypes.** Parts cross the wire with their spans, and the surface cuts left-out spans from the recorded line.
- **A part is marked only where cutting is safe.** It must stand in sequence with its neighbours. A part inside a substitution or a group is never marked. A pipeline is one command: it is left out whole when its first part is addressed to the record, and work piped into a record command is never left out.
- **The run's copy is the belt run's own.** A folder directly under the conversation's folder of copies also counts, because an ended run's copy has been given back while its steps still name it. A folder further down is the work. The row's `Folder` keeps the meaning a landed test pins.

## Where this came from

Two cells built most of this and neither brought it home. The first ended on the rig's wall and the second on its checker cap, both with their commits in the run's cut copy. Both sets were recovered by hand. One recovered commit moved a law test in `cmd/codeaf` outside the cell's fence and is dropped.

The hosted review of the recovered work found three faults, fixed here by hand:

- The surface rebuilt a command from trimmed parts. A line with nothing left out drew `ls;go test ./...&&go vet ./...` for a command typed with spaces, and a line ending inside a substitution lost its closing bracket.
- Rows were renumbered to close the gaps, so a page headed `12 steps` drew rows 1 to 6.
- Two shipped manual sentences were reworded and the new section sat under a heading the manual's search does not index. The shipped sentences are restored and there is one `## ` section with two probes.

## Hosted acceptance, real binary, on the Linux test box

`scripts/hosted-drive.sh` against `bin/codeaf` built with `make build` at the final head `1ec367172`, which sits on #1255: ALL PASS, exit 0, fourteen checks. The first run's page, as drawn:

```

 1  pwd && ls -la && echo "---GO FILES---" && find . -name '*.go' -type f | head -50
 2  echo "=== calc.go ===" && cat calc.go && echo "=== go.mod ===" && cat go.mod && …
 3  cat > muldiv.go <<'EOF' …
 4  cat muldiv.go && echo "=== status ===" && git status --short
 7  echo "=== show t-1 ===" && echo "=== show t-2 ==="
```

Steps 5 and 6 were the run's own bookkeeping and have no row. Rows keep their recorded numbers. No row names the run's copy or the record. Every command keeps the spacing it was typed with. On trunk the same page drew `cd <the run's copy> && go test ./... -v` and four rows of record commands.

Every drive removed its key copy first, ended the engine it started by socket holder and executable equality, and removed its home.

**One limit, stated plainly.** The dim line under a row is the head of everything that command printed. Row 7 above had two record commands cut from its middle, and the line under it is what those printed. Cutting a command's output to match is a separate change.

Two other things on these pages are trunk's and not this change, and each has its own cell running: a call the belt refused is drawn as a step with the refusal's sentence under it, and step numbers restart at 1 where a worker is woken again.

body:
## What
`startStandingTicks` launched a process-global endless ticker via a package `sync.Once`, and `closeAll` never stopped or joined it. After Close returned, the next pass created files under `<home>/v3/standing` (and appended `standing.log`), a writer outliving the process that left `<home>/v3` non-empty (the `<tmp>/v3 directory not empty` leftover class).

## Fix
The ticker is owned by `v3Process`: stop and done channels taken under `p.mu`, a select loop that exits on stop, and `closeAll` calls `stopStandingTicks` (closes stop, waits on done). The package `sync.Once` is removed, so a later process in the same test binary starts its own ticker. Behavior preserved: same interval, silence, at-most-once per process, ErrHeld silence.

## Interaction with #1250's settle-at-stop path (asked at review)
No adverse interaction. `closeAll` calls `stopStandingTicks` AFTER `stopPoolErrands` and BEFORE the agent-close loop where #1250's settle path runs. `stopStandingTicks` takes `p.mu` only briefly to lift the stop/done channels, then waits on `<-done` OUTSIDE the lock, so it neither runs concurrently with nor shares a lock with the main-agent settle path; the standing pass builds a separate standing session, not one of `p.agents`. Worst case, closeAll waits one bounded standing TickWindow for an in-flight pass, which is the intended no-writer-outlives-close guarantee.

## Verification (Spark, off eae7055ed, all via scripts/one-suite.sh for the heavy suite)
- Focused new test `TestCloseAllJoinsStandingTickerAndLaterProcessCanStart` `-count=8`: pass (zero writes under `<home>/v3/standing` after Close; second process starts its ticker).
- Whole `cmd/codeaf` + `internal/standing` `-count=5` under the one-suite lock: ok (459s, 0 FAIL).
- `go build ./...`; `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` (empty); `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`; `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` (ok). No em dash.

## Flake note
One earlier cmd/codeaf failure occurred on the prior base via a direct `go test` at load ~26 (not through one-suite); its goroutine dump pointed at chat.go:4622, the design-intentional detached worker-leaf flush goroutine, not this change's standing/close path. It did not recur across 5 one-suite runs on eae7055ed, and this change's own close-path tests pass 5x.
title: fix(chatv3): stop and join the standing ticker on process close

## What was wrong

The side list's rows of a run were read inside the freshness check that every drawing path comes through. So a frame asked the engine for them. Three things made that read due, and each made it from a frame:

- the first reading of a conversation
- a row of this window's own graph moving, which includes every verb that lands on a run's page
- the run's three second beat

In a hosted conversation that read is a call to another process with a ten second deadline. A frame that waits on it holds every key a person presses. An earlier cell moved the beat's read off the frame and left the other two. The law that keeps engine calls off the update loop never reported any of this, because it could not see a call reached through the surface's own plan reading.

## What changed

- The run's rows are held on the surface and asked for after a message, one read at a time, beside the ordered line. The frame re-files what is held and asks the engine nothing.
- What makes a read due is unchanged. A conversation at rest still reads nothing.
- A verb that lands while a read is out is answered by exactly one more read.
- Opening the run's tab used to read the rows and the run's page on the key press itself. It opens on the held rows and asks for the page through the one door every stored page already arrives through.
- The off-loop law now counts the plan reading as handing the agent back, so every plan call is under the law. The rows read is named in the ledger of reads asked beside the line, with its reason.
- The named budget of calls still made from the loop does not drop. The rows read was never in that budget, because the law could not see it. What changes is that the blind spot is closed.
- The hosted drive script opens the side list with its own key when the copied profile starts a conversation with it hidden. Without that, every side list check fails on the Linux test box on any binary, trunk included.

## Measured, on the Linux test box

The real remote client and a real engine, with 250 ms injected on the run's row read. Each trigger is raised and the very next frame is timed.

| what made the read due | trunk `eae7055ed`, frame | reads inside that frame | this branch, frame | reads inside that frame |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| first reading of the conversation | 258.1 ms | 1 | 0.7 ms | 0 |
| a row of this window's own graph moved | 254.2 ms | 1 | 0.1 ms | 0 |
| the run's beat came due | 256.6 ms | 1 | 0.1 ms | 0 |
| the chat was renamed | 0.2 ms | 0 | 0.2 ms | 0 |

The rows are held in both arms after the message that follows.

## Hosted acceptance, real binary, on the Linux test box

`scripts/hosted-drive.sh` against `bin/codeaf` built with `make build` at `27ca2daf5`: ALL PASS, exit 0. Fourteen checks, including the second hand-off showing on the side list, no row still running after the run ends, and a press on the first run's row opening its page.

The same drive against trunk `eae7055ed` passed the side list checks and failed two page checks in its one run, because the page it opened drew no `brief` line on its first screen. I did not chase that; it is one run and it is not this change.

Every drive removed its key copy first, ended the engine it started by socket holder and executable equality, and removed its home. The folders a failed drive leaves for reading were checked for a key copy, held none, and were removed.

## Tests

- New, on the real wire with reads counted: no frame path reads the rows under any of the four triggers, and the message after each costs exactly one read where one is owed.
- New: while a read is out the frame draws what it held, no second read is asked, and a stamp that moved in the meantime costs exactly one further read.
- Tests that called the freshness check and expected fresh rows now fold the read first, the way a window does after a message.
- Two tests that count every command or every call over the wire take their count after the window's first rows read.

## Suites, on the Linux test box at `eaf4ee6bc`

| what | exit |

| whole `internal/tui3`, under the box's one-suite lock, 324 s | 0 |
| `internal/manual`, `guard`, `namelaw`, `iconlaw`, `e2e` | 0 |

| `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` | 0, no lines |
| `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/tui3` | 0 |

## What
`make check` (vet fmt-check test test-packed-manual size) never cross-compiled, so a platform-specific undefined symbol compiled clean on the host and surfaced only at nightly/release. New `build-cross` target cross-compiles every shipped platform, compile only, and is wired into `check`.

## How
- Reads the platform list straight from `.github/workflows/release.yml` (the release source of truth), so it tracks the shipped set with NO GOOS/GOARCH names hardcoded in the Makefile. Current set: darwin/amd64, darwin/arm64, linux/amd64, linux/arm64, windows/amd64, windows/arm64.
- `CGO_ENABLED=0 GOOS=.. GOARCH=.. go build ./...` per target, compile only (no tests, no packing).
- The six builds share the normal GOCACHE, so a warm box pays little.
- Prints its own duration, rounded up as an upper bound, and names the target it FAILED on (not just a non-zero exit).

## Cost (measured on Spark)
- Warm (shared GOCACHE): ~11s added to make check.
- Cold (empty cache): ~111s (upper bound; a fresh box only).

## What was wrong

Every ask the surface makes of its engine stood in one ordered line, so the engine sees a person's gestures in the order they were made. The run's summary stood in that line too, and the summary asks a model with a ten second budget. A press made while a summary was out waited behind it.

Separately, an open task page asked for its page again from the paint clock: about six reads a second over the wire for as long as the page was open, ended tasks included.

## What changed

Two commits, each with a failing test first.

1. **Nothing a person did not press stands in the ordered line.** A second road off the update loop, `besideLine`, asks on its own goroutine and folds the same way. Its property: a read nobody pressed for, where nothing a person does next depends on the engine having seen it first. The run's summary is its one caller. A ledger law (`doorsBesideTheLine`, `TestOnlyReadsNobodyPressedForAreAskedBesideTheLine`) lists every caller, and the structural law that keeps engine doors off the loop accepts both roads.
2. **An open page reads on a beat.** Once per three second beat, counted from the last page read, and only while the task is queued or running. A page on an ended task is read once, to open it. The follow stays in the ordered line, because its answer replaces the page and a note re-reads the page too.

## Who stands in the ordered line

Autonomy reads and writes, the replay on attach, the gestures that resolve a question, the plan's spend, the plan verbs, a note, and page reads. Of all of them only the run's summary was a model call or had a budget in seconds. One more finding is not in this PR: the tasks place reads the plan synchronously on the frame.
