## What was wrong

With the belt on, nothing a person pressed could stop a run. Measured on the real binary, hosted, at trunk 12840eeb5 on 2026-09-19:

| gesture | what happened | count |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `x` over an empty box, then `stop it` on the card | `there is no task 1 in this session`; the run carried on and landed by itself | 4 of 4 |
| `x stop it` on the run's own page | `the harness owns the root task` | every time |
| `p pause` on the run's own page | `the harness owns the root task` | every time |

Cause, read in the code. A run's rows wear task numbers and are not in the task graph, and the stop a surface sends for a row is `task:N`, which only the graph answered. The run was started on a context nothing could cut, and no cancel was kept anywhere. The store refuses every verb on the run's own task for every caller, and the page offered two of them.

## What changed

**The store** (`internal/plandb`). `StopRoot` is the runtime's verb for a person's word. It ends the run's own task and every task still open in one write, and leaves ended tasks as they ended. A run left open in its store is adopted by the next hand-off, so a stop has to be written there.

**The session.** The id a surface already sends is resolved to whoever owns the row: the live run first, the graph second. Nothing on the wire changes, so a window built before this change stops a run through an engine built after it, and the model's own stop ends a run too. A stop goes in this order: the store first, so no part reads as a failure and the next hand-off cannot adopt the run; the context next, so every worker and every call it has out ends now; the work last, committed on the run's own branch with the copy given back. Nothing is merged into the folder and no model turn is bought to narrate the ending. A stop on a row that joined a run ends that work only. The page's stop on the run's own task is the same stop, and on a run nobody is running any more it ends the run in the store.

**The surface.** `x` on the run's own page raises the stop card, and the page steps aside for it the way a background job's page does. `p pause` is not offered under the run's own task and is a letter there. `ctrl+c` is read before a page that is on its way and before the page. Every ending of the page's read ends the key hold, including an answer for a tab the person has left. That read is already bounded by the wire's own call deadline, which answers no page. A key that leaves the page ends the replay, so `x` typed while the run's own page opens reaches the card.

**What a person is told.** On the run's page and once in the conversation:

```
stopped · its work so far is kept on <branch> and did not go into <folder> · merge that branch to bring it in, or delete it to drop it
```

A run stopped before it changed anything says `stopped · it had changed nothing`, and then neither the sentence nor the row names a branch.

**No further model call.** A surface asks for a run's four-line summary again whenever its rows move, and a stop moves them. The engine declines a summary for a run a person stopped; the last reading stands.

## Two laws

- `internal/session`: every function that publishes a row in a state a stop means something in is listed with the cancel kind that reaches its owner and the test that proves it by stopping one. A new publisher fails the law until it has both. I removed the run's entry to check it: the law named `startKnownTaskRun` and its line.
- `internal/tui3`: for every kind of row a run's store can hold, every verb word the foot offers is pressed against a real store over the real wire, and none may be refused. I put `p pause` back under the run's own task to check it: the law quoted the store's refusal.

## Not in this change

`ctrl+c`, `/quit` and a closed window do not stop a run today: the window closes, the run carries on in the engine and its work lands by itself. Measured three of three for each at 12840eeb5, and ten of ten in a separate reproduction with the terminal killed under the window. That is unchanged here. It is a separate open question and not a regression of this change.

## Hosted acceptance, real binary, belt on

Nine drives at 8ca974cb4, the same code without the summary commit, then eight ledger probes on the later heads.

| path | card raised | row out of `running` after `stop it` | landed in the folder | copy given back | work on the kept branch |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `x` in the conversation | 3 of 3 | 0.26, 0.27, 0.27 s | 0 of 3 | 3 of 3 | 26, 14 and 8 files |
| `x` on the run's own page | 3 of 3 | 0.27, 0.27, 0.54 s | 0 of 3 | 3 of 3 | 18, 14 and 22 files |
| `x` typed in the page-load gap | 3 of 3 | 0.27, 0.26, 0.26 s | 0 of 3 | 3 of 3 | 6, 6 and 12 files |

Child pids: the engine's pid and its child pids were recorded before each stop. Five drives had no child alive at that instant and four had one shell child. Every recorded pid was gone after the stop, and the engine had no children, nine of nine.

Page foot on the run's own task, every page drive: `↑↓ scroll · enter send · x stop it · esc back`.

Usage ledger rows stamped after the stop instant, read 60 s after it:

| head | path | rows before | rows after |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| f55c27ebe | conversation | 4 | 0 |
| f55c27ebe | page, three probes | 4, 3, 3 | 1, 1, 1 |
| f55c27ebe | gap | 2 | 0 |
| cdd8e777a | page, three probes | 5, 12, 9 | 0, 1, 0 |
| cdd8e777a | conversation | 6 | 0 |
| cdd8e777a | gap | 6 | 0 |

No billed row was ever stamped after a stop. The one kind of row that was is a marker, not a call: a model name, `unbilled: true`, no dollars, no tokens, no role, about 20.5 s after the stop. The engine writes it when it looks up the receipt of a call whose stream ended before its usage block and finds none. A stop cuts a call mid-stream, so the marker is the bookkeeping of a call that began before the stop and was cut by it. I first read it as a new summary call. The summary commit is still right, because a test shows the engine did make that call when asked, twice, and now makes none. It is not what the marker is, and the body says so rather than claim zero.

**The day figure on screen lags by a beat.** In one drive it moved after a stop. The ledger had no row for that; it was earlier spend drawn late. Nobody should read that figure as spend after a stop.

One drive took 7.09 s for the row to leave `running`, with a shell child alive at the stop. The row says `running` for that time. A small follow-up branch gives the row the `stopping` reading a stopped task already has; it is not in this PR so this head stays the one that was proven.

All drives used a throwaway home with private permissions. Each removed the key copy first, ended its own engine by socket holder and executable equality, then removed the home. No drive home remains.

How "the worker is gone and the spend has ended" is checked. The worker is not a process: it is a goroutine in the engine, and its steps are short-lived shell children. So each drive records the engine's pid and its child pids before the stop, and checks those pids are gone after it. Spend is read from the usage ledger's rows stamped after the stop instant. The day figure on screen is drawn on a beat and can show earlier spend late, so it is not the evidence.

## Proof

- Head aad44e486 sits on #1251's head bd0c2af56. It is cdd8e777a plus one line in the change entry.
- Spark, tree at cdd8e777a, under the one-suite lock: whole `internal/tui3` exit 0 in 324 s, whole `internal/session` exit 0 in 246 s.
- Spark, same tree: `internal/plandb`, `internal/run`, `internal/manual`, `internal/guard`, `internal/namelaw` ok; `make test-laws` exit 0; `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` empty.
- Failing tests first, each seen red with the sentence from the real screen: `there is no task 71 in this session`, `the harness owns the root task`, the foot offering `p pause`, `ctrl+c` held with the page's keys, the hold left standing, two summary calls after a stop.
- Manual: two new sections in `worker-harness.md` with three probes, and the sentence about the run's own task in `task-controls.md`. The store's old refusal is no longer quoted as the answer.

## What

Test only. `TestJobShellEnvCannotReachTheHostTmux` and `TestBackgroundJobShellCannotReachTheHostTmux` (internal/exec/tmuxenv_test.go) now assert on a single marker line instead of dumping and parsing the whole environment.

## Why

runShell and the background job log are captured through a capped output collector (preview budget). A full `env` dump overflows that preview on a machine with a large ambient environment, so the TMUX_TMPDIR line is cut off and the test reads it as absent although the job shell had it. That failed the foreground test on macOS (large ambient env) while passing on Spark (small env), and it made the TMUX and TMUX_PANE checks pass vacuously on any large env, since absence in a truncated dump proves nothing.

Confirmed on Darwin with an uncapped tee: the full env output was 25264 bytes but the captured preview was 4234, and the full output did contain TMUX_TMPDIR at the private dir. So the product was already correct; only the test could not see it.

## Fix

Both tests ask the job shell to print exactly the three variables on one short line, `JOBTMUX TMUX=[...] TMUX_PANE=[...] TMUX_TMPDIR=[...]`, with an explicit `unset` marker for any that is absent, through the same bash login path the product runs. The shared helper fails if the marker line is missing from the captured output, so a future truncation can never read as a pass. One short line always fits the preview.

## Scope note (capped-collector class)

A grep of internal/exec test files found no other test asserting on a full environment or other large dump whose asserted line position depends on ambient size; the rest assert on short, deterministic outputs (printf of a known string). The two fixed here are in the same file. The repo-wide capped-collector class is being swept by a separate cell.

## Verification

Darwin (macOS laptop), one focused test each: both PASS. Spark: whole internal/exec through scripts/one-suite.sh (green), plus `go build ./...`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` (empty), `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`, `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw`.

## Related

Supersedes the c316 approach (a product change based on a login-shell-clears theory that does not hold on macOS); this is the real cause and a test-only fix.
title: test(exec): read the job shell tmux floor by a marker line, not a full env dump

body:
## What

`writeProfileValues` (internal/config/budget.go) now takes a cross-process exclusive lock on a stable `config.json.lock` across the whole read-copy-rename, inside the existing in-process `profileWriteMu` (mutex outer, file lock inner). New `internal/config/profilelock.go` wraps `internal/filelock` (cross-platform Lock/IsBusy) with a bounded 2s wait built from IsBusy polling, so no second lock primitive is introduced.

## Why

Two codeaf processes writing config.json at once, a person running chats side by side, each read the file, add their own key, and rename; the later rename discarded the other's key, so a setting saved in one chat silently vanished. #1242 serialized concurrent writers within one process; this closes the cross-process case a person actually hits.

## Lock semantics

- Bounded wait: 2 seconds of IsBusy polling, then a plain `timed out` error, so a write never hangs a chat.
- No stale lock: the hold lives in the OS lock on the open file, released on close and, on a crash, when the OS closes the dead process's descriptor. The `.lock` file is never unlinked.
- Cross-platform: taken through internal/filelock, which the repo already ships for unix and Windows.

## Test

A forced two-process test re-execs the test binary twice, holds both at a real-flock barrier until both are contending, then shows both keys survive. A second test shows the 2s timeout; a third shows recovery after a holder crashes. These forced tests are `//go:build unix` (they build the barrier with flock); Windows recovery is by handle close, provided by internal/filelock. The test states which platforms it proves.

## Verification

`go build ./...` (linux), `GOOS=windows go build ./internal/config` AND `GOOS=windows go build ./...` (both pass; this is the check that catches the undefined symbol), `go test ./internal/config -count=5` (ok, includes the two-process/timeout/crash tests), `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` (empty), `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`, `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw`, all green on Spark.

## Gate gap noted

`make check` is `vet fmt-check test test-packed-manual size`; it does NOT cross-compile Windows (cross builds are staging/nightly per the Makefile), so the Spark gate would not catch a Windows-only undefined symbol. This PR was verified with an explicit `GOOS=windows` build. A build-only cross-compile step for the platforms the repo ships (read from the release config, no hardcoded names) is worth a separate small PR.

## Related

Reworked from the cross-process profile-lock cell, which first shipped a unix-only flock that broke the Windows build and duplicated internal/filelock. This is the cross-platform version.
title: config: make a profile write safe across processes with a cross-platform lock

body:
## What

The unread-config-key notice (#1223's load-time log, #1239's chat notice) named top-level `config.json` keys that a shipped version once wrote as a real settings row but that nothing reads at head, telling a person about an ignored key they never typed. Seven such retired keys are now skipped silently.

## The seven retired keys

`linear_mode`, `nerd_font`, `rail_state` (readers removed by 74e16993c), `work.workers` (05b995376), `memory.consolidation` (10dcdfdd4), `practice_demand_pct`, `propose_new_skills` (84ba8503e). Each was a real settings-registry row in a shipped version and is read by nothing at head. A person on an older profile (nerd_font and linear_mode were shipped v3/tui2-era settings) was being told these keys are ignored.

## How

- `retiredProfileKeys` in `internal/config/config.go`, each entry dated by its reader-removal commit; `warnUnreadProfileKeys` skips them silently.
- `consumedProfileKeys` is extracted as the single definition the unread check and the ledger law both read, so the two cannot drift.

## Regression-proof by property, not memory

- `internal/config/testdata/profile-keys.ledger` lists every top-level key the product has ever written (current writers plus the seven retired).
- `TestProfileKeyLedgerLaw`, two halves: (a) every key a current writer can produce is in the ledger; (b) every ledger key is either consumed at head or in `retiredProfileKeys`. Adding a settings row forces a ledger line; removing one leaves its line behind and turns the law red until the key is retired on purpose.
- `TestRetiredProfileKeysAreNotReportedUnread`: each retired key alone is silent, and a genuinely unknown key alongside them is still named.

## Real-binary capture (this branch head)

- profile `{linear_mode, nerd_font, work.workers}`: nothing on screen.
- add a genuinely unknown key: only `genuinely_unknown` is named.

## Method and its blind spot

The seven were found by a static history sweep (c312): grep the settings-registry key literals across the dev history, subtract head's consumed set, confirm each remaining key was a shipped registry row with no reader at head. A key retired BEFORE the settings registry existed would not appear as a registry-row literal, so the sweep would not catch it; such a key is not covered here. The ledger law will still catch any FUTURE writer added or removed.

## Verification (Spark; full package never on the laptop)

- `go build ./...`, `go vet`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` empty
- `internal/guard` + `internal/namelaw` ok
- `internal/config` whole package under the one-suite lock: ok
- `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check` clean (after the pr-number reconcile)

body:
What a person types right after pressing a run's row in the side list now goes to that task's page. Before this, it went to the conversation and was sent to the model.

## What was wrong

A task's page is read off the update loop. On a hosted conversation the answer took 2.4 s on a real screen, and up to 7.7 s under load. Until it arrived the conversation was still drawn and its box still took the keyboard. On the real binary, `keep the examples short` and `enter`, typed at once after the press and meant as a note for the task, was answered by the model and saved as a standing preference nobody asked for.

## What changed

- **The gap's keys belong to the page.** From the press on, keys are kept in order and handed to the page's own keyboard when it opens, `enter` included. `esc` withdraws the press. A second press replaces the first. A row that turns out to have no page opens its room as before, and those keys are dropped.
- **The stop card stands down while a page is on its way.** Its key is read above every page. With a task running, a note holding that letter still raised the card in the gap and lost the rest. This was found at review with a failing test first and is the same class as the fault #1240 fixed for a page that is already up.
- **Manual.** The section on opening a run's task from the side list says the page can take a moment and what happens to keys meanwhile.

The first two commits are the cell's. The third closes the stop card hole and documents the pending state.

## Hosted drive on the real binary

`bin/codeaf chat` from this branch, hosted as it runs by default, throwaway home and repository, 2026-09-19.

1. Handed off one task. Pressed its row on the side list, then typed `keep the examples short` and `enter` at once, with no wait.
2. The page drew with:
   ```
    notes
    you · now
    keep the examples short
   ```
3. Back in the conversation there was no message and no reply. The words exist in the run's record and nowhere else under the conversation's folder.

## Where the seconds go, measured

A temporary timer on the ordered door line, removed before this commit, on the same drive:

| Door | Asked | Took |
| --- | --- | --- |
| The page's read | once | 2 ms, after waiting 7586 ms in line |
| The run's summary | once | 10002 ms |
| The open page's follow | 509 times in about 90 s | 2 ms each |

The wire, the store read and the fold are two milliseconds together. The wait is one door: the run's summary asks a model with a ten second budget on the same ordered line as a person's gestures, so a press made meanwhile waits behind it. That is its own change and follows this one. The follow reading about six times a second is reported separately.

## Proof

Laptop, this head: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/tui3`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` clean. `make test-focus PKGS=./internal/tui3 RUN='Rail|Plan|Page|Note|Stop|Frame|Hosted|Manual|Work'` ok. `make test-laws` ok. `go test ./internal/e2e/ ./internal/iconlaw/ ./internal/manual/ ./internal/namelaw/` ok. `make changelog-check` ok. tui3 only: no session, prompt or schema change.

## What

`writeProfileValues` (internal/config/budget.go) reads config.json, copies in the update, marshals, and renames a temp file over it. A process-wide `profileWriteMu` now holds the whole read-copy-rename as one transaction, and update values are marshaled before the lock so a user-defined marshaler never runs inside the profile critical section.

## Why

Two goroutines in one process that both read config.json before either rename lose one update: the later rename discards the earlier writer's key. Serializing the transaction makes concurrent writers in one process compose.

## Scope, said plainly

This composes concurrent callers of `writeProfileValue` / `writeProfileValues` inside ONE process. Today's callers are settings writers that mostly run one at a time, so this hardens the writer against concurrent use rather than fixing a known concurrent caller. It makes no claim across processes: two codeaf processes writing config.json at once (chats side by side) still rely on the atomic rename to avoid partial JSON, and the cross-process lost update remains open. That cross-process case is being addressed separately.

## Verification

`go test ./internal/config -count=20` (ok, 69.9s), `go build ./...`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` (empty), `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`, `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw`, all green on Spark. `TestConcurrentProfileWritesCompose` forces both writers past the profile read before either rename with blocking JSON marshalers and asserts both keys survive; it fails without the mutex.
title: config: concurrent profile writes in one process compose

Adds `scripts/hosted-drive.sh`, a repeatable drive of a run on the real binary in hosted mode. It is the acceptance a person would do by hand, written down so anyone can repeat it.

**Lands after #1234.** Phase 3 asserts that an earlier run stays readable, which #1234 brings. On this trunk without it, phase 3 fails and phases 1 and 2 pass.

## What it does

```
make build
scripts/hosted-drive.sh bin/codeaf
```

It opens `codeaf chat` in a tmux server of its own, with a throwaway home and a throwaway repository. It types three hand-offs and reads the screen and the folder back. It prints PASS or FAIL per check and exits with the number that failed. A failed check keeps the screen it judged.

The fifteen checks, in a person's words, are in the script's header. In short:

1. **The run works in a copy of its own.** Your folder holds only your own unsaved file while it works.
2. **Its work comes home.** One new commit, your file untouched, the copy given back, no task branch, the card says merged, nothing still running.
3. **An earlier run stays readable.** Its record is kept, a press on its row opens its page with no id of the record's own, a note on it is answered in words, and esc returns to your draft.

## What it is careful about

- It makes real model calls, so it is wired into no make target.
- It never writes to your own home's state. It copies the profile's config file if there is one and otherwise relies on the key in the environment.
- It ends only its own tmux server, by its own socket name. It selects no process by command-line text.
- It removes only the folders it made, and only when everything passed.
- `shellcheck` is clean. One info class is disabled with its reason: the checks are functions handed by name.

## Proof

ALL PASS, 15 of 15, on the real binary built from the merge of 4e176a59a, #1232, #1234 and #1240, on 2026-09-19. `shellcheck scripts/hosted-drive.sh` exits 0. `go test ./internal/namelaw/` and `make changelog-check` ok. No Go change.

Follow-up to #1231. Four things a run task's page said that were not true, each with a failing test first.

## What changed

- **An ended task is offered no refused verb.** A `done` or `incomplete` task's row and page name no `x stop it` and no `p pause`. The store refuses both.
- **A note's author is a word a person knows, or nothing.** A note you left reads `you`. Any other note names no author. The page test now asserts that no id of the store's appears anywhere on the page.
- **An ended task's page promises no next step.** The sentence `the worker reads a note at its next step` is absent once the task has ended. One helper answers "has this task ended" for the key line and for that sentence.
- **A letter typed into the note is a letter.** The stop card's key is read above every page. The page opened from the side list sits over a conversation whose own box is empty, so a note holding that letter raised the card mid-word and the card swallowed the rest. A run task's page is now on the card's precedence list wherever it was opened from. The page still reads the key itself over an empty box. This fault came in with #1231 and was found by the hosted drive below, not by a test.

## Hosted drive on the real binary

`bin/codeaf chat` from this branch, hosted as it runs by default, throwaway home and repository, run switch on, 2026-09-19.

1. Handed off one task with `/task`. Clicked its `#1` row on the side list. The page drew over the conversation.
2. Typed `keep the examples short` and pressed enter while the task ran. Before the fix the box held `keep the e` and the store held no note. After it the page shows:
   ```
    notes
    you · now
    keep the examples short
   ```
   and the foot reads `the worker reads a note at its next step` over `↑↓ scroll · enter send · x stop it · p pause · esc back`.
3. Waited for the task to end. The same page's foot reads `↑↓ scroll · enter send · esc back`, with no sentence about a next step.

body:
## What

A chat conversation now shows a one-time notice when `config.json` carries top-level keys that no reader consumes, naming them, in both hosted and `--no-host` mode. Before this, the unread-key finding added in #1223 went only to process logs that a chat user never sees.

## Why

`config.json` is a flat dotted-key map. A nested block like `{"models":{"tiers":{...}}}` or a mistyped dotted key reads as all-unset, silently, and every affected setting falls to a shipped default with nothing on screen saying why. The log line #1223 added lands in a per-profile file (chat) or `host.log` (hosted), neither of which a person reads.

## How

- **Single source of truth.** `config.warnUnreadProfileKeys` now returns the sorted unread-key list (the once-per-process log is unchanged); `Config.UnreadProfileKeys` carries it. The notice never classifies keys a second way.
- **Both transports converge on `newApp` -> `showUnreadProfileKeys`:**
  - `--no-host`: `settings` -> `v3Process` -> `runSurface(tui3.Options)`.
  - hosted: `proc` -> `bootEngine` -> `remote.Engine` -> `Welcome.UnreadProfileKeys` wire field -> client `hostOptions` -> `tui3.Options` (engine and surface are separate processes, so the list must cross the wire).
- **Gate.** The existing `noticeBoard`/`noticeLedger`, key `unread-profile-config-keys-<sha256 of the sorted keys>`. Shown once per profile; re-shows only when the unread set changes.

## Real-binary hosted acceptance (real engine + client, default hosted mode)

Captured from a build of this branch head, `codeaf chat` (hosted; a daemon spawned), throwaway profiles:

| Scenario | On screen |
|---|---|
| nested `{"models":{"tiers":{"reflex":...}}}`, first launch | `config.json keys are not read: models; anything set under them is ignored and defaults apply.` |
| same profile, second launch | (nothing) |
| same profile after adding a second unread key | `config.json keys are not read: models, workers; anything set under them is ignored and defaults apply.` |
| a correct flat config (`models.tiers.reflex`) | (nothing) |

The wording is general ("anything set under them is ignored and defaults apply") rather than the earlier "models fell back to defaults", which overclaimed for non-model keys: a real profile carries `display.theme`, which no reader consumes. Model config, the motivating case, still reads correctly under this wording.

## Tests

- `internal/config` `TestLoadWarnsOnceForEveryUnreadTopLevelProfileKey`
- `internal/tui3` `TestUnreadProfileKeysNoticeTracksTheSet` (nil silent / named / repeat silent / changed shows / prior silent, across ledger persistence on disk)
- `cmd/codeaf` `TestHostedWelcomeCarriesUnreadProfileKeysToSurface` (a real `remote.Loopback` engine and client carry the list into `hostOptions`; not a fake agent)

## Verification (Spark; full suites never run on the laptop)

- `go build ./...`, `go vet` (scoped), `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal` empty
- the three focused tests plus `internal/guard` and `internal/namelaw`: all ok
- `internal/session` full package under the one-suite lock: PASS
- `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`: clean
- the real-binary hosted captures above

Base: 4e176a59a.


## No product-written key is ever flagged (review follow-up)

`display.theme` (seen on one Spark profile) was never written by the product: its only trace in history is a comment in `internal/tui3/styles.go` showing `settings.Get("display.theme")` as an example. It was never a settings row and is never persisted, so that key was hand-added, and the notice correctly names a genuinely unread key. Santosh's live laptop profile (its exact top-level keys) yields no notice. `TestNoShippedWriterKeyIsReportedUnread` locks the property: a profile of every settings-registry row plus every non-setting field the loader writes has an empty unread list, so the notice can never flag a key a person never typed.
title: chat: name unread config.json keys once before defaults apply

body:
## What

The leaf-end survivor test now identifies a survivor by process identity, not a bare PID. After leaf teardown it reports a survivor only when the PID is still live and its start time matches the one captured while the survivor was proven running; a missing PID, or a recycled PID that now denotes a different process, is a settled success.

## Why

The test asserted a survivor lived by probing kill(pid, 0) on a bare integer PID. After cmd.Wait reaps the original process, Linux can reuse that PID for an unrelated process, so the probe succeeds and falsely reports the original survived ("process N survived leaf end"). This is a test-side observation hole, not a product leak: product close cannot return while a job's waiter is unsettled, the waiter cannot settle before cmd.Wait reaps the recorded shell leader, and product signaling uses the captured group identity with an ownership check, never a bare PID. The false positive is reachable only in the assertion.

## Verification

A forced-ordering reproduction (a probe seam that returns success only after the real kill(pid, 0) reported the original gone) made the false positive deterministic; the identity-aware assertion then passes 20 of 20 focused runs while still failing on a real survivor whose PID and start time both match. The fix reuses the existing production ProcessStartTime helper, with no second identity scheme. build, go test ./internal/exec, gofmt, codeaf-changes, guard and namelaw all pass. Test-only, no change entry.
title: test(exec): identify a leaf-end survivor by process identity, not a bare PID

body:
## What

The internal/connect tests that prove begin-auth falls through to the second door no longer bind the machine-global fixed ports. During those tests the package address list is swapped for test-owned dynamic loopback listeners and the busy-first-door condition is forced in-process, so the anchor test and its two neighbors assert the second-door behavior without competing for 8765 or 18765.

## Why

8765 is real product code, the preferred fixed callback with an 18765 and then an ephemeral fallback, so any unrelated process holding it could fail or stall these tests, and the heavy-suite lock cannot cover a holder that is not one of our suites. The product does not require that exact port for the behavior under test, so the tests use dynamic ports and force the busy-first-door condition themselves. The production address order and binding path are unchanged.

## Verification

go test ./internal/connect passes and no test binds 8765 or 18765. build, gofmt, codeaf-changes, guard and namelaw all pass. Test-only, no change entry.
title: test(connect): the second-door tests use dynamic ports, not the fixed callback ports

body:
## What

A reconnect no longer introduces the identity a second time when it can reuse the one it already registered. On reconnect the manager reads the saved registration and tries its loopback redirect before the ordinary listener candidates; when that address is free the reconnect serves on the redirect the service already knows, so the identity check passes and no second introduction is issued. The fixed listener candidates and their order are unchanged.

## Why

After a first connection persisted its registration on a fallback ephemeral redirect (both fixed ports were busy), a disconnect kept the registration but a reconnect could bind a different ephemeral redirect. mcpRegistration.fits then rejected the saved identity, because the service was never told the new redirect, and the reconnect issued a second real registration request: codeaf introduced itself twice where once was wanted (mcp_auth_test.go:283). This is a real reconnect path, not a test counting artifact; the fake counts only requests to its own registration endpoint.

## Verification

A forced-ordering regression injects preselected listeners at the listener.New seam so the initial connection and the sequential reconnect receive distinct ephemeral redirects; on the base the reconnect introduces a second time, with the fix it reuses the saved redirect and introduces once. go test ./internal/connect passes; the fixed-port constants and selection order are untouched. build, gofmt, codeaf-changes, guard and namelaw all pass.

## Releasing the callback listener before a reconnect (follow-up)

Reusing the saved redirect first is not enough on its own. The callback listener was torn down by a fire-and-forget goroutine on the flow's context, and Flow.finish signaled done before that shutdown had closed it, so Flow.Wait could return while the saved loopback port was still bound. A reconnect that followed at once then found the port busy and, through the product's listener.New falling through to the next candidate, bound a fresh redirect and introduced the identity again. beginToolServer now captures when server.Serve returns and the flow's completion cancels its context and waits for that return before reporting done, bounded by the graceful shutdown's own timeout, so a finished flow has released its callback listener and a reconnect finds the saved port free. TestAFinishedFlowReleasesItsCallbackListenerBeforeItReportsDone gates the listener close open and proves Flow.Wait does not report done until the listener is released; without the wait it fails by construction. internal/connect passed through one-suite at -count=20.
title: fix(connect): a reconnect reuses its registered identity instead of introducing itself again

body:
## What this changes

A wait whose stream has stopped arriving paints at the spinner's cadence instead of thirty
frames a second. `internal/tui3/app.go` gains `streamFresh()`, which reports whether a
delta has landed within `streamFreshFor` (250 ms), and `paint()` multiplies the frame
interval by `spinnerStep` when the only live term is the wait on the model and the stream
has gone quiet. Animations that count in paints land exactly where they would have at full
cadence, one stride at a time. Any other liveness term, or a stream still arriving, keeps
the full cadence. 31 lines.

It also adds `bench/idle-surface/`, the harness and the measurements that found it.

## The claim, and its exact scope

**This changes the WAIT path only: a turn in flight with no delta arriving.** It does not
touch idle at rest, and the numbers below are not interchangeable with each other.

Three idle figures exist and they differ, because they measure different states on
different profiles:

| state | figure | profile | mode |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| settled, nothing in flight | 0.8 to 1.1 percent of a core, flat at K=5, 50, 200 | pinned FRESH | suppressed host |
| turn in flight, no delta arriving | 3 to 6 percent of a core | pinned FRESH | suppressed host |
| settled, on the operator's own live profile | 1.92 percent of a core, and the resident set never settled | operator's live profile | hosted, 2 processes and a daemon |

**Idle at rest on the operator's live profile is open and unexplained.** It is not what
this changes, and cell c300 is investigating it separately. Nothing here should be read as
addressing it.

### Before and after on the wait path

| point | before, percent of one core | after | saving | ranges |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `5:stream`, both windows held open by a slow stream | 1.639 (pairs 1.600 to 1.667) | 1.033 (1.033 to 1.034) | 0.61 pp | disjoint |
| `5:nodelta`, the held wait, window 1 | 2.589 (2.467 to 2.700) | 2.011 (1.967 to 2.067) | 0.58 pp | disjoint |

**The absolute saving is the same 0.6 percentage points of a core in both cases**, which
says more than the two percentages do: what comes off is a fixed cost, not a proportion.

**Why window 1 alone for `5:nodelta`.** Its second window is not a wait. The stub holds the
first delta for 90 s, the hold expires mid-window, and w2 reads 1.0 to 1.17 on BOTH sides
because by then the surface is simply settled, a state this change does not touch.
Averaging it in dilutes the effect. What makes that choice safe rather than convenient is
that **the cell put the same asterisk on its own nodelta rows before any after-figure
existed**, so it was not made by looking at the result. On the two-window mean the same
point reads 1.845 to 1.500, a saving of 0.34 pp, also with disjoint ranges: **the
conclusion holds under either reading.**

Method for those rows: three pairs per point, the ORDER FLIPPED between pairs
(before-after, after-before, before-after), so a monotone load drift pushes both sides the
same way in one pair and opposite ways in the next. Both binaries built with `make build`
in the same tree with only `internal/tui3/app.go` swapped; they are byte-for-byte the same
size, 52,429,065, so the guard is the **sha256 of the file `/proc/<pid>/exe` points at**,
printed per row. A row is VOID rather than absent if the hash is wrong, if the stub saw no
POST, or if no table row appeared. Runs refuse to start above a printed load limit. Load
recorded at both ends of every run.

**Profile for every row above: the pinned FRESH profile plus one key, `daily_budget_usd`.**
See the reproducibility note below for why that key is there.

## Acceptance, and what is not yet done

Measured here, suppressed-host mode: the wait-path figures above. **Not yet measured in
hosted mode**, which is the mode a person runs; a narrow follow-up cell is briefed for it,
because the harness launches `chat --yolo --no-host --max-cost 5`
(`bench/idle-surface/ns-wait.sh:47`) and every figure in `attribution.md` and `results.md`
therefore describes one process with no engine daemon. Its own `results.md` says the daemon
column reads "none" for every point, which is that flag showing through rather than a
property of the product.

`streamFresh()` decides on `lastDelta`: the stream counts as arriving while a delta landed
within the last **250 ms**. The window matters in both directions and is worth reviewing on
that basis: too long and the clock stays slow into resumed text, so the first words of a
reply stutter; too short and a normal inter-delta gap reads as quiet and the clock returns
to full cadence for nothing. Deltas in a working stream land a few hundred milliseconds
apart, so 250 ms sits below the gap that means "stopped" and above the gap that means
"still going", but it is a judgement and not a measurement.

Still to confirm on the real binary with a real engine and client: that the spinner still
moves during a stalled stream, and that when tokens resume the paint returns to full
cadence with no visible lag.

## Reproducibility note, and four explanations that turned out to be wrong

**The measurements in `bench/idle-surface/attribution.md` and `results.md` are real** and
the stub traffic proves it: every one of the cell's runs shows the expected POST count for
its K (6 at K=1, 26 at K=5, 251 at K=50, 1001 at K=200, and 998 to 1004 across the wait
points) with `first_deltas` matching and a pane state word of `working` or `idle` that
exists only on a real chat surface.

**They are not currently reproducible.** Running the committed harness with the recorded
binary commit and the pinned profile, on a quiet box, produces no rows at all: the surface
stops on the first-run settings screen, the harness polls 300 times at 0.5 s for the
composer, never finds it, falls out of the loop with no failure branch, logs `surface up`
as though it had, and types a turn into a settings page. Adding `daily_budget_usd` to the
profile fixes it, which is why the rows above carry that key.

Why the cell did not need that key is **unknown**. Four explanations were tested and
withdrawn, recorded here so nobody spends the time again:

- **Machine load.** Wrong: it fails identically on a quiet box at load 3.07.
- **The rebase onto newer trunk.** Wrong: the four files that decide first-run are
  byte-identical between the cell's commit and trunk.
- **The build.** Wrong: the cell's own commit, built with `make build`, fails the same way.
- **The profile.** Wrong: the profiles the cell's successful runs left on disk carry nine
  keys with neither `setup_seen_at` nor `daily_budget_usd`, and the harness re-extracts the
  tarball on every point, so the cell's runs reached the composer without either marker.

The first-run screen itself is by design: it opens when stdin is a terminal, the launch is
not a `--host` connection, the conversation was not resumed and has no entries,
`setup_seen_at` is absent, and at least one setup step remains unanswered. A profile
carrying an API key and every model key still meets it until `daily_budget_usd` exists.
That is a product fact for the owner, not a regression, and it is not what this changes.

**The harness's silent non-row is a real defect** and belongs to the follow-up cell rather
than to this PR: a poll that exhausts its attempts should fail, not log success.

## What exactly was measured

The numbers above came from two binaries, and this section pins them to content rather than
to commits, because a rebase changes every sha in this branch and the measurement does not
move with it. The identity that survives is the blob hash of the one file that differed.

| side | binary sha256 (first 16) | `internal/tui3/app.go` blob |
| --- | --- | --- |
| before | `ace79e7e0ae61a84` | `34ee6e566d1dc42858c8a2127eb984e03aa6858d` |
| after | `b7b2ce659b50786a` | `fb40344e917650121daf4a60fa438a85ec938fe7` |

Both were built with `make build` in the same working tree with only that file swapped, so
nothing else differed: no build-tag difference, no regenerated asset, no second worktree.
They are **byte-for-byte the same size, 52,429,065**, which is why the per-row guard is the
sha256 of the file `/proc/<pid>/exe` resolves to and not the size. Every `before` row in the
run carries `ace79e7e0ae6` and every `after` row `b7b2ce659b50`, so no row compared a binary
with itself.

An earlier attempt built the baseline in a fresh worktree and produced a binary 3.5 MB
smaller, which would have compared two different programs rather than one change. That is
why both sides are built in one tree.
title: tui3: a wait whose stream has stopped arriving paints at the spinner cadence, and the harness that measured it

body:
## What was wrong

A second hand-off in one conversation renames the first run's store to `plandb.db.1` and seeds a fresh one. Every read opened only the live store. The first run's row stayed on the rail, but its page, its parts and its notes could no longer be opened, and the `tasks` tool could no longer answer for it.

## What changed

- Reads take every ended store oldest first, then the live one. The listing carries each run's rows, and a task of any run opens by the id the rail shows. A root's id is the rail's number and is never reused; a part's id is random.
- Only the live run takes the six steering verbs. A task of an ended run answers `that task's run has ended`, and a test asserts the ended store's bytes are unchanged after every verb.
- An ended store never changes, so it is opened once and kept for the life of the conversation. The handles are given back when the conversation closes. The live store is still opened per read so another process's writes are seen.
- One function names the archives for the door that makes them and the reads that find them.
- With no archive the listing is byte for byte what it was, pinned by a test.

## Hosted drive on the real binary, 2026-09-19

Built from this branch merged with #1231 and #1232, because a rail row is not a door without #1231. `codeaf chat` with no flags, belt on. Two hand-offs, the second typed after the first had ended.

1. The session folder held `plandb.db` and `plandb.db.1`. The rail drew `#1` and `#2`.
2. A click on `#1` opened the first run's page: brief, folder, its three notes, its steps.
3. A note typed on that page was answered `that task's run has ended` on the page's own line, with the words left in the box.

## A defect this PR had, and how it was found

An earlier head of this PR froze a conversation's engine for good. It passed the cell's checker and the whole `internal/session` suite, and was found only by a real-binary drive in hosted mode.

- **What happened.** The reader that opens every run's store takes the plan's lock and returns a closer that releases it. With a plan armed and no store to open yet, it returned no stores, and all three callers returned on that before the line that deferred the closer. Nothing released the lock.
- **What a person would have seen.** A run whose rows stop moving, a third hand-off that never ends, and an engine that does not leave when the terminal is closed. It is a race on the first hand-off, so one drive in six hit it.
- **How it was found.** The engine from a failed drive was still alive an hour later and ignored a terminate signal. A goroutine dump showed `Agent.Close`, the plan listing over the wire, the run's driver and the turn loop all waiting on the same mutex.
- **The fix.** The helper unlocks before it answers that there is nothing to read, as the shipped single-store opener does, and each caller defers the closer on the line after the call. The failing test came first.
- **The law.** `internal/guard/lockcloser_test.go` covers every lock handed out through a returned closer, in two halves. The helper never answers nil while locked. Its caller writes no return before the closer is deferred or called, except on the first result being nil. Pointed at the leaking head it names the three exact lines. Two older helpers of this shape are on trunk and neither is exposed.

This is the argument for #1241, which puts that drive in the repo.

## Proof

- Whole `internal/session` on Spark under the box lock at 87dac1550: `ok github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/session 238.001s`, exit 0, 2026-09-19T04:04:37Z.
- Hosted, real binary, this head: `scripts/hosted-drive.sh` three times in a row, 15 of 15 each time.
- Laptop: build, vet, gofmt clean; the focused session set with the road ratchet, Schema, Prefix, Landing and Stand tests; `make test-laws` including the new law; manual and name gates; change entries. No prompt, schema or tool description changes.

## Order

Head 87dac1550 sits on santos/dev 1cbcb4b7d, which carries #1231, #1232 and #1240.

body:
## What

A `codeaf do` run whose root finishes itself now seats its review before the run ends. When the root's status is terminal Done but its worker goroutine is still in flight (the root task is still in the supervisor's cancel set), the pass no longer accepts the stored ending; it waits for the worker return, which is what seats the review. A root whose return has already been absorbed, or whose terminal status is not Done, proceeds as before, so a completed tree that left an unrelated worker behind still drains and the stored-result path from earlier work is untouched.

## Why

A root worker can write its Done to the store before its goroutine returns. A supervisor pass that observed that stored Done first accepted it and ended the run, so the review round was never seated and the run exited with no check task (do_engine_test.go:551, "check tasks in store = 0, want exactly one"): a real `codeaf do` run whose root finishes itself could skip its review. The deferral is narrowed by the root task's identity in the supervisor's cancel set, so it holds back only the self-finished root return and not a worker the completed tree left behind.

## Verification

The forced-ordering regression `TestSupervisorChecksASelfFinishedRootBeforeAcceptingItsStoredEnding` delays the root worker return across several supervisor passes so a pass deterministically observes Done with no return available; on the base tree the run ends with no check, with the fix it waits and seats one, without machine load. Focused `TestDoOnTheRunEngineChecksASelfFinishedRootAndExitsZeroWhenItHolds` passed 30/30. Full `internal/run` is green, including the completed-tree left-behind-worker law and the root review laws. `go build ./...`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal`, `go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check`, and `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` all pass.

## What bounds the wait

The deferral holds only while the root task is still in the supervisor's cancel set, and it is bounded by exactly the limit that already bounds every in-flight worker: the run's own context. The root worker is launched with that context (`context.WithCancel(ctx)`). If it is killed or errors, its goroutine returns on the run's `finished` channel and is absorbed, which records the root failure and ends the run (`OutcomeIncomplete`) and removes it from the cancel set, so the next pass no longer defers. If it hangs, the caller's wall fires `ctx.Done` in the run loop, which cancels that same context, drains the in-flight workers so their endings land, and returns `OutcomeIncomplete`. The change adds no new wait: a self-finished root whose goroutine had not yet returned was already an in-flight worker keeping the run alive under that same bound; the pass simply stops accepting its stored Done before the return. Covered by `TestRunAnswersIncompleteWhenTheRootWasCancelledAfterItRan` and `TestSupervisorNeverCancelsAWorkerThatWroteItsOwnDone`.
title: fix(run): a self-finished codeaf do run seats its review before it ends

body:
## What was wrong

With the bash belt on, a hand-off's workers typed in the person's own folder. The run's landing committed straight onto the branch the person had checked out. The receipt said `in a copy of its own`, which was false. Two hand-offs on different folders would have shared one tree.

## What changed

- A run works in a copy cut by the shipped ground ladder from the folder the task is about, as that folder stands. Every part of one run works in that one copy.
- A second hand-off joins the run underway only when it is about the same folder, and its answer says so. A proposed task about another folder is refused with both folders named and what to do next. That is the one refusal that stays at the run's door. Every other failure still falls through to the shipped engine, which cuts its own copy from the same stand.
- When the run ends its work comes home through `taskTree.comeHome`, the function every shipped task lands through. The copy's work is committed, merged into the folder it was cut from, and the copy is given back. The run is then cleared, as on trunk, so the next hand-off starts a run of its own.
- Work that will not go in keeps its branch in the person's repository, and the outcome note says so once.
- The card says `merged` when the work is in the folder. It used to say `branch kept` for every run that named a branch.
- A hand-off that joined a run ends with it. Its row used to stay `running` after the run had ended.

## What I did not take from the cell

The cell made landing a separate step that a person triggers. That had three faults. A later hand-off joined a run whose workers had stopped and never ran. The waiting door lived only in memory and was lost when the window closed. The conversation was told the work was done while the folder held none of it. The cell also rewrote the shipped road's receipt and two manual pages to say `until you land it`; those are restored, and the worker page gains the sections that are now true.

## Hosted drive on the real binary, 2026-09-19

Built from this branch merged with #1231, because the run is not visible on a hosted screen without #1230. `codeaf chat` with no flags, belt on, a two-file repository with an unsaved file of my own in it. Two hand-offs typed six seconds apart.

1. While the run worked, `git status` in my folder showed only my unsaved file. One copy existed, under the conversation's `trees`. The second hand-off's row hung under the first on the rail.
2. When the run ended the folder held one new commit with the three files the run wrote. My unsaved file was untouched. The copy was gone and no task branch was left behind.
3. The card read `done · 30s · 3 files · merged`. The joined row had settled under the run's row.

On the first drive the card read `branch kept · work` and the joined row was still spinning. Both are fixed in the second commit and pinned by tests.

## Proof

- Whole `internal/session` on Spark under the box lock: see the comment below for the tree and result.
- New tests: a real file comes home committed and the copy is given back; a run that only read changes nothing; a person's commit during the run keeps the branch and never says merged; a hand-off after an ended run is a fresh run in a fresh copy that holds the first run's work; the joined row settles.
- Every belt test now waits for its run to end before cleanup. That removes the intermittent `directory not empty` failure at its cause.
- Focused set with the ratchet, schema and prefix tests, `make test-laws`, manual and name gates, `gofmt -l`, `go vet`: green. No prompt, schema or tool description changes.

## Owed after this and #1231 both land

The task page's folder line reads the conversation's folder. While a run is live it should name the run's copy, and the step rows should drop a leading change into that copy. It is a small follow-up that needs both changes on trunk.

body:
Stacked on #1230. It needs that pull request's wire to be seen at all in a hosted conversation, so read only the commits after `docs: the #1230 change entry`.

## What was wrong, on the owner's screen and on mine

- A run task's page opened with `t-qax3xr is your task in the plan.`, a line written for the worker, and never showed what the task was asked. The owner's words: "task details is not shown like actual task it just says like internal name task4".
- Every step row spent its width on a change into the task's own folder, and the command was cut off.
- With a run on the rail, the run had no row of its own, only its parts. A click on a row did nothing. A run's rows were text with no door.

## What changed

- The page opens with the title, the brief folded with the rest one key away, the declared checks, and the folder said once.
- One function draws a command on the page, the rail and the tree. It drops only a leading change into the folder the head names, and draws a command of many lines as its first line and a mark. The record of what ran is unchanged, and a test pins that byte for byte.
- The rail keeps the run's own row and hangs the run's rows under it. Two rules each hid the other's row: the reading hides the run's plan row because a node row wears its title, and the rail hid that node row because the store held its title.
- The frame and the pointer read one drawn view. The press used to be answered from the rows before the run's were spliced in.
- Every row of a run opens that task's page over the conversation, through the single off-loop page door from #1230. A row with no stored page opens its room as before.

## Hosted drive on the real binary, 2026-09-19

`make build`, throwaway home, two-file repository, `codeaf chat` with no flags, belt on, tmux at 170 by 50.

1. A two-part task ran. The rail drew `two independent parts,… #1` with three parts and three checks under it.
2. I typed a draft, then clicked the last part's row. Its page opened: title, `done · 4 steps`, brief, folder, four steps. The step that wrote a file read `cat > muldiv.go <<'EOF' …` on one row, and the note box and the foot were on screen.
3. `esc` returned to the conversation with `my draft stays` still in the box.
4. A click on the run's own row opened the run's page with its brief, folder and notes.

## What was wrong

`codeaf chat` hosts its engine in another process by default. The surface reads a run through one optional method set: the run's rows, one task's page, six steering verbs and the run summary. The wire carried none of them, so in every hosted conversation the rail drew one row and nothing under it, a task's page could not open, and no verb reached the store. All of it worked under `--no-host` and in tests with a scripted agent.

## What changed

- `session.PlanAgent` is the one method set. The surface names it, and the local engine and the remote client both implement it.
- `internal/remote` carries all ten methods, and holds this line so a method added later fails the build until it is carried:
  `var _ session.PlanAgent = (*Agent)(nil)`
- The surface-door ledger shrinks from 23 to 22 and its law follows an interface alias.
- Plan reads and verbs leave the update loop through the ordered door line. The page's follow read is one at a time, and an answer is folded only into the page that asked.
- The run's plan is re-read on a three-second beat of its own, and only while the reading holds a row that is queued or running. It used to ride on the reading of other windows' work, which a hosted conversation does not have.
- Something does paint at rest: the re-read runs from every frame that draws the rail or the tasks place, and from that place's tick. Before the condition below, that was twenty plan reads a minute over the wire for ever in a hosted window nobody was touching.
- At rest the count is zero. A hosted conversation always has a plan reader, so the beat asks a second question: can any held row still move by itself. The read that finds every row settled is the last. A row of this window's own graph moving starts it again, and a hand-off publishes its row after its store is seeded.
- The run summary's refresh carries how long the caller will wait, never the instant it stops waiting. An engine reached with `--host` runs under another machine's clock, and an instant read against a clock one minute ahead is a refresh cut before it starts.

## Hosted drive on the real binary, 2026-09-19

Built with `make build`, a throwaway home and a two-file repository, `codeaf chat` with no flags and the belt on, driven in tmux at 170 by 50.

1. The same two-part task was handed off hosted and unhosted side by side, and the rail was captured every ten seconds. Before the beat fix the unhosted rail drew the two parts at 70 s and the checks at 80 s, and the hosted rail drew one row until the run ended. After it the hosted rail drew the parts at 10 s, a third part at 20 s, and each check as the run added it.
2. The tasks place listed the conversation with its seven pieces of work, their state, steps and cost.
3. Enter on a part opened its page over the wire: the state line, the description, and four steps with their commands and first output lines.
4. A note typed on that page was drawn under `notes` on the same page a moment later.

## Proof

- `internal/remote` and `internal/enginehost`, whole packages, green. The enginehost test seeds a real store, serves a real agent over a real pipe and reads the rows back through `remote.Dial`.
- Focused `internal/tui3` set, `make test-laws`, `gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal`, `go build ./...`, `go vet`: green.
- `TestTheRunsPlanIsReadAgainOnItsOwnBeat` fails with the beat removed and passes with it.
- Two tests go through a real store, a real session agent, the real remote server and the real client, with the client's plan reads counted. `TestAHostedConversationAtRestReadsNoPlanOverTheWire`: twenty beats at rest cross the wire no times after the first read. It fails with twenty extra reads when the condition is removed. `TestAHostedRailLearnsOfAnAddedPartWithinOneBeat`: a part added to the store by another handle is on the rail one beat later, at the cost of one read.
- Rebased onto santos/dev fe9eb62af; every proof above was re-run on the rebased head 42bbdc38e, and the hosted rail drive was repeated with the conditional beat: parts at 10 s, checks as added.
- No prompt, schema or tool description changes.

## Seen on the drive and not fixed here

- Once a run has ended the rail draws its parts and not the run's own row. It does the same unhosted.
- A click on a rail row does not open its page yet. That is the next pull request.
- A step whose command is a multi-line document spills over several rows of the page.

## What

Orders the late-first-token rescue test by a transport signal instead of elapsed-time slack. Lane A now carries a `FirstTokenUntil` channel closed only at cleanup, so A cannot emit its first token until B has completed and the rescue has committed a winner. The winner, loser, and cancellation assertions are unchanged.

## Why

The test asserts B wins, A is unnamed, and A is cancelled, but it ordered A after the rescue only by giving A a 300ms first token against B's 5ms: an elapsed bound (`took < 300ms`) with about 80ms of slack. Under gate load that slack could be eaten and A could complete first; the product then correctly commits A and cancels B, and the fixed B-wins expectation flips.

This is a test-side timing expectation, not a product defect. The rescue commit path names the first completed arm the winner under the race mutex and cancels every other registered arm, so a real request cannot overwrite a winner or leave an uncancelled loser (decide/commit at `internal/provider/hedge.go:1521-1564`, settlement at `hedge.go:2007-2065`). Forcing B to complete before A's first token makes the winner follow the transport ordering the product actually guarantees, at any speed.

## Verification

Focused, no heavy lock:

```
go build ./...
go test ./internal/provider -run '^TestALateFirstTokenIsRescuedByTheAlternativeAndTheLoserIsCancelled$' -count=20
```

20/20 forced-order runs pass. `internal/provider/pool` untouched. The whole `internal/provider` suite runs in the gate.

Deliberate negative: with B forced before A there is no wrong product outcome to encode; making A win and still demanding B would only assert an invalid expectation. No product change is supported by this seam.
title: test(provider): order the late-first-token rescue by a signal, not elapsed slack

body:
## What

The place sweep note is now sealed at process close instead of joined. `startPlaceSweep` runs the walk fire-and-forget; `noteSweep` writes under `sweepMu`, and `v3Process.closeAll` calls `sealPlaceSweep()`, which takes that lock and marks the sweep sealed. A note already mid-write finishes; no note writes after the seal. Close does not wait for the walk.

## Why

The sweep was started and forgotten. On an error it resolves the current home and appends `sweep.log`; a process or test that closed quickly could see that write land after close, under a directory being torn down (the cleanup race that leaves "directory not empty"). Joining the whole walk at close would fix the race but move a pause that grows with the number of conversation folders the machine has held from launch onto quit. Sealing the note gives the same guarantee (no write after close) in O(1): quit waits only for one line already in flight, never for the walk.

## Verification

Focused, no heavy lock:

```
go build ./...
go test ./cmd/codeaf -run TestClosingSealsThePlaceSweepWithoutWaitingForTheWalk -count=2
```

The test blocks the sweep as an unbounded walk, asserts `closeAll` returns within a small fixed bound while the walk is still blocked, and asserts a note attempted after the seal writes no `sweep.log`. Without the seal the late note recreates `sweep.log` after close, so the test fails by construction. Whole `cmd/codeaf` and the rest run in the stacked gate.

## Attribution of the gate cleanup failure

The property test proves a note attempted after close writes `sweep.log` without the seal and nothing with it. The sweep has one writer and one file (`noteSweep`, `sweep.log` under the process home), and `closeAll` seals before a v3-process test's `t.TempDir` RemoveAll runs, so a gate run's "directory not empty" cleanup failure in such a test is consistent with this writer. It was not reproduced in 200 quiet runs on either the sealed or unsealed tree; a raw loop cannot force the interleaving that fails, only the property test's blocked walk can.
title: fix(chatv3): seal the place sweep note at close instead of joining the walk

## What

A single resident dispatch pass no longer reclaims a leaf that the same pass just released. claimNext records each leaf it dispatches in a new pass.dispatched set and skips those leaves for the rest of that pass; a later pass picks them up normally.

## Why

Under the busy gate a leaf that ran out (StopBudget) and was released by its worker mid-pass could be reclaimed and re-executed by the same Tick. What a person running background self work would have seen: the same leaf executed twice in one pass, spending its budget twice, before the pass ended. The ordering is forced deterministically, not by load, with an afterDispatch test seam that holds the pass until the worker lands (nil in production). The new test asserts one pass executes the leaf exactly once and leaves it Pending for a later pass.

Change entry: docs/changes/unreleased/1225-resident-dispatch-no-double-run.md.

body:
A design page only. No code changes. The owner answered both of its questions on 2026-09-20, so it is settled rather than proposed and three cells follow it.

## The rule

Closing a window never ends work and never loses it. Work is always in one of three conditions the screen names: running, interrupted, or settled. While the engine is alive a run keeps running. When nothing is driving it, it is interrupted, never failed, and everything it did is kept. On the next launch the person is asked once and `enter` continues. Nothing restarts silently, and the five-minute tick never continues a run.

## What it records as true today

- A live run does not count as work, so the engine retires its conversation at 30 minutes, mid-run.
- A run's context belongs to the turn that proposed it, not to the conversation.
- On reopen an unsettled run row is stamped failed and stopped, over a store that holds every row.
- The supervisor can already release dead claims and carry on from a store. Nothing calls it on reopen.

## The owner's answers

Both yes, in his own words, quoted at the foot of the page:

> 1. `interrupted` is the state word. Yes.
> 2. Continuing always asks first, and the five-minute tick never continues a run on its own. Yes.
>
> The design is settled on those two points. Build it as written.

So `interrupted` joins running, finishing, done, incomplete and your call, and means only "nothing is driving this". The fourth row in the order of work, the tick continuing a run on its own, is refused by that second answer. It is written down as refused rather than merely unbuilt.

## The three cells

| # | Cell | Size | New words |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| a | a live run counts as work; the run's context is the conversation's; the engine stays while a run lives | S | none |
| b | on reopen, an unsettled run reads `interrupted` from the store's own state, never failed and stopped | S | `interrupted` |
| c | the card, and continue through the existing supervisor on the existing store | M | none beyond b |

The order is not arbitrary. Cell b reads a condition that cell a is what makes truthful, and cell c draws the word cell b introduces.

Two acceptance notes are now on the page beside that table, because they are the parts most likely to be dropped under time pressure. A cell that has to end an engine ends it by the process id recorded when it was launched, confirmed by reading that process's own executable, never by matching a pattern against a command line and never by signalling a group. And cell b carries the manual in both directions: the new word has to reach the pages, and the page that today tells a person their run ended when codeaf closed has to be found and corrected in the same change, because a page that names a word while denying the thing around it satisfies every gate and still lies.

## Proof

Docs only, so the light gate is the level. On Spark, plain ssh, a detached tree of head `c97770f35`. Exit codes read directly.

| Step | Result |
| --- | --- |
| `go build ./...` | exit 0 |
| `make test-laws` | exit 0 |
| `internal/manual`, `internal/namelaw` | ok |
| `make changelog-check` | exit 0 |
title: design: closing the window never ends work, and interrupted work continues with one key (settled)

## What was wrong
Profile config.json is read as a FLAT map of dotted keys (readProfileConfig, internal/config/budget.go; per-key lookup persistedValue, settings.go). A key at the wrong depth (a nested {"models":{...}} where "models.tiers.reflex" was meant) or a mistyped dotted key is silently ignored: it is not the dotted key any reader looks up, so every affected seat falls to the shipped defaults with NO error. A fresh profile that set model.talk and all five models.tiers but NESTED sent 16 requests in one chat --once turn, none the configured model (8 google/gemini-2.5-flash reflex, 4 ~deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-latest talk, 4 deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731 low). A misshapen config was silently the same as no config.

## The change (internal/config/config.go)
At load, warn ONCE per profile (sync.Map guard) naming every top-level config.json key that no reader consumes (the settings registry Rows() plus the known non-setting fields). By property, any key the reader does not know is named, at any depth, including a nested object used where a dotted key was meant. It is a log line, never an error that stops a session, and it does not change how a correctly shaped flat config resolves.

## What a person sees
- 12 nested file {"models":{"tiers":{"reflex":"..."}},"model.talk":"..."}: `codeaf: <profile>/config.json has unread top-level config key(s): models`
- one mistyped dotted key {"model.tark":"..."}: `codeaf: <profile>/config.json has unread top-level config key(s): model.tark`
- a correct flat config (api_key, model.talk, models.tiers.*, effort, model_sources, tools.approval, tools.approvalMode): NO output.

## Scope
Surfaced through the process logger, once per load. Whether it should also appear on the chat surface at turn time is a separate product decision (chat-time attribution), out of scope here.

## Tests and checks (Spark, focused, rebased onto 39ffbc548)
- internal/config/config_test.go TestLoadWarnsOnceForEveryUnreadTopLevelProfileKey: nested + typo named, flat keys NOT named, resolution unchanged, warned once across two loads.

body:
## What changed

The S2 router-movement gate (TestS2TheDefaultGoesSlowAndTheRouterMoves) now scores each request on the SCRIPTED first token of the lane that answered, looked up from the sheet, and reinstates the design's own ship gate on that figure. The verdict no longer reads measured wall time, and it is no longer the weaker request-count check.

## Why

Two problems, in order:

1. The original gate read p90 first token off measured wall time. On this hundredfold clock a healthy answer carries about 2.5 s of loopback overhead around 1.2 s of script, and that overhead sits in the numerator AND the denominator of the improvement ratio where it does not cancel. Under load one scheduler delay on the eighteenth of twenty answers dragged a healthy 45% improvement to 28.7% and failed the 30% gate. That is the flake.

2. The interim fix replaced the gate with a request-count check, routedVictim >= pinnedVictim. The pin sends 20 of 20 to the slow default, so a router that moved a single request of twenty passed. That lowered the bar the design set.

## The fix

Each request's first token is scored as the scripted median of the lane that answered it (e2eSheet), with a lane that was rescripted slow scored at its slow figure. This value is fixed by the script, so the same routing decisions give the same verdict on a quiet box and a loaded one. On that figure the test restores both clauses of the design gate:

- a p90 first-token improvement of at least 30 per cent (provider-routing.md, Part III, C3), and
- the moving arm's p90 below the pinned arm's median.

The measured wall figures stay in the test as logged diagnostics.

## Load independence and the bar

Stressed on a box at load about 80, five runs of S2 in a row gave routed scripted p90 of 768 to 844 ms against the pin's 4 s every time, a 79 to 81 per cent improvement, no flake. The earlier measured-wall attempt had failed one of the first three runs on the same box at 29.3%.

## The deliberate negative

A router configured not to move (the routed arm pinned to the victim) scores the pin's own scripted p90 and fails by construction:

    e2e_test.go:449: victim Baidu scripted p90 first token routed 4s, pinned 4s (pinned p50 4s); ...
    e2e_test.go:468: the router's scripted p90 first token is 4s against the pin's 4s, 0.0% better, and the gate is 30%
    --- FAIL: TestS2TheDefaultGoesSlowAndTheRouterMoves

## Verified on Spark

Tree ed368fcc5. go build ./... clean; go test ./internal/lane/... ok; gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal clean; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check clean; go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok. Combined exit 0. Test-only change, no changelog entry.

The review round's contract becomes the command or commands the worker declares as the proof of its work, judged only by properties any project shares: the checker ran the command in this check task, its exit was recorded, and it passed the shipped read-only audit law. A holds conclusion requires every declared command to have a recorded zero-exit audited run; a does not hold conclusion is never gated, so a reading checker can still report a defect on an empty or partial contract; a leaf that declared nothing is judged by reading, and reading can hold. Each verdict records its basis on the leaf, by run with the commands and their exit codes, or by reading, so a later reader and a grid see how a verdict was earned. The trajectory-guessing backfill and its runner set are removed, and the check seat stays read-only.

This closes #1206. Its check-contract line of work lands here as one small PR onto santos/dev rather than a long-lived wave branch.

Provenance, plainly: the product commit on this branch was written with a second agent present in the worktree during the run. It was accepted on review and on tests, not on the cell's own say-so. The seven test-first commits specify the behavior; the change passes them, the internal/plandb, internal/run and whole internal/session suites, the complexity ratchet, and the prompt prefix budgets; and its store.go was read line by line for anything beyond scope. The learning crew's fit row for the originating run is flagged two-agent and excluded from crew fit and the arbiter.

Verified on Spark at tree b61129dde: go build clean, gofmt -l clean, go test ./internal/plandb/... ./internal/run/... ok, the whole internal/session suite ok through one-suite.sh (259s, including the ratchet and prefix-budget tests), go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check clean, and go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok.

## Update: one quote-aware reader, shared with the store (folds in #1215)

santos/dev 39ffbc548 (with #1215) is merged in. The check door's quote-aware reader now lives in one place, internal/approval: FirstCompositionOutsideQuotes and FirstBarOutsideQuotes, with the composition character set as approval.ShellComposition. Session's three files (task_audit.go, task_checks.go, task_divide_scope.go) and the store's auditableDeclaredCheck all read through it. The store's duplicate declaredCheckComposition const and its non-quote-aware strings.Fields composition pass are gone, so a check the proposal door admitted with a quoted bar can no longer be refused a holds verdict by the store.

A store-side acceptance test (internal/plandb, through checkVerdictBasis) reuses the proposal door's own eight-form never-run table: a quoted-bar check is admitted, run, its exit 0 recorded, and holds is allowed; every form that is more than one command is refused by the store even with a zero exit on file.

Verified on Spark at tree a8a1ddf12: go build clean; whole internal/session suite ok through one-suite.sh (217s), including the complexity ratchet, both prefix-budget tests, and the door's quoted-bar contract test; internal/run, internal/plandb, internal/approval ok; gofmt -l ./cmd ./internal clean; go run ./cmd/codeaf-changes check clean; go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw ok. Combined exit 0.


## Recording the command's real exit (round 2)

The verdict now rests on the command's own exit, recorded by the belt as it runs. A bash tool that ended is exit zero; one that failed carries the non-zero code the belt appended to its output (read back, or a plain non-zero when the output was cut); a harness refusal and a non-bash tool record no exit. The exit is a pointer on the step, so a step written before this field, or one whose exit is unknown, decodes to nil and is never read as a zero a real exit could equal. A holds verdict rests only on a recorded zero exit for every declared command.

A build that records exits stamps an opening line, before any step, and the ending line with exits_recorded, so a trajectory cut off mid-run is still known to be from a new build. On a new-build record a declared check with no recorded run refuses the holds verdict: a checker that ran nothing has not earned it. A record from before exits were recorded cannot be judged that way, so it holds as a reading and names, in VerdictBasis.Unobserved, the declared checks it never observed, so no reader mistakes it for a holds earned by running them.

Acceptance drives a real command through the real belt recorder into the store, with no hand-written exit line: a passing command yields holds, a failing one is refused.
title: run: declared checks are the review contract, judged by observable properties, with the verdict basis recorded

The owner proposed three tasks in one message on 2026-09-18 and nine calls were refused over three rounds. Every refusal was about the shape of a check.

Inside double quotes a dollar, a backtick and a backslash still refuse the check, because the shell still expands them there. An unclosed quote is refused. Nothing the shape law stopped before starts running: only what the shell passes to the one program as an argument is newly allowed, and it reaches the checker byte for byte.
