body:
`internal/tui3`'s test floor points an empty profile directory at **one** state root for the whole
package run, so every test whose surface named no profile read and wrote the same directory — and an
earlier test's `setup_seen_at` decided what a later one saw. That hid a red for a week:
`TestTheOpeningHintNamesBothDoors` passed in the package run and failed alone, from #680 until #1153
fixed that one test. This closes the class **at the helpers**.

## What changed

| helpers | what they do now |
|---|---|
| `newTestApp` (**663 call sites**) and `benchApp` (9) | no `*testing.T` in hand, so they mint a directory with `mintProfileDir()` — a fresh subdirectory of the run's own `CODEAF_HOME`, thrown away with the run |
| the sixteen others that take a `t` | name `ProfileDir: t.TempDir()` — attachLab, mixedLab, newRewindApp, modalLab, browseLab, fileLab, asyncApp, hostLab, welcomeApp, recallApp, memoryPlaceApp, hostedSurface, exportLab, folderLab, aliasApp, completionApp |
| `newTestAppWithProfile(dir, agent)` | the escape hatch for a test that means two surfaces to share **one** profile, used by the crew test that seeds a profile and has two surfaces read it |

**The 663 call sites are untouched, deliberately.** Threading a `t` through them would collide with a
branch that carries `internal/tui3` changes and is rebasing onto trunk; `mintProfileDir()` is what
makes that avoidable.

## The law, and proof that it bites

`TestEveryHelperThatBuildsASurfaceNamesAProfile` reads this package's `_test.go` files with `go/ast`
and fails any helper that builds a surface without either naming a profile or moving the state root
itself. It is honest about its own scope in its own comment: **it is a law about helpers, not about
test bodies.**

A law test can be made to pass by weakening what it asserts, so I checked it by mutation rather than
by reading. Removing `ProfileDir: t.TempDir()` from one helper (`aliasApp`):

```
--- FAIL: TestEveryHelperThatBuildsASurfaceNamesAProfile
    A helper must give each app a profile of its own: t.TempDir() where a *testing.T is in hand,
    mintProfileDir() where none is. A helper that means two surfaces to share one profile passes
    the same directory to both on purpose.
FAIL	github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/tui3	0.183s
```

and reverted, `ok 0.201s`. Both runs mine, on Spark.

## Tests that legitimately depend on a shared root: none

The brief required these to be **reported, not hidden**, and the honest answer is that none were
found. Isolating every helper produced exactly one failure, and it was not a shared-root dependence:
`TestAnEmptyProfileDirectoryIsTheOrdinaryProfileAndStillHasACrew`, whose *subject* is the launch that
names no profile, asserted `a.profileDir == ""` and so could no longer be built by `newTestApp`. It
now builds through `ordinaryLaunch`, which names no profile and still pins a root of the test's own.
The tests that do carry a setting from one surface to another already name the directory themselves —
`TestTheColumnsPostureIsRememberedAcrossSessions` (railaway_test.go:220),
`TestChoosingAModelWritesItWhereTheNextLaunchReadsIt` (modelmemory_test.go:17), `noticeApp`/`sheetApp`
— so nothing had to be shared implicitly.

## Still exposed, and said plainly

**45 direct `newApp(` calls inside test and benchmark bodies still name no profile** and still share
the run's root (62 direct calls in test bodies, 17 of them naming a `ProfileDir`). The law does not
read those sites, and this PR does not change them: that is the call-site sweep the scope forbade.
Widening the law to test bodies is a separate change, and it would need to give each site an
`ordinaryLaunch`-style root.

## Evidence

Log: `~/src/trees/check-bfabb11e84a920d347cb43c87022f3648c9e6c20.log` on the Spark cluster, from a
fresh clone of this head.

- `go test ./internal/tui3 -run '^TestTheOpeningHintNamesBothDoors$'` — **ok 0.180s**, alone, which is
  the whole point: it no longer depends on a marker some earlier test happened to write.
- `go test ./internal/tui3 -count=1 -timeout 600s` — **ok 314.8s**, the whole package, run once.
- `go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` — ok.
- The mutation run above.

## Summary

`codeaf exec` is a headless door: its worker's provider calls never reached the usage ledger (`usage.jsonl`), because `internal/exec`'s loop runs outside `internal/session`, so no row was ever minted and every spending surface under-counted an exec run.

- `cmd/codeaf/exec.go`: after `linear.Run`, `recordExecUsage` mints one row from the outcome's usage — the run's own id as `Root`, the worker model, `worker` role and worker seat (the same shape a chat seat's row has; `TagUsage` + `RecordUsage`) — and flushes the async writer before exit, the way the chat surface does on its way out.

## Summary

Three things a fresh install does that `codeaf pool status` never showed, each one status-line item in `cmd/codeaf/pool.go`:

body:
An unattended `codeaf chat --yolo` run pushed two commits onto a shared branch from its own bash,
after the task road had refused the same push and the task had read the refusal. #1160 is the
diagnosis; this is the fix, and the failing test is the **first commit on this branch** so the two can
be read against each other.

## Why it was possible

| gate | what it did |
|---|---|
| the consent gate | `--yolo` replaces the policy default with allow (`cmd/codeaf/chatv3.go:1662`), and `git push` is on neither floor that survives a blanket allow, so **no card was drawn** |
| the git guard | `whoseCopy` leaves a **Person**-headed session unguarded on purpose, and an unattended run with no ceiling is Person-headed — so the line was **passed through unread** |

## The fix: one narrow register beside the existing two

`refusedUnattendedBranchMovement` — **an unattended run may move a branch it cut itself, and no
other.** A run that is unattended (`Config.Unattended`, the door's own record of `--yolo`) and is
standing on a branch it did not cut is refused `push`, `merge` and `rebase` on that branch. Everything
else it did before stays: reading refs, committing into the working copy, unstaging, creating a fresh
branch.

**Ownership, not names.** The branch a run found its checkout on when it began is not one it created,
whatever it is called — which is what covers `santos/dev` without touching
`protectedBranchNames`, where a name merely *containing* a protected word is not protected and
teaching that list to catch `santos/dev` would refuse a person's own similarly-named branch. Ownership
is read from the two places a run records what it cut: its standing copies (`StandingTree.Branch`) and
its graph's task branches (`TaskNode.branch`).

**Attended sessions are untouched**, and `TestASessionCarryingItsOwnWorkAnswersToTheSameGitList` —
which pins that Person contract deliberately — still passes unchanged.

**The rejected alternative**, stated in the code: a `git push` entry on the critical-command floor
(`internal/approval/bash.go`). It loses twice — it would refuse an *interactive* session's own push,
the act `taskgit.go`'s header calls deliberately the person's, and it matches command **text**, so it
can say nothing about which branch a push would move.

## Failing test first, proved inside the branch

```
at d13e7e95 (the test alone):   FAIL — "…git push -u origin fix/…" was ALLOWED for a --yolo run
                               standing on a branch it did not create; the gate answered
                               "default → allow" and no citizen refused it
at 91826f60 (the branch head): ok  github.com/Agent-Field/codeaf/internal/session  0.259s
```

Both runs are mine, on Spark, on this branch.

## The test's shape moved, and that needs saying

The first draft set `Interactive` and the `--yolo` policy but **not** `Config.Unattended`, and stood in
no checkout — so it could never have reached a register gated on exactly those facts. It now records
the `--yolo` fact and stands in a real repository on `santos/dev`, which is the posture the incident
actually had. **It still replays the three command lines that really ran**, unchanged, and still
asserts a refusal of each; the strengthening is in the session around them, not in what is asserted.
A companion test covers the three scope lines apart: the run's own branch still pushable, an attended
session untouched, and a foreign branch's push, merge and rebase each refused.

## Known limits

- **The branch is read off the session's own workspace, not off the command.** That is deliberate and
  argued in the code — the guard refuses the *act*, and which branch a run stands on is a fact about
  the checkout it was launched in rather than about a directory a chain happens to `cd` into. The
  consequence is worth stating plainly: an unattended run whose own workspace sits on a branch it cut,
  which then `cd`s into a second clone and pushes a foreign branch there, is **not** caught. The
  incident's third command is caught only because that run's workspace was itself foreign. Closing that
  would mean reading the target of each command, which is the pattern-matching road this fix rejects
  for good reasons; it deserves its own decision rather than being smuggled in here.
- A detached HEAD, a workspace that is not a repository, and a session with no workspace all answer
  "not foreign" — there is no branch to be wrong about, and refusing on an absent reading would refuse
  a run sitting in a plain folder.
- The resident's consequence classifier (`internal/head/head.go:1123`) still never sees a chat door's
  tool call: `internal/session` imports `internal/head` in no non-test file. Wiring that up is another
  product's road and is left alone.

## Evidence

- The two runs above, and the whole `internal/session` package plus `internal/approval`,
  `internal/guard` and `internal/namelaw` from a fresh clone of this head — log path in a comment
  below, HEAD on its first line.

## What

Two things under `relay/`:

- **A purge for fixture-vendor rows.** `relay/src/purge.js` selects the `sheet/<install>/<day>/<cellKey>` keys whose model or judge vendor is in a named set (both cellKey shapes read) and lists or deletes them through the two calls the Worker's KV binding and the tests' fake KV both answer. `relay/tools/purge.js` is the thin wrapper over `wrangler kv key list` / `wrangler kv key delete` (`--vendor` repeatable, `--dry-run` prints the keys, otherwise deletes and prints the count; `--binding`, `--prefix`, `--local`). `seen/` and quota keys are untouched. The published `judges` list is derived from stored keys, so a purge followed by a publish drops the judge.
- **An allowed-vendor rule at the door.** `validateRow(line, now, vendors)` refuses a row whose model or judge vendor is not in the set, naming the field; `worker.js` reads the set from `ALLOWED_VENDORS` (comma/space-separated, lowercased) through a `listVar` beside `intVar`. Unset or blank, the rule is off and every vendor passes as before.

RUNBOOK: two operator steps (set the variable from the vendors the published index already carries; dry-run, delete, publish). `wrangler.toml`: a commented `ALLOWED_VENDORS`.

## Why

Fixture rows (model vendor `crew`, judge vendor `other`) reached the public pool from a package test and keep refolding into every publish; nothing in the relay could refuse them or remove them short of one `wrangler kv key delete` per key.

## Why

A bash call the model runs inherited codeaf's own environment, `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE` included, so a bare `tmux` it ran targeted the very server hosting the chat. Tonight a worker ran `tmux kill-server` and killed the server hosting its own chat (issue #576; killwatch 00:47:31, SIG=15, sender==target, comm="tmux: server"); on a shared socket earlier it reached every run on the box. A person running codeaf inside tmux has the same exposure. `runShell` and the background-job registry also left `cmd.Env` nil on the bare path, inheriting everything.

## What changed

`JobShellEnv` (internal/exec/tools.go) is the environment every model-run shell now gets:
- `TMUX` and `TMUX_PANE` removed (`withoutEnv`);
- `TMUX_TMPDIR` pointed at a profile-owned socket directory (`jobTmuxDir` = `<profile>/tmux`, created; per-profile, not per-process);
- a nil slice is read as `os.Environ()` and stripped the same way, so the previously-nil `cmd.Env` bare path is covered.

**The floor is both halves** (argued in the code): unsetting `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE` alone leaves the user's own tmux reachable; a private `TMUX_TMPDIR` alone leaves the inherited vars pointing at the host server. Together they name a namespace a job's `tmux` reaches and nothing outside it — and a test that needs its own tmux still works (it gets the private `TMUX_TMPDIR`, not a broken env). Applied at `runShell` (tools.go), the background-job env (jobs.go), and the bare streaming env (bare/streaming.go).

## Tests

`internal/exec/tmuxenv_test.go`: with `TMUX`/`TMUX_PANE` set in the process, a command run through `runShell` sees neither, and sees `TMUX_TMPDIR` = `<profile>/tmux` (which exists). `internal/exec/bare/streaming_test.go`: the bare streaming env carries the same.

Verified on Spark: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/exec/...`, `go test ./internal/exec/...` (exec 103s, bare 6.8s) — all green.

## What

`relay/src/sheet.js`:
- `judgeSeverity` holds each judge's fitted offset β inside ±10 after every sweep's re-centring (the rubric is 100 wide; a judge further off than a tenth of it is a different rubric, not a severity).
- `aggregate` clamps the severity-adjusted scores back into [0, 100] before folding, at the triple level: adjusted mean `clamp((s − n·β)/n)`, adjusted sum of squares `s2 − 2β·s + n·β²` (the exact shift), or `n·b`/`n·b²` when the mean clamps to a bound `b`.
- The published `sd` is pooled from the same adjusted triples as the mean, so both are on one scale.
- `huberMean`'s zero-MAD case answers the median instead of the plain mean.

## Why

A judge fitted far enough below the fit's centre lifted every score it gave past the rubric's top: the live index published a `role_quality` cell at mean 103.5 from rows every validator had held to 0–100, with an sd that described the raw, unshifted rows. The zero-MAD fallback let one far install mean count at full weight.

body:
#1158 gave a surface a soft memory limit of half the machine's **physical** memory. Inside a container
that is the *host's* memory, so the limit lands far above what the process may use: it never binds, and
the kernel OOM-kills instead of the collector working — the exact failure `GOMEMLIMIT` exists to avoid.
This takes the smallest real bound instead.

## What changed

`surfaceMemoryLimit` now takes the **smallest finite bound it can read** of: physical memory, the
cgroup v2 `memory.max` for this process, and the cgroup v1 `memory.limit_in_bytes`. A bound that is
absent, unreadable, the literal `max`, non-numeric, or the v1 sentinel is **not a bound** — it does not
participate, and it does not become a zero either. If none is readable the surface behaves exactly as
it did before #1158's floor rule, which is unchanged: if the smallest bound halved falls under 512 MiB,
nothing is set at all.

**The reader walks the whole path, not just the leaf.** The process's own cgroup is the third field of
its `/proc/self/cgroup` line; the reader walks from there up to the hierarchy root and takes the
minimum, because a container often puts the real bound on a slice above the one the process sits in, or
leaves the leaf at `max` while a parent is bounded. Walking can only tighten the answer, never loosen
it, and it costs a few stats at startup. Both generations are read: v2 has an empty controller list on
the `0::` line with the bound in `<path>/memory.max`; v1 names `memory` among its controllers with the
bound in `memory/<path>/memory.limit_in_bytes`.

`hostCgroupMemoryLimit` is the reader seam, the same shape as `hostTotalMemory`, so the tests stand a
hierarchy in front of the derivation without one existing.

## Why the naive version would have been dead code

Measured on the machine this was written on, and these went into the brief for exactly that reason:

- the box is cgroup **v2** (`stat -fc %T /sys/fs/cgroup` → `cgroup2fs`);
- **`/sys/fs/cgroup/memory.max` does not exist** — the root cgroup has no `memory.max`, so the obvious
  path always fails. The file for a process is under its own cgroup path, here
  `/sys/fs/cgroup/user.slice/user-1001.slice/session-….scope/memory.max`;
- every level on this box reads the literal **`max`**, so this change must not lower the limit here,
  and no test on this box can see a real cgroup bound — which is why the tests read **fake files**;
- cgroup v1's "no limit" is a huge sentinel (`9223372036854771712`), not a word.

## Tests

An unattended `codeaf chat --yolo` run hosting a `/task` landed two commits on a shared branch from
its own bash — after the task road had refused the same push and the task had read the refusal. This
is the diagnosis. **No behaviour changes here.**

## The road, in three gates

| gate | what happened |
|---|---|
| the consent gate (`loop.go:3246` → `approve`) | **ran, answered allow.** `git push` is on neither floor that survives a blanket allow — not the critical-command table (`approval/bash.go:245-271`: rm -rf, mkfs, dd, shutdown, fork bomb) and not the acts-in-your-name table (`approval/approval.go:91-101`: gmail, calendar, slack) — so the decision fell to `Policy.Default`, which `v3Policy` replaces with allow under the flag (`cmd/codeaf/chatv3.go:1662`). An allow short-circuits before any card, so **no card was ever drawn** |
| the git guard (`taskgit.go:117-128`) | **ran, passed the line through unread.** `whoseCopy` leaves a Person-headed session unguarded on purpose, and `newPrincipalFor` gives a Person to an unattended run with **no ceiling** — `--yolo` with no `--max-hours`/`--max-cost` is exactly that. A Steward (unattended *with* a ceiling) is refused the same push outright, and `taskgit_test.go:215-245` pins both sides |
| the high-stakes classifier (`head.go:1123`) | **never ran.** `internal/session` imports `internal/head` in no non-test file, so a chat door's tool call cannot reach it. Nothing on the chat road classifies a bash command by verb at all |

## And the branch was not protected

`protectedBranchNames` (`task_branch_protection.go:28-42`) is a fixed list matched with `EqualFold`
(`63-77`), so **`santos/dev` is not protected although it contains `dev`**. The landing path asks
three questions about the branch it merges into — detached HEAD, moved from `t.home`, protected name,
moved by a person — and **never asks whether the run created it**. That merge is codeaf's own
(`groundcarry.go:352-354` under `codeafGitIdentity`, which is the attribution the worktree reflog
carries); the push that followed was the door's shell, and nothing in the tree connects the two.

## The failing test is deliberately not in this PR

It fails by design. A red test on the trunk would make every other branch read as broken, and this
repository burned `.github/known-red.txt` to zero on purpose in #1012 — a standing exception would
undo that. It waits on **`task/c206-yolo-push-test`** as `internal/session/yolopush_test.go`, it
replays the three command lines that really ran, and its verbatim red output is quoted in the note so
the fix can be judged against it. The gate's own words are the finding in one line: **`default →
allow`**.

## What was checked by hand

Four claims here are load-bearing and each was read in the source rather than taken from the
diagnosis: the missing `internal/head` import, the `--yolo` default at `chatv3.go:1662`, the
`EqualFold` matching that leaves `santos/dev` unprotected, and the absence of any
did-this-run-create-it question on either road.

## One deviation worth flagging

This was asked for as docs-only with no changelog entry, and it carries one anyway
(`1156-yolo-bash-push-road.md`, to be renumbered): the check job demands an entry for every pull
request, so a PR without one is red for a different reason. The entry says plainly that no behaviour
changed and why it exists.

`tuneForTheSurface` raises the heap target for the commands that draw a screen — `GOGC` 400, a heap
target five times the live heap — and nothing bounded what that permits. A surface left open for a day
is exactly the shape that finds the ceiling by exhausting the machine. `debug.SetMemoryLimit` is the
other half of that bargain: a **soft** limit over all runtime-managed memory, not the heap alone,
which the collector works to stay under rather than cross.

## What the limit is

**Half the machine's physical memory**, and **nothing at all** — no call, no variable — where half
would fall under a **512 MiB floor**, or where the machine's memory could not be read.

The floor is a refusal rather than a value, and that is the whole safety argument: a limit below the
live heap makes the collector run continuously against a bound it cannot meet, which is a worse
failure than the unbounded growth the limit was added to prevent. 512 MiB is five times the ~104 MB a
surface's resident set was measured at, so the runtime still collects on its own schedule long before
the soft limit binds.

It keeps the three laws the tuner already states beside `GOGC` and `GOMAXPROCS`:

| law | here |
|---|---|
| an explicit setting decides | a set `GOMEMLIMIT` is left untouched — not rewritten, and the runtime's limit not moved |
| a machine that cannot be tuned safely is left completely alone | under the floor, or unreadable: nothing is set |
| the setting crosses the process boundary | the engine host is a separate process and reads `GOMEMLIMIT` at its own startup, so the variable carries it |

Per-OS readers are split out: `/proc/meminfo`'s `MemTotal` on Linux, `sysctl` on darwin, and a zero
answer elsewhere, which lands on the refusal. The reader is a variable so a test can stand a small
machine in front of the tuner without owning one.

## What this does not claim

**Nothing about whether it helps.** No benchmark, no RSS figure, no timing. The claim is exactly "a
surface now has a bound, and an explicit setting still wins". Measuring it is a separate piece of
work, deliberately not attempted here — a measurement taken inside a test process would be worthless.

## The open question I want a second opinion on

The derivation reads **physical** memory, and the code argues that a cgroup limit is "only ever
tighter than the one physical memory already gives" and that over-estimating inside a container is
"the safe error: it makes the limit loose, never tight".

I think that reasoning is worth challenging, and it is the one thing in here I would not merge on my
own word. Inside a container with, say, 512 MiB, `/proc/meminfo` reports the **host's** memory, so the
limit lands far above what the process may actually use — the soft limit never binds, and the process
is OOM-killed by the kernel instead of collecting. Avoiding exactly that is the usual reason to set
`GOMEMLIMIT` at all. A loose limit is safe in the sense that it cannot cause thrashing; it is not safe
in the sense of doing the job in the case that most wants it done. The counter-argument in the code is
real too — a container with no cgroup limit reads as unbounded and would leave the surface with
nothing — and it may be that reading a cgroup limit *when one exists* and falling back to physical
memory otherwise is the right shape. I have not changed it: the cell was scoped to code plus a unit
test, and this is a design decision rather than a defect.

## Evidence

- `go test ./cmd/codeaf ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw -count=1` on the Spark cluster over ssh
  from a fresh clone of this PR's head; log path in a comment below with the HEAD line first.
- Six focused tests: the derivation table (unreadable, negative, under the floor, one byte under twice
  the floor, exactly twice the floor, 16 GiB), an explicit `GOMEMLIMIT` left alone, the limit set with
  the variable carrying it, and the floor case setting nothing. Each restores the process's own limit
  through `debug.SetMemoryLimit(-1)`.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

## Why

An exhausted leaf's remainder was planned from scratch on every overrun round: `ReplanOverrun` ran a fresh `plan.Build` over a goal the job had already planned, so the round paid a second planning call, re-emitted the planner's phases onto the stream, and could drop the shape the job was planned with — the ds1 re-plan returned a fresh one-step remainder where a five-step plan was already recorded. (Root cause from the do-loop diagnosis, cause 1.)

## What changed

`internal/resident/overrun.go`: the splice now tells the planner WHY it is planning — `Growth.Reason` travels on the context (`withGrowthReason`/`GrowthReasonFrom`) to `replanOverrun`, the one seam every growing job passes.

Anything else — a cold start, a job with no plan, and every gap or cooperative round — keeps the full re-plan unchanged.

body:
## Why

A job is torn down by signalling its recorded process-GROUP id (`kill(-pid, SIG)`), which reaches WHATEVER process group currently holds that pgid. Pids are recycled — under load, within the minute — so a recorded pgid can belong to someone else by teardown, and a SIGKILL to a recycled pgid destroys an unrelated live group. Observed twice tonight from the kill tracer: a codeaf tearing several job groups down at settle SIGKILLed a pgid that had become the DOE's `tmux -L pareto` server, taking ~12 running jobs (~$12) each time.

## What changed (safe default: never signal on doubt)

New `internal/processgroup` seam:
- A `Group` is recorded at launch with its leader's identity — the `/proc/<pid>/stat` start-time (field 22), unique to one process within a boot (`identity_linux.go`; `identity_unix.go` for other unix).
- `Group.Terminate`/`Kill`/`Alive` signal only while that identity still matches the live process (`owned()`), and send NOTHING when it cannot be proven — leader gone, pid free, read fails. A missed kill leaks one process; a wrong kill destroys someone else's work, and the second is never traded away to avoid the first. A withheld signal can be reported via `OnRefused`.
- All teardown callers route through the seam: `internal/exec/jobs.go`, `internal/exec/services.go`, `internal/resident/services.go`, `internal/session/jobs.go`. Windows path preserved (`group_windows.go`).

## Tests

`internal/processgroup/group_unix_test.go`: a signal is never sent to a recycled process group (the reported failure), is withheld when the leader is gone, is sent to its own group, and a refusal records why. Seams (`processStart`, `groupSignalFn`) let the recycled-pid case be exercised without racing the kernel.

Verified on Spark, clean login run (HEAD e933b9a8, source-identical after a clean rebase onto trunk): build, vet, `internal/processgroup`, `internal/exec` (102s), `internal/resident`, `internal/session` (189s), `cmd/codeaf` (90.5s), `internal/guard`, `internal/namelaw` — all ok, EXIT 0. Log `~/src/trees/check-e933b9a8.log`.

Note: the non-linux unix identity path (`identity_unix.go`) and `shellwait_other.go` compile on their platforms but are not exercised by the Linux suite.

`go test ./internal/tui3 -run TestTheOpeningHintNamesBothDoors` has been red on its own since #680
(2026-09-09) and nobody saw it, because that package only runs when it is touched and the test is
green inside a package run.

## Why it was both

The test named no profile, so its app read the default profile of the state root — and
`internal/tui3`'s TestMain moves that root to **one directory for the whole package run** and clears
`CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` to the empty string, so every test that names no profile shares it. Whether
this test's keystroke dismissed the greeting therefore depended on whether some earlier test had
written a `setup_seen_at` marker into that shared directory.

Measured with a probe in the test, on the same tree in the same minute:

| run | probe | result |
|---|---|---|
| the test alone | `profileDir="" setupSeen=0001-01-01 recent=0 first=true` | FAIL |
| the whole package | `profileDir="" setupSeen=2026-09-18 03:32:49 recent=0 first=false` | PASS |

With `first` true, `welcomeStandsThroughTyping` makes the first conversation's greeting stand
through typing **on purpose** — the composer must not move out from under a sentence somebody has
started — so `dismissWelcome` never ran, `noteLandingKeys` never ran, and the hint was absent. The
contract changed in #680; the test did not.

## What changed

The test, only. Every app it builds reads a profile the test made, and it pins both halves of the
contract instead of one:

- **a profile the setup has never met**: the greeting stands through typing (the starter keys are
  still on the frame, no hint), and the hint lands at the **send**;
- **a profile that has met the setup**, marker written by the test into its own directory: the same
  keystroke dismisses and the hint lands then.

The other three assertions are unchanged — the greeting must not teach the exit before the entrance,
a resumed session gets the line on its first frame, help names `alt+enter`.

## What this does not do

The package-wide coupling is untouched: `newTestApp` alone is 663 call sites that name no profile,
and 18 of the 23 app-building helpers name none. That is a separate change, already planned, and it
will have to report the tests that depend on the shared root rather than paper over them.

This change was pushed onto `santos/dev` directly as `da491059`+`72de3bca` and reverted there
(`beb31ecf`, `499083d1`). The content is identical; the changelog entry is renumbered to this PR.

body:
`codeaf --version` on a build with no revision said it was **built without `make build`**. That is
the wrong cause, and the remedy it names does not work in the case where the sentence appears.

## Measured, on go1.26.5 at `2ab365d6`

| build | what the binary carries | what `--version` prints |
|---|---|---|
| `go build ./cmd/codeaf` inside the checkout | `vcs=git`, `vcs.revision=2ab365d6…`, `vcs.time`, `vcs.modified=false`; module `v0.2.2-0.20260918035413-2ab365d6cb3e` | `codeaf v0.2.2-0.20260918035413-2ab365d6cb3e · go1.26.5 linux/arm64` |
| the same tree copied without its `.git` | no vcs rows at all | `codeaf dev (no revision stamped …) · go1.26.5 linux/arm64` |

So a plain `go build` is not the condition — `internal/buildinfo` already falls back to
`vcs.revision` and it works. **What leaves a binary with nothing to name is having no VCS to read**:
a tree that is not a checkout, an archive, a vendored copy, `-buildvcs=false`.

And `make build` cannot fix that case, because its own stamp is
`BUILD_REV := $(shell git rev-parse --short HEAD)` — it needs the same checkout the plain build
needed. Both roads need one, so the line names the checkout:

```
codeaf dev (no revision stamped — built outside a git checkout) · go1.26.5 linux/arm64
```

## The test had to change with it, and that is the part to review

`cmd/codeaf/polishrows_test.go` asserted the sentence must contain `make build` — it encoded the same
wrong belief, so it could not survive a correct message. It now asserts the sentence names the
condition, and its comment carries the measurement above so the next reader does not restore the old
claim. **I am flagging this deliberately**: changing a test's expectation is a claim about intent, not
a mechanical fix. The intent I kept is the one the row was written for — an unstamped build must not
wear the bare word `dev` like a release name, and must say something a bug report can act on. The
intent I dropped is that the something must be a Makefile target.

## Also corrected in place

`docs/design/polish/audit-commands.md` row 29 recorded **`debug.ReadBuildInfo` was not the fallback
row 29 assumed it was**, stating the tree embeds no `vcs.revision` under a plain `go build`. That is
not true on this toolchain. The row keeps its history and carries a dated correction with the
measurement, rather than being quietly rewritten.

## Evidence

- `go test ./cmd/codeaf -run 'TestPolish|Version|version'` ok, and
  `go test ./internal/buildinfo ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw` all ok, on the Spark cluster over
  ssh. Full scoped log for this head is linked in a comment below.
- The two builds in the table above, run on Spark, `go version -m` read on each binary.

## Not claimed

Nothing about the laptop. The report that started this was `go build` on a laptop printing the `dev`
line, and the cause there is that the tree in question is not a git checkout at all — no code change
reaches that, which is why this PR changes only what the line says.

body:
PR #1145 stopped four `cmd/codeaf` tests from writing into a profile the environment named, one test
at a time, and proposed the real stopper without doing it. This is the stopper.

## What was wrong

`isolateTestEnvironment` (`testenv_test.go`) is the floor `TestMain` gives every test in the
package. It moved `HOME` and `CODEAF_HOME` into a temp root and left `CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` alone —
and `config.ProfilePath` answers an exported profile **before** it falls back to the state root. So
the floor covered every variable except the one that outranks both, and a harness that exports a
profile at a live `chat.log` reached the whole package rather than the four roads #1145 had named.

**The obvious version of this fix is a no-op**, which is worth stating because it is the trap here:
`pinTestEnv` deliberately skips any variable already set to a non-empty value, so adding the profile
to the map it is handed would do nothing in exactly the case that matters and would pass on every
developer machine, where the variable is unset. The profile is therefore **cleared unconditionally**
and restored in the cleanup — the way `internal/tui3`'s `TestMain` already does it. Empty reads as
unset everywhere in `internal/config`.

## Failing test first

`testfloor_test.go` holds the floor from the outside, because a test that pins the variable itself
cannot fail on a floor that does not clear it — which is why #1145's four pins could not be the
failing case any more. A child of the test binary is started with `CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` exported at
an empty stand-in; the child takes the real fault road and asserts what the floor left it; the parent
reads the stand-in back. Assertions are on *where* the write landed and on what the child inherited,
never on a byte of any real profile, and the stand-in is a directory the test created.

Verified by hand on the unfixed tree — `testfloor_test.go` alone, dropped onto `santos/dev` at
`7231347e`:

```
testfloor_test.go:75: a package test wrote into the profile the environment named despite the
floor: [chat.log]
    --- FAIL: TestTheFloorLeftThisProcessNoInheritedProfile
        the floor left CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR in this process's environment:
        "/tmp/TestThePackageFloorClearsAProfileTheEnvironmentNamed.../001/profile"
```

## What is deliberately not here

#1145's four per-test pins stay, belt and braces under the floor. Removing them is a separate
decision.

## Review note

The child guard's own comment claimed it never runs in the suite's process. That was wrong — it is
an ordinary `Test` function and does run there, where it reads the floor's clear and passes. The
comment now says so and says why that pass is worth having; the second commit is only that comment.

## Evidence

- `go test ./cmd/codeaf ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw -count=1` — **all ok, exit 0**
  (`cmd/codeaf` 87.9s) on the Spark cluster over ssh from a fresh clone, on this change's content.
  Re-run against this branch head is attached below in a comment if it differs.
- The failing-first run above, on `7231347e` with only the new test file added.

## History

This change was briefly pushed straight onto `santos/dev` as `5e257557` by mistake — a push from a
local branch that carried a shared branch's name — and was reverted there by `4dd1c562`. It is
unchanged apart from the comment fix and the changelog number, and it is here for the review it
should have had.

## What

`codeaf pool show --cells` lists the held index's cells, one per line, under a `cells:` header after the metric lines: the metric, the role and model the cell is addressed by, the dims it spells in the order the metric declares them, the measurement (`mean` for a gaussian metric, `share` for a bernoulli one, from the document's `kind`), `sd` where it is non-zero, `n`, and `installs` where the cell carries them. A metric with no cells says `none`. The order is the index's own — never a sort by a number.

`--json --cells` adds a `cells` array of `{metric, role, model, dims, mean, sd, n, installs}` beside the existing summary; without the flag neither the words nor the object change.

`internal/pool/index`: `Cell` now carries `Installs` (the count the floor reads; zero where the cell spells none) instead of dropping it after the floor check.

A flag rather than a fourth verb: the cells are what show shows, read one layer deeper, so they ride show's own answer and its `--json`.

Manual: one sentence on the flag in the pool section of running-from-the-terminal.

## Testing

On the Spark host, fresh clone of `pool/show-cells` at `bd687f2cc`, log `~/src/trees/check-bd687f2cc.log`:

```

go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw -count=1   → ok
```

New tests: `TestPoolShowCellsListsEachCellWithItsInstallsAndItsDims`, `TestPoolShowCellsSaysNoneForAMetricWithNoCells`, `TestACellCarriesTheInstallsItSpells`.

## What

The seed index the binary carries (`internal/pool/index/seed.json`) is regenerated from the live relay by one in-repo command, and the trusted pool key has one importable home.

- `internal/pool/poolkey`: the index signer's ed25519 public key, spelled once; `cmd/codeaf/pool.go` and the generator both import it (`Keys()` hands back a copy). The pin test moves with it.
- `internal/pool/index/cmd/seedgen`: `go run ./internal/pool/index/cmd/seedgen [-url] [-mirror] [-key … ] [-out] [-cells] [-check]`. It fetches `index.json` + `.sig` through `internal/pool/pull` (signature under the build's key, size cap, mirror when the relay does not answer), refuses a document `index.Parse` refuses, and renders the seed deterministically: fixed key order, cells grouped by metric and sorted by the metric's declared dims. It copies by declaration — every metric with its declaration, every cell verbatim by its metric's dims — so a metric or a dim this build has never seen passes through unchanged. The embedded seed's aliases are merged under the live document's. It refuses a missing or non-integer `version`, an unparseable `generated`, a cell below the live floor, an undeclared metric, and a rendered seed over 1 MiB. `-check` diffs and writes nothing, exit 1 on drift. It also writes `docs/design/model-pool/data/seed-cells.csv` (the `role_quality` cells) from the same document.
- `seed.json` regenerated once with the tool: it now carries `version`, `installs` on every cell, both metric declarations and rubrics, the relay's floor and judge list. `seed_test.go` grows: every cell in the file survives `Parse` per metric, both metrics and rubrics declared, `installs` on every cell, a positive integer version and a real day, a size bound.
- `pool_test.go` reads the seed's day from the seed instead of pinning a date.
- RUNBOOK: one release step (`-check`, review the diff, regenerate when it drifts).

## Why

Nothing in the repository generated the seed; it was a hand-authored snapshot that lagged what the relay publishes, and a fresh install picks from it until a signed index is cached.

## Testing

On the Spark host, fresh clone of `pool/seedgen` at `4fe0b19e8`, log `~/src/trees/check-4fe0b19e8.log`:

```
go test ./internal/pool/... ./cmd/codeaf -count=1   → ok (index, index/cmd/seedgen, judge, outbox, poolcfg, poolkey, pull, record, tally, cmd/codeaf)
go test ./internal/guard ./internal/namelaw -count=1 → ok
go vet ./internal/pool/index/cmd/seedgen ./internal/pool/poolkey → clean
go run ./internal/pool/index/cmd/seedgen -check → "seed.json and seed-cells.csv are what the relay would write", exit 0
```

body:
## Why

Do-loop diagnosis cause (b), "gate-after-grown", reduced to a proof test. The concern was that a job which grew earlier (an overrun spliced a continuation) might not be gated when it finally lands its top-level root — the shape awilix landed in. Investigation showed the gate is already correct once pacing (#1144) lets the grown job reach its root landing: the delivery gate reads the root's OWN landing, and the growing flag is set only for the leaf landing that grows, never for the top-level job node that later gathers the pieces. So the root's landing arrives with `continuing=false` and is gated. The awilix miss was the wall cutting the job off before that landing, which #1144 fixes.

This PR pins that law so a future refactor can't silently drop it.

## What

`cmd/codeaf/gate_after_grown_test.go` (new, test-only): table test over `shouldGate`. A top-level job node (`Parent==store.RootID`, non-reflex, non-nil outcome, not continuing) is gated; the growing-leaf landing (`continuing=true`), reflex group, non-root child, and nil-outcome shapes are exempt.

Note: at this revision the growing flag reaches `shouldGate` as its `continuing` argument (3-arg signature; there is no `carriedOn` parameter in this tree).

## Tests

`go test ./cmd/codeaf/ -run ShouldGate` PASS. `go build ./...`, `go vet ./cmd/codeaf/` green. Test-only; no production code changed.

body:
A test in `cmd/codeaf` wrote a fake crash — `runtime error: slice bounds out of range [:-1]` —
into a live profile's `chat.log`, where it read as a genuine crash. The test had moved `HOME`
and `CODEAF_HOME` to directories of its own. That is not enough, and the gap is the whole point
of this change.

## What was wrong

`reportFault` appends through `config.ProfilePath(config.ProfileDir(), "chat.log")`, and it has
to: the surface's running log and the crash's append are one file, so a profile that moved
the first must move the second. **`CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` therefore decides where a fault test's
fixture lands, and it outranks both variables a test naturally reaches for** — an exported
profile wins over `CODEAF_HOME`, which only answers where the state root is when no profile
was named. A harness that exports a profile points every such test at somebody else's log.

## What changed

Tests only. Four tests and helpers now name every variable that decides where their writes go:

| file | what followed the inherited profile |
|---|---|
| `nopanic_test.go` | the fault fixture itself, into `chat.log` |
| `telemetry_test.go` (`telemetryHome`) | the profile's telemetry row through `config.WriteTelemetry`, and the spool read back |
| `chatv3_belt_test.go` | the model catalog (`catalog.LoadLazy`) and the pool's index refresh, both seated by `openV3Process` |
| `vocabulary_test.go` | `pool/install` and `pool/outbox.jsonl`, minted by the launch `do` and `exec` seat |

**Reading found three of the four.** The fourth was found by running the roads instead: every
`cmd/codeaf` test that seats a launch or writes a profile path was run with
`CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` pointed at an empty directory, and the directory was then read. The other
launch-seating rows in `vocabulary_test.go` stopped at a missing key before any errand started
and wrote nothing across three runs each.

## Failing test first

`faultprofile_test.go` holds the fault case down **from the outside**, because a test that pins
the variable itself cannot fail on the tree that leaked. It runs the fault test as a child
process with `CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` at an empty stand-in directory and then reads the stand-in.
The assertion is on *where* the file landed and never on a byte of its text, and it reads only
directories it created, so no real profile is touched — not even to check it.

Verified by hand on the unfixed tree: `faultprofile_test.go` alone, dropped onto `6c98ddca`
with none of the fixes,

```
--- FAIL: TestAFaultTestKeepsItsFixtureOutOfAProfileItInherited (0.03s)
    faultprofile_test.go:65: the fault test wrote into the profile the environment named
    instead of one of its own: [chat.log]
```

## What would stop the class, proposed and not done

`cmd/codeaf`'s `TestMain` already gives the package a floor — `isolateTestEnvironment` in
`testenv_test.go` — and that floor pins `HOME` and `CODEAF_HOME` but not
`CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR`; `pinTestEnv` also leaves alone any variable the process was deliberately
started with, which is exactly the harness case. Clearing `CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR` unconditionally
there, the way `internal/tui3`'s `TestMain` already does, would cover all 170 test files in the
package at once. **It is deliberately not in this PR**: it changes what every test in the
package inherits, which is a wider claim than this leak needs, and it wants its own review.

## Evidence

- `go test ./cmd/codeaf -count=1` — **ok, 81.2s, exit 0** — on the Spark cluster over ssh from a
  fresh clone of this PR's head `44791a3da4023680a02bbfe110706348d51eaa41`, rebased onto
  `santos/dev` at `49760fb4`.
- The failing-first run above, on `6c98ddca` with only the new test file added.

## One inconsistency left alone

`vocabulary_test.go` writes the literal `"CODEAF_PROFILE_DIR"` while the other three use
`config.ProfileDirEnv`. It matches the literal `"CODEAF_HOME"` on the line above it in that
file, so it was left as the local idiom rather than made consistent across files.

body:
## Why

`internal/resident/grow.go` reads how near the wall is from the job's own measured round pace, and `jobPace` returns 0 for a job with no measured round yet. Zero pace meant "not near", so a FIRST replan round was admitted however close the wall was. It then ran long and the clock killed it mid-round: the job was released with its root unlanded, no delivery gate was ever cut, and broken work shipped. ds1 bought a first round at 40m22s of a 45m wall; awilix ended the same way with a `src/awilix.ts` a build would have caught. (Root cause from the do-loop diagnosis.)

## What changed

- When `jobPace` returns 0, `wallNear` is now read against a conservative floor, `roundFloor(node)`: the elapsed runtime of the leaf that just overran (it has run that long without finishing, and a round replanning the same remainder can hardly cost less), or `noPaceRoundFloor` (4 min, the benchmark's median round, biased low) where no start was stamped. A first round the wall cannot hold is handed over via the existing `RefusedOutOfWall` path — which closes the job out so a gate precedes the wall — instead of being killed mid-flight. The measured-pace branch and every other refusal (rounds, ceiling, rail) are unchanged, and the floor leans toward finishing: the wall refuses a round only when it cannot hold even that much.

## Tests

`internal/resident/grow_test.go`: a first overrun round with no measured pace is refused (`CauseOutOfWall`) when the wall cannot hold the floor, and admitted when it can. `go build ./...` and `go test ./internal/resident/` green.

The chat screen manual says the status row's ledger, meter and job counts all stay the
conversation's. That has been false for the ledger since `c7142ca4` (2026-08-31) made the
bill tree-inclusive, and the same page already contradicts it two screens earlier.

## What is wrong

`internal/manual/chat/screen.md` describes the bill as **what this conversation and its
tasks have spent** where it introduces the groups, and then, in the paragraph about a task
room, says:

> The ledger, the meter and the job counts on the same row stay the conversation's, because
> those are measurements of a session.

The code says the first one. `internal/tui3`'s `spendShown` draws the larger of the subtree
receipt (`session.UsageTree`) and the conversation's own books, and every call a task
subtree makes writes one ledger line rooted at the chat conversation's session id, so a
running node's spend is in the bill whether or not its room is open. `/cost` is where the
two halves are taken apart.

Nothing catches the stale sentence: the Manual CI step checks commands and aliases only
(`manual_test.go`), so a prose claim about a figure can go out of date silently.

## What changed

One paragraph in `internal/manual/chat/screen.md`. The meter and the job counts keep the
sentence they had — those really are the conversation's, and the meter is the only one of
the three with a defined window, which is the reading the compaction decision uses. No code,
no behaviour, no test.

## Where this came from

A read-only diagnosis of what the status row draws while a task subtree is running, which
found the manual claim while establishing that the bill is already correct. The same
diagnosis recommends one behaviour change that is **not** in this PR and is waiting on a
decision: while the chat door is at rest and its subtree is working, the state word says
`idle`, and it could say what the subtree is doing instead — everything needed is already in
hand at draw time, and the cost is about thirteen `idle` assertions in `internal/tui3` plus
the vocabulary table on this same manual page.

`codeaf pool status` counted the outbox's rows and named the last live judge, but said nothing about the landings the headless doors leave in `pool/pending.jsonl` for the restart sweep (#1132, #1137–#1139) or about the sweep itself — so a person could not tell whether their `exec`/`run`/`do` runs were being scored at all.

**What changed** (`cmd/codeaf/pool.go`, `cmd/codeaf/poolrecord.go`): status prints `pending judge: 1 · oldest do run 3h` (unjudged rows of the pending file — rows with no `pool/judged/<id>-<attempt>` marker — with the oldest one's door and age) and `last sweep: 2m ago · judged 3 · 2 still pending · 41s of 10m`, in the last-judge line's shape; `--json` carries `pending_judge` and `last_sweep` beside the outbox count and judge record. The sweep leaves one record of itself at its end, `pool/sweep-last.json` `{at, judged, left, budget_used, cut}` (`sweepClaim`/`sweepPending` now answer what they judged and what the deadline left). Pending rows carry `at`, the moment they were written; rows from before the stamp say an unknown age. An install with nothing waiting says `pending judge: none` / `last sweep: none yet`.

**Tests first** (`pool_test.go`, `poolrecord_test.go`): two pending rows (doors `do`, `exec`, one judged) and a sweep record → the two lines and the `--json` fields; an empty profile → the two "none" forms; the sweep writes its record. Failed on `santos/dev`.

The `--json` answers of show, status and verify carry `metric_list` (`name, kind, unit, dims, cells, sources`) beside the `metrics` count, which stays an integer so today's readers keep working. A headless `codeaf do` run was never scored by the Model Pool: the do door runs the resident's brain over a store journal and builds no `session.Agent`, so `Config.TaskLanded` — the seam a chat landing reaches the live judge on — never fired for it.

**What changed** (`cmd/codeaf/do.go`): `errandRun` leaves the run's landing in `<profile>/pool/pending.jsonl` through `writePendingLanding(profileDir, "do", landing)` (#1132's contract) after `priceErrand`, so the run's own bill is settled first — the judge's later spend stays in the usage ledger under its own seat and never enters this envelope, whose `Spend` is a read of `SpendSinceSeq` and may not disagree with it. The row carries the run's worker (`seats.Work.Model`), the root's deliverable, the artifact count and the tokens `priceErrand` summed, state `unverified`, an id minted from the run's start in nanoseconds (the sweep dedups on `<id>-<attempt>`). A run this process handed to a resident writes no row (that work settles elsewhere), and neither does a pool that forbids reading. Nothing waits on a judge.

**Tests first** (`cmd/codeaf/do_pending_test.go`): one `do` row with the run's model, deliverable, artifact count and tokens; pool off → no file; a run handed to a resident → no file. Failed on `santos/dev`.

A headless `codeaf exec` run was invisible to the Model Pool: it builds no session graph, so the chat door's live landing hook (`Config.TaskLanded`) never fires for it, and nothing reached the judge.

**What changed** (`cmd/codeaf/exec.go`): at the run's tail, after `linear.Run` returns and before the envelope is written, the door appends one row to `<profile>/pool/pending.jsonl` through `writePendingLanding(profileDir, "exec", landing)` (#1132's contract) — model, answer, files, tokens, state `unverified`; the restart-time sweep judges it later under the `exec` door. Nothing waits on a judge: one `O_APPEND` and the process exits. A pool that forbids reading, or a run that left nothing (error with no text and no files), writes no row. The row's id is the run's start in nanoseconds, since the sweep dedups on `<id>-<attempt>` and two runs must never share one.

**Tests first** (`cmd/codeaf/exec_pending_test.go`): a run with the pool on leaves exactly one `exec` row with the run's model, text and tokens in the unverified state; with the pool off no file appears. Failed on `santos/dev`.

After #1128 a submit batch cost one KV `get` and one KV `put` per row (the sheet triple and the per-row `seen/<install>/<nonce>` key) plus reads: an install re-sending a 200-row outbox spent 400 writes to fold a handful of cells, and KV writes are metered per day.

**What changed** (`relay/src/worker.js`): a day's folded nonces live under one key, `seen/<install>/<day>` (newline-joined, one-week TTL), read once per day in the batch; fresh rows are grouped by sheet key and folded in memory before one `put` per key; the seen set and the quota counter are written once per day with fresh rows. Per batch: writes = distinct (day, cell) keys + days with fresh rows × 2; reads of the same order; neither scales with rows — 200 rows over ten cells on one day is 12 writes where it was 400. The idempotence contract is unchanged (a stored nonce is neither folded nor charged; a wholly remembered batch is `202 accepted: 0`), and its KV-consistency limit is now stated on the one key. A quota raised past what one value holds is refused (500) rather than allowed to drop nonces. Retries straddling the deploy may fold once more — the same window the per-row key had.

**Test first** (`relay/test/worker.test.js`): the fake KV counts its operations; six rows over two cells on one day cost 4 puts (two sheets, the seen set, the quota) — 12 on `santos/dev`; the retried-batch, mixed-batch and repeated-nonce tests keep their assertions on triples, quota and `accepted`.

`docs/design/model-pool/RUNBOOK.md`: what a batch costs the meter, the seen set's bound against KV's value limit, and the plan's daily write limit (`plan: <operator fills in>` — neither the runbook nor `wrangler.toml` names the plan; the free tier's figures are beside it).

Change note: `docs/changes/unreleased/1136-the-relay-writes-once-per-cell-per-batch.md`.

## Why

The finished-tree verify reading is taken at the errand's workspace root. A corpus task clones its project into a subdirectory of that root (awilix under `./repo`, bandit under `./bandit`), so discovery at the bare root opened no manifest, Makefile or script and the reading came back "this project declares no way of checking itself" — nothing ran, and awilix shipped a `src/awilix.ts` a build would have caught. (Root cause from the do-loop diagnosis.)

## What changed

- `internal/verify/photograph.go`: when the workspace root declares no check, `locateProject` looks one level down and takes the reading at the single immediate subdirectory that declares one (`subdirectoryProject`, sorted for determinism, skipping built/foreign dirs by the same `SkipTree`/`skipBuilt` the walk already uses). The reading is re-rooted onto that project so every downstream reader (second reading, journal, delivery gate) runs the command where the project is. When the root itself declares a check, behavior is unchanged.
- `internal/exec/photograph.go`: honors the discovered project root so the before- and after-readings are taken at the same place.

Only `internal/verify/photograph.go` is touched in the verify package, per the split with #1125.

## Tests

body:
The outbox file (`<profile>/pool/outbox.jsonl`) was append-only with nothing that ever rewrote it: a line for every row an install ever judged, and later the marker that retired it. Every `Send` and every `Pending` read the whole file back, so a long-lived install's work per judgement grew with everything it had ever judged.

**What changed** (`internal/pool/outbox/outbox.go`): a `Send` whose file has grown mostly into retired rows — more lines than twice the pending rows, past a floor of 1024 lines — rewrites it to exactly the pending rows (`compactLocked`): a temporary file in the same directory, fsynced, renamed over the original, then the handle reopened; never truncated in place. A crash before the rename leaves the old file whole, one after it leaves the same pending rows — no row lost, no retired row back to be sent twice. It runs under `mu` at the start of `Send`, before its first POST, so no `Send` of the process is between a POST and its markers; a failed rewrite is not a failed `Send`. The one-writer-per-profile assumption the append-only file already rested on is now stated: a second process holding the old file writes to the unlinked inode.

**Tests first** (`outbox_test.go`): a file seeded past the floor with retired rows and two pending rows compacts to exactly those two, in order, on `Send`; rows appended after a compaction survive a reopen. Both failed on `santos/dev`.

Change note: `docs/changes/unreleased/1133-the-outbox-file-is-compacted.md`.

## Why this must land

The Model Pool judge only ran when a live process reached a node's terminal state, on a fire-and-forget goroutine. A process death mid-run left the node final in `tasks.json` but never judged, so those runs never reached `own.json`/`outbox` — and the headless doors (do, exec, run), which own no session graph, were never judged at all. This closes both gaps with one bounded restart-time sweep, and lays the seam the learning-crew door tails and #1123's grader build on.

## What changed

- **door parameter** threaded through `poolJudgeHook`/`poolJudgeLanding` into `recorder.Record` (default `"task"`).
- **per-run judged marker** `pool/judged/<id>-<attempt>`, written at every terminal judge outcome. The live hook writes but never gates on it, so a resettle still re-judges; only the sweep gates, so each run is swept at most once.
- **CheckedOn** persisted on `taskRecord` and **Attempt** on `session.TaskLanding`, so a run rebuilt from the checkpoint keeps its high seat.
- **writePendingLanding** appends one `O_APPEND` line to `pool/pending.jsonl` — the seam the headless doors record a landing on. The row is forward-compatible (optional `by_model`/`propensity`/`acceptable`/`source`).
- **poolJudgeSweep** wired in `chatv3.go` on a `guard.Go` goroutine: key-gated (no key, rows wait), budget-bounded, claims `pending.jsonl` by atomic rename (torn last line tolerated), and judges the resumed session's own final-state nodes via `session.LoadLandedForJudge` — each run once.

## Tests

New: `TestPoolJudgeSweepJudgesAPendingRowOnceThenNeverAgain`, `TestPoolJudgeSweepWithNoKeyLeavesRowsWaiting`, `TestPoolJudgeSweepToleratesATornPendingLine` (cmd/codeaf); `TestLoadLandedForJudgeRebuildsAFinalNodeWithItsHighSeat`, `TestLoadLandedForJudgeSkipsNodesStillInFlight` (internal/session). Existing pool/judge tests updated for the door param and green.

Full make check log attached in a follow-up comment.

The signed index carried every cell, the ones below its own `min_installs` floor sorted after the ones that meet it. A cell with `installs: 1` is one contributor's mean, `n` and `sd` for one model, public in the document although every client drops it unread (`internal/pool/index` floors on `installs` since #1127). The floor exists so no single install's numbers are published; a cell below it must not leave the relay.

**What changed** (`relay/src/sheet.js`): `aggregate` drops the cells below the floor before the sort, so the sort's floor-split goes and every cell in the document meets the floor. The seam is the sheet, not `buildIndex`: `aggregate`'s only caller is the publish path, and a sheet that never produces a below-floor cell needs no second reader to remember the rule. A document whose every cell is below the floor is a signed document with an empty `cells` array.

**Test first** (`relay/test/sheet.test.js`): triples from one install for model A and from three installs for model B under `min_installs: 3` — the cells hold B alone; the old below-floor ordering test is rewritten to assert the drop. Failed on `santos/dev`.

body:
An outbox `Send` that met a refused batch left every row of it, and every row behind it, pending. The relay refuses a whole batch on the first line it cannot validate (`400 {"error":"line N: <why>"}`), and that refusal is permanent for the row — a payload from an older or newer client, or schema drift — so it was retried at the head of the batch on every judged run and every start-up, refused again, and nothing from that install reached the pool again.

**What changed** (`internal/pool/outbox/outbox.go`): `sendHTTP` posts through `postBatch`; a 400 whose reply names `line N` marks row N of the batch as posted `dropped` (the marker that keeps it gone across a reopen) and posts the rest of the batch again within the same `Send` — one POST per refused row at most, inside the `Send` budget. A 400 that names no line, a 413 and a 429 still return the error and keep their rows pending (none names a row; retiring one would be a guess); 5xx unchanged.

**Tests first** (`outbox_test.go`): a destination that answers `400 line 2: role must be …` while the bad row is in the batch and 202 otherwise — after `Send` the bad row carries a `dropped` marker, the two good rows are `sent`, count 2; a 429 leaves all three pending and returns the error. Both failed on `santos/dev`.

The relay folded a resubmitted batch again. `handleRows` (`relay/src/worker.js`) keyed nothing by a row's identity, while the client keeps every outbox row that did not get a 202 and re-sends it on the next judged run and at start-up — a timeout after the relay had already stored the batch is the ordinary case. The retry was summed into the install's running total a second time and charged against its daily quota a second time. The row's nonce was already required on the wire (`validateRow`) and unused at storage.

**What changed** (`relay/src/worker.js`): a folded row's nonce is recorded under `seen/<install>/<nonce>` with a one-week TTL; rows whose nonce is already stored are neither folded nor charged, a nonce repeated inside one batch folds once, and `accepted` counts the rows folded now — so a wholly remembered batch still answers 202 (`accepted: 0`), which is all the client needs to mark its rows sent. The comment states the limit: idempotence is as strong as KV's eventual consistency, no stronger.

**Tests first** (`relay/test/worker.test.js`): the same two-row batch posted twice folds `n: 2`, quota 2, both 202; a batch repeating a stored nonce and adding one row folds only the new row; a nonce repeated inside one batch folds once. The existing fixtures now carry distinct nonces per row.

The relay computes `min_installs` over distinct contributors (installs) and folds their rows into a cell's `n`; the client held cells against the floor by `n`. So a cell one contributor filled with nine rows passed a floor of three, and a cell three contributors shared over three rows was held below it — the opposite of what the floor is for.

**What changed** (`internal/pool/index/index.go`): `addCell` counts the floor on the cell's `installs` where the document carries it, on `n` where it does not (the seed document carries rows alone); `installs` is now a reserved cell field, never a dim. `crewpick.PriorFromCells` keeps its floor on rows, with a comment saying why that still holds (rows cannot be fewer than the installs that produced them; the cells built from an install's own sheet carry rows alone). `N` keeps meaning rows everywhere, so the learn blend is unchanged.

Adds `docs/benchmarks/`: a script that measures any command-line agent's footprint the same way, the method it follows, and one day's numbers for seven CLIs on one machine.

## Procedure

One Linux machine (aarch64, 20 cores, 119 GB RAM), one repository (a CodeAF checkout, 3,249 Go files), one session, every CLI on its own authenticated profile, folder-trust dialogs cleared first. `docs/benchmarks/measure-cli.sh --name <cli> --home <profile> -- <command>` once per CLI:

- **On disk**: bytes of the installed binary plus everything it needs to run.
- **Cold start**: wall clock for `--version`, best of 20 (hyperfine when present).
- **First frame**: launch until the first non-blank character in a 160x48 tmux pane on a private socket.
- **Memory, idle**: 30 s after the first frame, whole process tree, RSS, PSS (shared pages counted once), peak RSS, idle CPU.
- **Memory, one turn**: the same prompt to each, sampled every 0.5 s over 40 s.
- **Startup work**: `strace -f -e trace=openat,connect,execve` over `--version`, invoked directly.

The script kills only processes it started, by pid. Full method and limits in `docs/benchmarks/README.md`.

body:
Two changes that cost a launch less, each measured on the same machine, and a short account of
three more that were tried and are not here.

## What changed

**`internal/verify`'s regexps compile on first use.** All 78 of its patterns were package-level
`regexp.MustCompile` vars, so every one was compiled before `main` on every invocation —
`--version` included, which reads no runner output and needs none of them. Each is now behind a
lazy holder. The patterns, the captures and the order a vocabulary is tried in are untouched, and
`MustCompile`'s panic on a malformed pattern is kept: it now fails loudly at first use rather than
at package init.

```
internal/verify init   1.5 ms, 1539664 bytes, 11143 allocs
                  ->   0.033 ms, 15216 bytes, 243 allocs
--version best-of-20   14236 us -> 12455 us      (interleaved runs)
```

**A surface caps the scheduler at 8 Ps, and its engine host inherits the cap.** The Go runtime
holds one GC-worker goroutine per P for the life of a process, so on a 20-core box an idle daemon
carries 20 of them. `tuneForTheSurface` already makes one trade of this kind for the interactive
surfaces and leaves every other command on the Go default; this is the same bargain in a different
unit. An explicit `GOMAXPROCS` still decides, exactly as an explicit `GOGC` already does in that
function, and a machine no bigger than the cap is left alone — the variable is not even set.

```
idle engine daemon, 20-core box, two runs each side
  goroutines / GC workers / OS threads
  unset (20 Ps)   33 / 20 / 13
  capped (8 Ps)   21 /  8 / 11

live chat pair
  host      52 -> 40 goroutines, 20 -> 8 GC workers
  family   ~29 -> ~26 OS threads
```

## What this does not do, stated plainly

- **The surface process keeps its 20 GC workers.** `GOMAXPROCS` is read at runtime startup, before
  any Go code runs, so a cap set inside `tuneForTheSurface` lands after those workers are born.
  Only the engine host gets 8, because it is a separate process and inherits the variable. Chasing
  the surface's own workers would need a re-exec, which is not worth it: parked mark workers cost
  no wakeups.
- **RSS does not move.** ~104 MB for the live pair before and after. This change removes
  goroutines and threads, not memory.
- **Idle wakeups are not demonstrably improved.** The figure ranged 0 to 84 voluntary context
  switches per second across repeated runs of the *same* build, so the spread is reported rather
  than a number, and no claim is made from it.

## Three things tried and not included

- **The syntax-highlighting lexer registry** is the single largest remaining startup cost: chroma's
  `lexers` package builds its registry in a package-level var that XML-parses every embedded lexer
  at init — 7.3 ms of clock, 2.75 MB, 31,517 allocs on this build, now the dominant entry in
  `inittrace`. It cannot be made lazy from our side: the var is upstream's, and importing the
  package at all runs it. The routes are vendoring the registry, carrying a fork, or an upstream
  lazy registry — a dependency-policy decision rather than an optimisation, so it is raised, not
  taken.
- **Dropping the eager catalog warm** would move a fetch and parse onto the first frame: the v3
  first-frame path reaches the catalog's resolve eleven times through the waiting door, which is
  the stall the eager warm exists to prevent. Left alone.
- **`CGO_ENABLED=0`** is worth about a millisecond and removes the loader pass, but it switches the
  binary to Go's pure resolver, which behaves differently under split DNS and unusual `nsswitch`
  configurations. Proving that behaviour unchanged across darwin, linux and windows is not
  something one Linux box can support, so it stays out.

## Evidence

Spark cluster over plain ssh, from a clone at this head.

- `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/verify/ ./cmd/codeaf/`
- `go test ./internal/verify/ -count=1` — ok
- `go test ./cmd/codeaf/ -run 'Tune|Surface|GOMAXPROCS|GC' -count=1` — ok
- `GODEBUG=inittrace=1 ./bin/codeaf --version`: `internal/verify` no longer appears in the top
  entries; best-of-20 wall clock **12513 us** on this head against 14236 us before.
- Full `make check` log path is appended below once the run on this head completes.

`TestTheLaunchesBlockingCatalogReadsDoNotGrow` failed once with `TempDir RemoveAll cleanup: unlinkat …/pool: directory not empty` and passed on the rerun: a race, and it will recur.

**Cause**: `wirePoolIndex` starts the Model Pool's two start-up errands fire-and-forget through `guard.Go` — the index refresh (writes `doc.json` + `.sig` under the profile's pool directory) and the outbox push (rewrites the outbox, writes the install nonce). Nothing joined or cancelled them when the process closed, so a closed process left writers running against its profile. In a test that is the TempDir being removed under a live writer; on a door that reopens on another profile it is a write into a directory the process no longer owns. The errands' own budgets do not keep this: a budget bounds one fetch, not the goroutine's life.

**What changed** (`cmd/codeaf/poolindex.go`, `cmd/codeaf/chatv3_process.go`): the errands are seated per profile on one context and one `sync.WaitGroup` (`poolErrandsStart` / `poolErrandGo`), still through the `poolRefreshGo` seam; `v3Process.closeAll` calls `stopPoolErrands(profileDir)` first — cancel, then wait — before it closes the conversations and the stores. Idempotent; a profile with no live errands is a no-op. Neither errand is on a run's path, so the join costs nothing at the prompt.

**Test first** (`cmd/codeaf/poolleak_test.go`): an endpoint that holds the index fetch open makes the race certain; open a launch, `closeAll`, then every goroutine started through `poolRefreshGo` must have returned within a fraction of the pull budget. It failed on `santos/dev`.

**The other road** (`chatv3_local_test.go`): the first run of the scoped suites failed `TestAPlainLaunchKeepsThisMachinesDoorsWhileAHostLaunchDoesNot` with the same cleanup error. `hostOptions` (`chatv3_host.go`) wires the pool on the terminal's profile too; the host doors exit the process behind their errands, that test does not. Measured 4/30 failures on `santos/dev` alone — pre-existing. Two things follow: `poolErrandsStart` keeps a profile's tracker on a second wiring (replacing it would orphan the first wiring's errands — the test wires the same profile twice), and the test closes what it wired through `stopPoolErrands` in its cleanup.

Change note: `docs/changes/unreleased/1124-the-pool-writers-stop-when-the-process-closes.md`.

## What this is

The crew picker's one dial is now a **stake in dollars** — what a failed task costs you — and the thing it learns from is a **model-free grade** of what the task left in the tree. The paper (`docs/design/model-pool/pareto-crewing.tex`, PDF committed) is the design; the code lands the decision rule, the grade, one scoreboard, learned seat shapes, the relay side, and the manual pages.

## Code

- `crewpick`: `AtStake(front, stake, tokens)` picks the crew with the least `Loss = bill·tokens/1e6 + stake·(1 − quality/100)`. `frugal` = \$1, `balanced` = \$10 over `TypicalTaskTokens` (4.4M, the median of 133 measured runs); `max` = top of the front. `knee` is deleted. `ShapesFrom` learns each seat's volume and in/out from real tasks, shrunk N/(N+30). `PriorFromCells` folds cells of one seat and model by count.
- `internal/pool/grade` (new): gofmt over the files the task wrote, `go build ./...`, `go vet` and `go test` on the touched packages under 2-/3-minute budgets → `Pass`, `Source` (`codeaf/grader` when tests ran, `codeaf/grader-build` when they did not finish), stage and detail. No `go.mod` → no grade, nothing recorded.
- `internal/pool/record`: metric `acceptable` (100/0 per held seat, `source` dim) is what the picker reads; the judge's 0–100 stays under `role_quality` as evidence. `seed.json` re-keyed to `acceptable`/`reviewer`. `index` holds the floor on `installs` when a cell carries it. `internal/pool/shape` (new) reads the usage ledger into per-task seat spend.
- `config`: `AutoShapes` seam beside `AutoOwnCells`; `PoolQualityMetric = acceptable` (bernoulli); catalog prices scaled to \$/1M at the one seam — a dial in dollars makes the scale matter.
- `cmd/codeaf`: the landing hook grades first, then asks the judge, records both, writes `pool/grade-last.json`; shapes are learned once at start-up.
- `relay/`: accepts both metrics, keys `acceptable` under its own name so stored triples never move, publishes graded cells per source, declares both metrics. **Deploy the relay before this client** — an older relay refuses a batch holding an `acceptable` row.

## Evidence

- Fixture catalog (`crewpick` tests): all-family `balanced` moves from **\$2.60/task at Q 95.4** (glm-flash / fable / fable — the crew whose checker ate 75–80% of real bills) to **\$0.65/task at Q 89.2** (glm-flash / qwen-max / qwen-max). \$50 of stake buys the old crew back. `frugal` and open-family `balanced` are unchanged.
- 133 measured runs: high seat mean token share 0.126 vs the default 0.08; median dollar share 0.45 — most of a dear checker's bill is price, the rest is the tail the learned shape now sees.
- Paper: proxies measured on 202 runs (a run's own `settled` claim ρ = 0.02 of a grade; an off-crew rating 0.42); calibrated simulation: Thompson-in-J does not repay exploration where every model has a catalog index — exploration belongs in a capped, separately-vehicled budget (design only here).
- Tests: `crewpick`, `config`, `pool/*` (incl. the new hook test that grades a real module both ways), relay (35), manual gates, `make test-quick` green locally. Touched-package suite running on Spark from `~/src/af-pareto-v2` at `167329d06` — result to follow, plus a live `/task` smoke under `learn balanced` with the branch binary.

## Base

Temporarily based on `fix/judge-unverified-restart` (b1's judge-restart fix, `cc405486a`) at their and the manager's request, so the grader sits on their hook shape; when that merges to `santos/dev` this PR is rebased and their commits drop out of the diff. Relay half already merged as #1129 and deployed.

## Still design only

Price bands, cascades, the capped exploration budget, the switch guard, a custom stake setting.
title: pareto crewing v2: one dial in dollars, a grade no model can move, and the paper behind it

body:
A bare `auto` seat that resolves under `pick=learn` reported its rung as
`crew balanced, computed from the catalog`. The learn word has its own rung — `learned` — and that
is the honest answer.

## What was wrong

Two functions produce these rungs, and only one of them read the pick word:

- `pickedModel` read it and returned `SeatLearned` under `learn`.
- `autoRow` did not. It returned a hardcoded `SeatComputed`, whatever the pick word said.

`autoRow`'s own doc comment describes it as *"THE ONE SEAM both ladders resolve a tier row that
says `auto` through ... A second copy in each would be a seat that means one thing in chat and
another headless, which is the defect this file exists to prevent."* The rung had become exactly
that second copy.

## What changed

The rung decision now lives once, in `computedRung`, which both seams call. `autoRow` asks
`CrewPickAt(profileDir)` for the word and names the rung from it; `pickedModel` passes the word it
was already given. Neither can name one computation two ways.

The rule is `pickedModel`'s existing one, kept deliberately: **the rung names which pick ran, not
whether the prior moved the id.** `SeatLearned`'s own comment defines it as "a seat computed at
the crew's budget under the `learn` pick", and `pickedModel` has always returned it whenever the
pick is `learn` without asking whether anything changed. Inventing a "only if it moved" rule here
would have made the two seams disagree again, in the other direction.

**The model id does not diverge under `learn`.** `autoRow` computes through `AutoPick`, which is
`AutoPickWith(..., autoPrior(autoIndex()))` — the same pool prior `pickedModel` passes under
`learn`. So only the label was wrong, and only the label is changed.

## A pre-existing divergence found on the way, and deliberately not fixed here

Under `pick=catalog` the two seams **do** disagree about the model, and have all along:

- `pickedModel` leaves `prior` at its zero value for any word that is not `learn`, so `catalog`
  gets the published figures alone — which is what `CrewPickCatalog` is documented to mean:
  *"the catalog's own published figures, with nothing measured on top."*
- `autoRow` calls `AutoPick`, which **always** wraps `autoPrior(autoIndex())`. So a bare `auto`
  row under `catalog` is picked with the pool's measurements on top.

That is a behaviour difference, not a label one, and fixing it would change which model a seat
answers under `catalog` — too big to ride along with a rung fix, and it wants its own test and its
own decision about which of the two is correct. Raised rather than folded in. Note that this PR
makes it slightly more visible: the rung now asserts which pick ran, so a `catalog` rung on the
`autoRow` path claims something the prior contradicts.

## Evidence

Test written and committed before the fix, failing on the tree without it:

```

1643827e  config: a bare auto row names the pick word's rung under learn
```

- `go test ./internal/config/ -count=1` — ok, 3.2s
- `go test ./cmd/codeaf/ -run 'Seat|Crew|Rung' -count=1` — ok, 3.6s
