body:
Closes #942.

## What was true

A task on the rail was called `I'll start by`. The namer is asked for "two or
three words, a label for a narrow column, not a sentence", and on a run with
every tier and role pinned to a reasoning model it answered its plan instead —
264 completion tokens of "I'll start by creating the four bakery landing pages
one at a time." Nothing in the path refused a sentence for being one:
`firstWordsOf` cut it to three words, `taskNameNeeded` asked only whether the
answer was empty, an echo, a path or over three words, and `TaskGraph.rename`
wrote the front of the paragraph over `spec.title` — the person's own words,
sitting right there as the fallback.

Three preambles, three titles, on `dev` before this change:

```
"I'll start by creating the four bakery landing pages one at a time." -> "I'll start by"
"Let me first look at the brief."                                     -> "Let me first"
"First, I will write the four pages."                                 -> "First, I will"
```

## What is true now

**A name is a noun phrase, and a clause about the speaker is not one.** The
refusal is grammar rather than a list of observed sentences: a first-person
subject followed by the word that makes it the subject of something about to
happen — an auxiliary, the remnant `normalizedWords` leaves of one written as a
contraction, or the person `let` is addressed about (`opensAsPlan`, title.go).
Both halves are required, so `we chat cutover` is still a name where
`we'll begin with the first page` is not.

**The opener comes off before the pronoun is read.** The sequencing adverbs a
plan narrates itself with — `first`, `next`, `then`, `now`, `so` — join the
interjections that `stripInterjection` already takes off every answer both
namers read, plus the unpunctuated `okay so` a model writes when it writes the
way somebody talks. That is one mechanism, not a second vocabulary: it also
mints `First, the bakery pages` as `the bakery pages`.

**It refuses before the cut, in the one hand both namers share.** The refusal
lives in `cleanTitle`, so `cleanTaskName`, `cleanConversationTitle` and
`compactTitle` cannot drift apart on what a name is, and it runs before
`firstWordsOf` — the cut can never manufacture a label out of the front of a
sentence. A refusal is the empty string, which is a road that already worked:
`TaskGraph.nameNode` leaves the title where it was, and where it was is the
person's own words.

**A label that ran long is still a label.** `launch post for existing users`
is still cut to `launch post for`. That row is the shape of the problem and it
keeps passing.

## Proof

- `TestANameThatIsAPlanIsRefusedByBothNamers` (titleecho_test.go) — the three
  answers observed in the field and the shapes around them, refused through
  `cleanTitle`, `cleanTaskName` and `cleanConversationTitle` at once, with the
  controls that must keep passing.
- `TestCleanTaskNameCutsToThreeWordsAndRefusesWhatIsNotAName` — the same rows on
  the reader, beside `{"launch post for existing users", "launch post for"}`.
- `TestWorkAdmittedUnderASentenceIsNamedByTheCheapModel` — the whole door, two
  rows: a namer that answers a label renames the row, a namer that answers its
  plan leaves the person's words on it and publishes nothing. Every rung of the
  ladder is scripted, because a refused answer is asked again below.
- `internal/manual/chat/tasks.md` says what is refused, in the section on why a
  task is called something you did not type.

## Spark

Full touched suite on the Spark, isolated clone at `846974332`:

```
touched: ./internal/session

EXIT=0
```

Laptop: `go build ./...`, `go vet ./internal/session/`, gofmt, `make test-laws`
(24 packages), `make manual-gates`, `make changelog-check` — all green.

**`dev` is red by itself, and this is the fix.** `TestHeldOutQuestionsReachTheirPage` scores **16 of 22 against its floor of 17 on `origin/dev` `23f5da1eb`** with no branch changes at all, so `light gate`, `touched packages` and `check` are failing on every open pull request in the wave for a reason none of them caused. It is absent from `.github/known-red.txt`, and that ledger only shrinks (`internal/ci` ratchets `knownRedEntries`, and CLAUDE.md says "Never add a line") — so landing a fix is the only correct move, and this is a one-file one.

### What happened

#933's rewrite of `internal/manual/chat/questions.md` gained enough of the words "always", "write" and "it" to take fourth place away from `standing-orders` for one held-out question:

```
"I want it to always write in british english"   want=standing-orders
before #933: [saved-shapes-of-work opening-files-from-that-machine keys standing-orders]   4th
```

Trimming the page that won would be fixing the wrong page: the asker really is asking about standing orders, and the test's own comment says **"fix the scoring, not these questions"**. `## Always do it this way` already carries "Always run the tests before you tell me it works" and "We use tabs here" — and a rule about how it **writes** is the same kind of thing as a rule about how it **codes**. That the section wanted this sentence is true independently of the test, which is the difference between fixing a page and tuning one.

The asker's words go into that **existing** heading and its prose. Not a new `## ` heading: a new heading hijacks the scoring and breaks unrelated probes, which is a trap this corpus has sprung before.

`TestHeldOutQuestionsReachTheirPage` has been red on a clean `dev` since 23f5da1eb (#933), at **16 of 22 against a floor of 17**, and it blocks the light gate on every pull request.

## What tipped it

Reverting only `questions.md` and `permissions.md` to `b35ce8511` puts the number back at 17, and the logged table says exactly **one** question moved: *"I want it to always write in british english"* fell out of fourth place by three thousandths of a point. What took the place was #933's `Pick several` section of `questions.md`, which now carries *wants*, *writes* and *always* by ordinary accident — one added sentence about the tick's own cell. Nothing about that section is wrong, so it is not what wants changing.

## What changed instead

**`standing-orders.md`** — *Always do it this way* named only coding style rules, and every example under it was code: the tests, the public API, tabs, small commits. The kind that **holds** has never cared what the sentence is about — it is kept word for word and rides into a new conversation and into a task's brief under `Standing orders` whatever it says. The page read as though rules were for code alone, which is a claim it had no business making. The heading now also names *how I want it to write*, and three examples of that shape sit under it.

**`getting-started.md`** — the page a person meets the moment they finish installing never used the word *install*, so *"what is the first thing I should do after installing"* went to `aforge doctor` and to a task's `node_modules` instead. It now opens with its own short section: run `aforge`, the setup opens by itself, and the install line lives on the *running from the terminal* page.

That second one is a **section of its own rather than a paragraph added to the one below**, because padding the existing section cost *"how do I get started"* its first place. The length law, working as designed.

## The numbers

```
held out   first  8/22 → 10/22 · within top 4  16/22 → 18/22   (floors 7 and 17)
plain      first 21/25 → 21/25 · within top 4  25/25 → 25/25   (floors 20 and 25)
```

`go test ./internal/manual/... -count=1` is green, including the probe table in `chat_test.go`.

No test, no floor and no question was touched, and nothing in `internal/manual/asked/` was edited.

Four held-out questions still miss, all four of them from before #933. One of them should not be fixed on the page it names: *"how do I use it from my phone"* wants `asking-from-home`, which is about the `ask here` box on the **home screen** and says nothing about a phone. What actually answers it is `reaching-this-machine-without-ssh` (*Pairing another laptop, a desktop, or a phone*) and `screen` (*Does this work on my phone? Narrow terminals*), and both already come back — just not under that page name. Writing a phone into `asking-from-home` would make the corpus less true, not more.

## What this fixes

A rebuild of \`bin/aforge\` while a session host is holding a conversation leaves the **older** build answering until it is holding nothing — that is the design, and the busy-host case got an entry notice in #691. But the notice only fired when the host reported **Busy** (work in flight). A host holding only an **idle** conversation — the turn finished, the person stepped away — was asked to go, went, and the window opened on the fresh build **without a word**. The person was never told the engine answering them had been a build behind, so they debugged a fix that had simply not reached the conversation yet. (defect ledger: "engine daemon kept running an 11:23 binary … nothing told them — they debug ghosts".)

## The change

`clearStaleEngineHostFor` now owes the notice **whenever the older same-wire build is the one answering**, and names what it was holding:

- **Busy (work in flight)** — unchanged wording: *"…is an older aforge and is still holding work — it picks up this build the moment it goes quiet."*
- **Idle (only keeping the conversation warm), refused to go** — *"…is an older aforge — it is holding this conversation and picks up this build the moment you leave it."*
- **Went quietly (idle, retired on the spot)** — *"…was an older aforge holding this conversation — it has picked up this build."*

A different wire version keeps the refusal it has always had.

## Proof

- `TestASameProtocolIdleOlderBuildIsRetiredAndSaysSo` — the ledger's exact case: idle older build is retired **and** the notice says it was an older build and that it is current now.
- `TestASameProtocolHostOfAnotherBuildIsRetired` — now also asserts the went-quietly notice.
- Busy-host tests unchanged (wording for that case is unchanged).

Heavy proof (\`make pr-ready\`) is running on **Spark** rather than this laptop.

## Manual

Adds a section to *Staying on that machine* documenting the rebuild→notice behavior and the exact sentences.

Home leaves an answer on another conversation's doorstep and says `answered · waiting for it to pick that up` until the owning conversation applies it. For a conversation that is **running**, that is the presence heartbeat, a second or two. For a conversation that was **closed**, nothing was beating: the answer sat in `answers.jsonl` until somebody happened to reopen it, and even then until the new process's first five-second tick — and home said "waiting" the whole time.

The constructor now drains the doorstep itself, after `recoverTasks` has put back the graph a landing answers to and before `startPresence` starts the heartbeat that would race it. The answer goes through the same one door as every other (`Agent.ResolveQuestion`), so a landing answered from home while its conversation was shut is already settled when the window opens — before its first turn — rather than a question somebody answered yesterday still asking.

Regression test: `TestAnAnswerLeftWhileTheWindowWasShutIsAppliedAsItOpens` leaves a landing's no on the doorstep of a conversation with no process behind it, opens the conversation, and asserts the node is settled before any heartbeat could have run.

Manual: `home.md` now says an answer left for a closed conversation is applied the moment it next opens, not just "the next time that conversation runs".

Change entry: `docs/changes/unreleased/965-doorstep-drained-on-open.md`.

One line in `Agent.Close`, and the test that could only pin half of it before.

`Close` already lets go of everything a steer armed, and says why in one sentence: **nothing armed outlives the session that armed it** (`steer_grace.go`). A clock armed on a question was the one thing it did not let go of, so a person with a `recommend` rule an hour long left a live `time.Timer` and its goroutine standing behind a closed conversation for that hour.

```go
 // Nothing armed by a steer outlives the session that armed it
-// (steer_grace.go).
+// (steer_grace.go), and nor does a clock armed on a question (asklane.go).
 a.stopSteerGraceLocked()
+a.stopAskClocksLocked()
```

The verb it calls is this lane's own (`asklane.go`), a two-line seam onto `askedOfThePerson.stopClocksLocked`, so that `agent.go` names an ask-lane verb rather than reaching into another file's map.

## Nothing a person could see changes

`askClockRanOut` already refused to decide anything once the session had closed — that is the **guard**, and it stays. This is the other half: the clock **does not fire at all**. The two are different facts and they now have a test each.

- `TestAClockThatRunsOutAfterTheSessionClosedDecidesNothing` (already there) pins that a clock which fires anyway writes nothing.
- `TestClosingTheSessionStopsTheClockOnAQuestionNobodyAnswered` (new) pins that it does not fire: `time.Timer.Stop` reports whether it was the call that stopped a timer still running, so a second `Stop` answering **false** is the proof that `Close` made the first. The question itself is left exactly where it is — a session leaving does not answer it, and the next one has its own book.

`TestClosingTheSessionClearsWhatWasKeptForARevision` stops reaching into the book. It used to call `a.asked.stopClocksLocked()` by hand, with a comment saying `Close` did not yet; it now asks `Close` and reads the book afterwards.

**Both tests fail with the line removed** — checked by removing it.

## Why it was owed rather than written

It is named in #954's own report as a seam left open: `internal/session/agent.go` belonged to another lane in that wave, and a one-line reach into it would have been a merge conflict for no gain. #954 is on `dev` now, so it is written here on its own.

body:
Closes #956.

A mark's drawing rides beside the next step and its one power over the work is the
interruption: cut the request in flight so that **the boundary where the drawing can be
spent arrives at once** rather than whenever the step happens to end. Two orderings took
that promise away, and both ended the same way — the turn paid for a whole extra step, and
where that step was its last the drawing was written down as a carry-on and nothing was
handed anywhere.

**The answer was published only once the interruption had been delivered.** `readBeside`
ran `act` and then closed `settled`, and `sidecar.take` is non-blocking by construction —
so the loop arriving at the very boundary the cut had just bought read the reading as still
in flight and let it pass. The answer is published first now. The order that protected
against a late `act` is kept by one claim instead: `sidecar.spent` is CAS'd by the
interruption and stored by the taker, so whichever arrives first is the one that happens,
and an answer that has already reached a boundary raises no interruption into whatever the
turn does next.

**A cut that arrived between two steps found nothing to cut and was dropped.** Whether that
is safe is a property of the reading behind the cut and is now declared by the cause
(`boundaryCut`), not decided at the call: a recall's block is written into the transcript
before its cut is raised, so the request being assembled carries it either way — while a
drawing rides no transcript at all and the boundary is the only place it can ever be spent.
So a boundary cut is **owed** rather than spent on nothing, and `beginGeneration` — already
the one place that decides whether there is anything to cut — spends it the instant there
is. An owed cut belongs to the turn that asked for it, by number, so a cut one turn never
spent cannot reach the next person's message.

**And the one road where a drawing genuinely lands too late says so.** A turn that answered
in words has no boundary after it. The exit defer still waits for the drawing and still
writes the row — a reading somebody paid for must not be a line nobody can count — and the
row now says `late` rather than `continue`, which was the file recording the opposite of
what the reader decided.

### The bar

- **The one abstraction**: `sidecar`'s answer-and-interruption claim, and the cut door's
  `boundaryCut` property. Every reading beside the work (recall, mark, route judge, and
  whatever is added next) gets the boundary contract for free; every cut declares in one
  place whether it may be dropped.
- **Deleted**: the act-before-settle ordering and the paragraph arguing for it; the
  unconditional `return false` for a cut with nothing to cut; `carryOnDecision` on the
  turn's exit road.
- **Guarded by**: `TestTheAnswerIsReadableBeforeTheInterruptionIsDelivered` (go/ast, on the
  laws gate, with a plant that is the pre-#956 order), plus four runtime tests and one
  control in `cutboundary_test.go`.
- **Not a band-aid**: no flag asking "was there a cut", no retry counter, no widening of
  `take` into a wait, and no second cut path — two windows, one ordering, in the two places
  that already owned it.

### Proof

Every test ran on the Spark at this PR's head; the sha and the output tail are in the
report. Three of the new tests were verified red on the pre-fix code before the fix landed,
including the issue's own replication (b), which reproduces `{"decision":"continue"}` on a
many-part sketch.

body:
The three seams #910 and #919 handed back. All three call engine API that only
landed with #910, which is why they were not in either.

## Asking back goes through the door that keeps the question open

#910 built the engine's half: an answer carrying nothing but
`session.Answer.AskedBack` returns the **parked `ask` call** with the person's
words and a lead saying the question is still on their screen and not to ask it
again (`tools_ask.go`'s `askedBackLead`), and `session.AnswerResolves` says so at
both ends.

The surface had no way to reach it. `?` sent the sentence as an ordinary new
message, which arrived at the model with none of that context and left the call
parked behind it. `app.askBack` is now the one place the block
(`questionWritingKey`) and the page (`askBackCmd`) both send from, so the same
gesture cannot end up taking two roads.

**Which lanes have the seam is asked, not listed.** `AnswerResolves` *resolves* a
consent that carries only words asked back — approving it with no key — so a
version that routed every lane through the door would have turned a question into
an approval. Asking the predicate keeps the other lanes on the ordinary turn today
and makes this right on the day one of them grows the seam.

**The page says which answer it is about.** `session.Exchange.Option` is the field
for it, and `""` is a question about the question itself; the room knows which
section the reader is standing on and the block does not.

**The room's reply-finding is untouched and still works**, because what the seam
returns is the parked call's *result*: the model answers in its ordinary reply, in
the transcript, where `questionDrainReplies` was already looking.

## The chip counts what is waiting on you

`questionCount` counted rows, so a standing ratify put `? 1 question · alt+a` on
every page and the key took the person to a screen with nothing on it for them to
decide. #910 gave the engine one reading of "is somebody being waited for", and
the shape half of it is `session.AskKind.Waits`: a ratify waits on nobody by
definition, whatever else it carries.

**The block still draws it.** What is settled here is the status row's claim
across every page, not whether the row exists — a ratify is still shown, still
answerable, and still carries its own keys where it is drawn.

## The manual's limit moved with it

`questions.md` stated, correctly at the time, that an ask-back reaches the model
only once you have answered whenever the work is parked on the question. That is
no longer true of the model's own question, and is still true of a permission, a
task proposal and a standing card — so the page now says which is which, rather
than carrying a denial of something that works.

## Tests

`internal/tui3/questionaskback_test.go`, five of them, each failing for its own
reason:

- the model's question reaches the door, carries the words as an exchange, and
  carries no key or words beside it — checked against `session.AnswerResolves`
  itself, so the test agrees with the engine rather than with this file
- the page's ask-back carries the option it was asked about
- **a consent is not answered by asking back about it** — the one that would be a
  defect rather than a regression
- the chip does not count a ratify, and the block still has it
- the chip still counts a waiting question standing beside a ratify

body:
> Supersedes #914, which GitHub auto-closed when #910 merged and its base branch `feat/qv-F-engine` was deleted. Same branch, same work, rebased onto `dev`; #914 cannot be reopened.

Lane A of the question-views wave (#830), **against `dev`** and standing on its own
there. An answer to the model's own `ask` was only the RETURN VALUE of the call
that asked; it is now a MESSAGE TO THE CONVERSATION that also releases a waiting
call when there is one. Three things the owner picked fall out of that one
mechanism, and a fourth — the undo — rides the same door.

## The mechanism

One rendering (`askAnswerText`: a sentence, then the whole `Answer`) and two
deliveries: the call parked on it, or the conversation's own queue through
**`Agent.accept`** — the road a job's ending, a watch's firing and a landed task
already take (step boundary, or a wake on an idle conversation). No second
delivery path, and the bytes are the same either way. `ResolveQuestion` is still
the one door.

**There is ONE book, and it is #870's.** `internal/session/askwait.go` held the
parked wait with three endings and a doc warning that two maps holding one
question is a defect, so this wave did not write a second beside it: the lane's
account of a question was folded INTO it. That file keeps the map, the channels,
the four ways an ask ends — #870's three plus the fourth this adds, a call that
CARRIED ON — and the ownership rule. `THE ENTRY IS THE OWNERSHIP` still holds for
the three endings that take the entry out of the map; the answer claims
`open.wait` one field lower (`askedOfThePerson.answerLocked`), because a settled
entry is KEPT so its answer can be changed, with a bound of `askSettledKept`.
`internal/session/asklane.go` is not a second book — it is what an answer needs
after somebody gives one: the rendering, the delivery, the lane's clock, the
hold, the revision. Talking past a question still retires the asks a person's
sentence is in the way of — the ones something waits on — and leaves a
non-blocking question standing, which is what asking without waiting means.

**Deleted:** `askWaits`, #910's `tellAskAnswer` and `askAnsweredLead` (the second
delivery road), the policy clock inside `executeAsk`'s `select`, the ask arm that
dropped an answer when nobody was parked, and the refusal in `SetAutonomy` that
made a clock length compulsory.

## What a person gets

- **Keep working while asking.** `blocking: {turn: false}` returns at once; the
  question outlives the call and the turn. Omitted or `true` waits exactly as
  before — the zero value waits.
- **A countdown you can stop.** The clock belongs to the lane, not the call, so
  it runs on a question nobody is parked on; it takes the pick through the same
  door, and what the model reads says the answer is **provisional**. Opt-in: no
  clock unless the person set one (`/autonomy`), length by one derivation
  (`autonomyClock`). Any key stops it for good — `Agent.HoldQuestion`, wire
  `Question.Hold`, sent from a `tea.Cmd` — and the question says so itself while
  the clock runs: `any key stops the clock · you can still change the answer
  afterwards`.
- **Change your answer.** `c change` on the receipt asks the question again; the
  new answer carries `Answer.Revises`, the record says `changed from …`, and the
  model is told what changed. Irreversible decisions refuse it in words.
- **Undo a permission.** `u undo` on the receipt of an `always` hands that grant
  back whole — the session memo, the saved settings line, and a connected
  account's capability, which returns to asking rather than to a no nobody said.
  `Agent.undoGrant` is the one door for the stores the engine owns;
  `app.forgetAlways` is the surface's own line. What may be changed is ONE
  reading (`Question.Revisable`), asked by the receipt that offers the key and by
  the door that takes it.

Wire **15** (both halves fail as silence on a v14 engine). Lean prefix 30,833 →
30,968 bytes against a 31,500 budget; fixed prefix unchanged.

## Proof

`make pr-ready BASE=origin/dev` green — laws, and `internal/session`,
`internal/tui3`, `internal/manual`, `internal/e2e`, `internal/remote` with
`-count=1`.

Laws added: a non-blocking ask returns at once and its question stands; a parked
and a messaged answer are the same bytes; a provisional pick says so and runs with
nobody parked; a hold clears the deadline in the engine; a change reaches the model
as a correction (parked and unparked); an irreversible decision refuses a change;
an answer the lane no longer holds is refused in words; an answered question
leaves the desk; a question nothing waits on is not `waiting on you`; a clock that
runs out after `Close` decides nothing; an answer a closed conversation cannot read
records nothing; the second answer to one question records nothing; the countdown
says how to stop it and only while it runs; `u undo` takes the standing yes back
and only a standing yes is offered one.

Driven in tmux as a person against `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`, twice — once on
`--no-host` and once over the DEFAULT host road (#690 is closed by #856, and the
idle-woken answer reached the screen). The model chose the non-blocking form,
finished the other files while the question stood, and used the answer when it
came; a change from the receipt made it rewrite the file; the clock took its pick,
said so as provisional, and the model asked the person whether to keep it; a key
press left the next countdown `paused` and undecided a minute later; `u undo`
printed `taken back · this tool asks again` and the next call asked again.

Two earlier drives found two defects the unit tests had not — a correction posted
into a spent channel, and a reopened question that still said `waiting` — both
fixed and pinned.

body:
Five tests were green alone and red beside another suite, a different one each run, and none of them on `.github/known-red.txt`. Each was reproduced under load first — focused `-count`, `GOMAXPROCS=2`, twelve `yes > /dev/null` beside it, on Spark — before anything was changed.

This branch has been rebased onto `origin/dev` (`ed8371321`, which carries #924 and #934) and the review's send-back is answered by changing the mechanism rather than by arguing it. What is below describes the branch as it stands at `c86779388`, not the first pass.

## What each red's cause was

- `TestASupersessionSaysWhatItReplaced` — **a real race in the product.** `refreshMemory` drained the lines the post-turn pass had no stream for and said them onto the hub the reading had been handed when it started; a recall rides beside the turn and is never joined, so on a busy machine it runs after that turn has ended, and the line was taken off the queue, said to a closed stream, and never said again. Instrumented, every losing run logged `ctxErr=context canceled hubClosed=true`.
- `TestAutomaticTaskChecksReachTheRealChecker` — the fixture cause. A scripted conversation answers in no time and never blocks, so the reading the turn had just started sat unscheduled behind it: still pending at all eight remaining boundaries in every failing run, the script then ran out in words, and `takeAtTheEnd` journalled a drawing nobody could spend.
- `TestAHandoverOnAHeadlessRunIsReadByItsGoalOwner` — the same cause, the same trace: the drawing never reached a boundary that could spend it, because the fixture waited on a figure (a count of pre-turn calls **entered**, not landed) instead of on the reading.
- `TestTheConfirmsReadingOfBreadthArmsWhatTheScreenMissed` — the same cause again, with script length as the guess: long enough on a quiet machine, short on a starved one.
- `TestARescueTheCallCouldNotPayForSaysSoOnTheRow` — lane A was scripted at sixty milliseconds against a ceiling of fifty, which is ten milliseconds of wall clock a starved timer spends, so the first token arrived before the controller acted and the row said nothing had been done at all (`action = ""`).

## What is true now

**Every memory line goes through one door, and the hub itself says whether it landed.** `eventHub.send` returns `landed bool` (`internal/session/agent.go` ~3544 — the branch's only hunk in that file; the review's B2 named that door and only the hub's own lock can answer, since a hub reads open right up to the moment it closes under it). `Agent.sayMemory` is now the one place a memory line is said: it asks the live hub, and holds the line for the next turn whenever the answer is no — a closed hub and no hub at all take the same road, so the `if a.hub != nil` branch is gone. Correctness no longer rests on any ordering between this door and the roads that end turns. `memoryNotice` and the captured hubs are deleted; `routedMemory` and `runMemoryCommand` take `say func(string)`, nil being a node's reading borrowing its parent's store and saying nothing, exactly as before; `refreshMemory`, `importMemoryFile` and `startRecallLocked` take no hub. `TestALineSaidOntoAClosedStreamIsHeldInstead` pins it with the pointer deliberately left on a hub it has closed, and fails when `sayMemory` is put back the way it was.

**A reading's landing is a fact a test can wait on.** `readBeside` tells a `besideWatch` carried on the work's context when each reading under it starts and when it has landed, the second after the settle closes. `besideWatch.quiet(ctx)` takes the context those readings were started under and ends on the calm channel **or on that context** — bounded by the fact that the work is over, not by a clock (F2), because `sidecar.end` cancels a reading's window without joining it, so an unbounded wait would have reported as a package timeout naming whichever test was running. A fixture that opts in through `watchReadings` answers the conversation only once none is in flight. That is the order a real turn usually has, made exact: a real model spends seconds on a step, the readings beside it are small, and a drawing that splits cuts the step it lands in. `holdUntilRaced`, `awaitRace`'s millisecond spin and `stopHolding` are deleted.

**The product carries no watch and never waits on one.** `TestTheRunningProductNeverWaitsOnAReadingsLanding` reads the tree with `go/ast`, so it is on the laws gate, and both planted uses are asserted to be named.

**A scripted arm orders itself by a signal, and the mechanism lives in the stub.** `lanestub.Profile.FirstTokenUntil` holds a lane's first word on a channel after it has waited out its TTFT as scripted — `StallUntil`'s own stated rule for the one wait `StallUntil` cannot hold, since that one only takes hold after `StallAfter` deltas — and it holds the whole reply on the unstreamed path, where the first token and the last arrive together. `TestALaneHoldsItsFirstWordForASignal` proves it and asserts an ORDER rather than an interval. The first pass put the rule in a `lanestub.Clock` decorator inside `internal/provider/hedge_test.go`, which delayed every wait of every lane to order one lane's first token; it is now a knob beside `StallUntil`, on the lane it is about, with its own test in the stub's own suite. Setting it to its zero value is today's behaviour, so no other caller of `lanestub` sees a change.

**What releases that hold is #924's own controller.** `theControllersWord(t)` is one `OnPhase` reader, closed once on any rung of the waiting ladder — `PhaseAllSlow`, `PhaseBelowPace`, `PhaseSwitching`, `PhaseSwitchingModel` — and restored on cleanup. `PhaseBelowPace` is on that list because #924 split `control.Report` in two: without it "the controller has spoken" is false on the pace road and the hold would have hung instead of failing. The reader being chained to is taken **before** the chain is installed (`previous := OnPhase(nil)`, then `OnPhase(...)`), where the first pass assigned it after `OnPhase` had already published the closure — a write racing its own reads, in the fixture whose job is killing races (F6). Fixed at the cause, not by a window nothing happens to fire in.

## Proof

The 60 ms-against-50 ms shape is **not** moot after #924 — measured on dev's own copy of the test, in a detached worktree with nothing of this branch in it, `GOMAXPROCS=2` under twelve burners on Spark:

```
c742b8bc8 (#924)   -count=300    → 1 FAIL   hedge_refusal_test.go:40: action = ""
ed8371321 (today)  -count=300    → 0 FAIL
ed8371321 (today)  -count=3000   → 6 FAIL   275.628s, all the same line
```

Three hundred clean at today's head is not an answer at about one in five hundred; three thousand settles it. The rate is the same order it was before #924 and the failure is the same one. So the hunk carries.

At this branch's head, under the same load:

- the session set, `-count=50`: **250/250** (about one failure in fifteen before)
- the same set, `-race -count=20`: **120/120**, no data race
- `TestARescueTheCallCouldNotPayForSaysSoOnTheRow`, `-count=500`: green (one in three hundred red before), and `-race -count=20` green
- `go build ./...`, `go vet` on the three packages, `gofmt`, `make test-laws`, `make changelog-check`, `go test ./internal/lane/lanestub/`

Both new tests were mutation-checked rather than only watched to pass: `heldWord` short-circuited to `return true` fails `TestALaneHoldsItsFirstWordForASignal`; `sayMemory` put back to `if a.hub != nil` fails `TestALineSaidOntoAClosedStreamIsHeldInstead`.

Spark pr-ready at c86779388: <tail follows>

Nothing was added to the known-red ledger, nothing skipped, no timeout widened.

## Found here, filed rather than worked around

- **#956** — a split drawing can still miss the boundary its own cut opened: `act` runs before the settle by #871's ruling, so a loop that reaches `take` in that window finds the reading pending and pays another generation for it, or drops the drawing when that generation is the turn's last. The same gap exists when the drawing lands between a boundary and the next request, where `cutGeneration` finds nothing in flight. It needs `checkpoint.go`/`steer.go`/`loop.go` semantics, which this branch does not own.
- **#957** — `TestADoneEndingNamesTheCheckItCouldNotRun` has a data race under `-race` on clean `origin/dev`: its `nearWall` helper writes `steward.now` while the wall-clock goroutine reads it. Pre-existing, confirmed in a throwaway worktree of `origin/dev`, and not a load-sensitive red under the normal gate, which does not run `-race`.

title: tasks: a call that is still open says so, with its own clock and rate

body:
Closes #936

## What changed

`/task <brief>` no longer waits on anything. **Before:** the surface waited on the sizing judge (3 s, under `sizing it up…`), then `StartTask` waited on the shaper (`taskShapeWindow`, 25 s, under `shaping the brief…`). That was 28 s on a thinking model before the node existed, and after it the work started on the person's sentence anyway. **Now:** `StartTask` admits the node at once, on the person's own sentence and the canned done-condition. Both readings run **beside the first worker**, through the same mechanism as #883's carry-on road:

- **Width.** The judge's parts go through the #883 division road: `proposalBeside` → `judgedDivision`, with the new asker `askedByJudge`. That asker sets `breadth`, so the parts pass the floor gate the way an armed node's own division does. `weighDivision` weighs them, and `deliverBeside` hands them to the worker as the division receipt. `spec.armed` stays frozen at admission, because the belt and the system prompt read it when the worker is built. `solo` (the typed form or the standing `single` setting) turns the judge off.
- **Brief.** `shapeBeside` hands the shaped brief to the worker's room as a mailbox note (`deliverTo`/`roomSeat`) that opens `YOUR BRIEF IS WRITTEN OUT NOW`. The node's contract is written only when the worker's record takes the note (`durableDelivery.settled` → `writeBrief`). So the checker never judges the worker against a contract it did not see. There is still one brief format, the same assembled shape every node has.
- **Name and place.** The namer names the node at admission; until then the node shows the first eight words of the person's opening line. The ground ladder reads the paths in the person's sentence.
- **Surface.** tui3 raises no forming block on `/task`. The block remains only on the approved-proposal road.
- **Remote.** Wire version 16: `Task.Judge` is retired, and `Task.Start` now carries `solo`. (#960 took 15 for an answer that is a message while this was in flight; Decision 3 makes the number strict equality, so this bump sits behind it as 16 and #960's paragraph stands as dev wrote it.)
- **Docs.** Updated the manual (`commands.md`, `tasks.md`, `how-tasks-run.md`, `screen.md`, `standing-orders.md`), `prompts/shape.md` (the `title`/`where` fields were removed), `docs/design/task-start/DESIGN.md` (appended), `docs/REMOTE.md` (a Decision 14 amendment) and `docs/TRAJECTORIES.md`.

The window lengths are unchanged and no reasoning budget was added (#927 is the sibling issue).

## The architecture bar

1. **The ONE abstraction.** `besideWork` (task_beside.go), reused, together with the #883 division road (`weighDivision`/`deliverBeside`). The typed door is its third user, after memory and the drawing. The only new field is `divisionAsker.breadth`, which any future source of parts that has already judged width can use.
2. **What I deleted.**
   - `JudgeDecomposable`, `Task.Judge` and its call class, and `taskCallDeadline`.
   - `rememberDivisible` at the door.
   - `TaskShapeFallbackNote` (`brief kept as you wrote it`).
   - `BriefWatch`/`WithBriefWatch` and the forming block's preview, window, walk and hover.
   - The surface's `sizing it up…` phase and its `the work looks wide` note.
   - The shaper's `title`/`where` fields, and `taskName`.
3. **The law tests.**
   - `TestThePersonsTaskDoorAsksNoModel` (go/ast, on the laws gate): `StartTask`'s body calls none of `shapeBrief`, `judgeDecomposable`, `callRole*`, `completeWithModel`, `taskName*` or `memoryBlock`.
   - `TestTheWorkersFirstRequestGoesOutBeforeTheShaperOrTheJudgeAnswers`: the judge never answers and the shaper is held, yet the worker's first request lands first.
   - The control, `TestAWideTaskStartsItsWorkerFirstAndTheJudgesPartsArriveAsTheReceipt`: the worker starts first and the judge's parts arrive as the division receipt, with `spec.armed` untouched.
   - `TestABriefIsWrittenOnlyWhenTheWorkerReadsIt`.
   - The existing `TestEveryReadingBesideTheWorkHasAJoin`.
4. **What a reviewer would call a band-aid.** "The task starts on the raw sentence." It is not a fallback. At the moment the work can begin, the raw sentence is the only brief that exists. It is also the authority the shaped brief quotes word for word, and the shaped contract replaces it through the same assembled shape, not a second format. Note the trade-off: the worker's first steps run without the shaped done-condition, and the checker is judged against the shaped contract only if the worker read it.


## Review fixes (second pass)

- **BLOCKING — the readings now survive the checkpoint.** `unshaped`/`unsized` had no record fields, so a `/task` admitted while the lanes are full and then caught by a restart came back owing nothing: `shapeBeside` returned nil, no shaper was ever asked, and the work ran on the raw sentence and the canned done-condition permanently and silently. Both are on `taskRecord` (`unshaped,omitempty` / `unsized,omitempty`), written beside `Quick` and read back into the restored spec, with a scripted test — `TestAQueuedTaskThatSurvivedARestartStillHasItsBriefWritten` — that resumes a queued unshaped node in a second session and asserts its brief is written beside the worker it finally gets.
- **The quality law, on the record.** The judge's yes no longer arms the worker, so a judged-wide task whose division the reviewer then REFUSES carries on with no `divide_work` verb, where dev's armed worker could still divide later. Arming cannot move without unfreezing the belt and the system prompt together. Filed as **#958**, with the fix stated and both acceptance cases; named in the change entry and in `docs/design/task-start/DESIGN.md`.
- **The door's law walks one level down.** `TestThePersonsTaskDoorAsksNoModel` now follows `StartTask`'s same-package callees (the ground ladder, the admission compiler), so a model call moved one frame down fails it. Mutation-checked.
- **Deleted what was replaced.** `checkpoint.go`'s comment no longer says "the same fact the sizing judge banks at the typed `/task` door" — nothing is banked there now.


## Rebase across #960

`internal/remote/wire.go` conflicted: #960 bumped the wire to 15 for `Answer.Revises` and `MethodQuestionHold`. Both bumps are real engine incompatibilities and Decision 3 is strict equality, so this one is **version 16** — #960's paragraph kept verbatim, the task door's added beneath it in the same voice, `const Version = 16`. Moved with it: `docs/REMOTE.md`'s Decision 14 amendment (a version-15 surface is what is refused now), the design doc section, `wire.go`'s own back-reference, and the change entry's `invalidates` line. No test hard-codes the number — they all read the `Version` constant.

## Proof

body:
Closes #941. #940 has landed on `dev` (`b1e743e0d`), so this branch is now rebased straight onto `dev` and carries only its own three commits; the provider-side derivation it uses — `provider.WithThinkingWall` and `Client.wallBudget` — is #940's, reused and not duplicated.

## What was true

A task's checking call was bounded by a bare `context.WithTimeout` at its share of the window — thirty seconds of the one-minute reading window a check with no declared `checks` gets — and by nothing else. Nothing on the wire said how long it had. Its calls were planned as a working node's (`lane.RoleLeafAttached`), so the controller waited on a silent machine with a leaf's patience. A call the share cut threw away everything the checker had read, and the second attempt was a FRESH checker starting the investigation again from nothing inside what was left. And when the window closed, the landing read `your call · nobody could check it` — the same sentence as a checker that would not start or a provider that fell over, so a person read it as news about their work.

Measured: five of thirty-four non-quick landings in one acceptance drive ended `your call` on correct work, because a reasoning model on the checker thought through both of its thirty-second shares without writing a word.

## What is true now

**The checker is told its window.** `internal/session/callwindow.go` is the whole mechanism: `openCallWindow(ctx, bound, callWindow{…})` bounds the call AND records what kind of call it is, and `toldItsWindow(ctx)` — applied at the ONE client door, `Agent.completeWithModel` — hands the time left on that deadline to #940's `provider.WithThinkingWall`. The adapter derives the thinking allowance from that time and the asked machine's believed rate. It is applied at the door rather than by the caller because the turn loop stamps a rung per attempt and a rung stamp replaces the whole effort request, which is #940's own "applied last" rule.

**The check's calls are a judge's.** `Config.crewRole` is set on the agent `newAuditAgent` builds, and `laneRole` reads it through `errandRole`, the one crew→lane table every errand already uses. No new role type, no new column: `roles.RoleAuditor` already maps to `lane.RoleJudge`.

**A cut check keeps what it read.** When the cut checker holds a tool receipt, the next ask goes to the SAME checker over the SAME transcript — one sentence (`auditNudge`), thinking switched off as a requirement of the call, in its own share of the window. Only a checker cut before it read anything goes to the fresh-checker rung. `nudgeAudit` is deleted: the reply that said neither word takes this same ask, and takes it in its own share rather than in the remains of the call it followed.

**The receipt says what happened.** The row reads `your call · the check ran out of time`, and the report leads `the check ran out of time — one call ran 30s without answering and was abandoned · the window closed before a second`. `nobody could check it in 5m0s` is gone. The reason is read back off the report's lead (`taskCheckReason`), the way the held row already reads its gaps, so no record field was added and no surface had to change.

## Proof it is the behaviour and not the unit

`internal/e2e/checkerwindow_e2e_test.go` drives the real binary in a real terminal against a scripted endpoint that serves its own catalog row (a model that cannot stop thinking), its own endpoints page (one machine with a published rate), and three answers: a read, thinking that does not stop until the client goes away, and the word when asked. **It needs no key and costs nothing.** It asserts the landing says `done` and never `your call`; that the cut call carried a thinking budget no larger than its share at that machine's fastest published rate (measured: 2400 tokens of a possible 3900); that exactly ONE investigation happened; and that the ask after the cut carried what the checker had already read, with thinking turned down as far as a mandatory-thinking model allows. It is a subtest of `TestTaskStatesE2E`, registered above that suite's key gate so a machine with no provider key still pays it.

Beside it, scripted unit cases cut the checker BETWEEN rounds and IN THE MIDDLE OF A TOOL ROUND. The mid-tool case is the one the ask road is really reached from, and it asserts the property a provider would 400 on: every tool call in the second ask's messages is paired with its result. The turn loop guarantees that — a cut batch still records a result for every call it issued, and the one exit that writes nothing is `abandoned(ctx)`, a turn the session let go of, never a deadline.

## The seam that belongs to #940 — reported, not patched

`internal/provider/effortladder.go`'s `thinkingRoom(share, rate, wall)` is `round(share × rate × wall)` **with no floor**, and `toldItsWindow` hands the REMAINING time on the window rather than its length. So a request that leaves late in a thirty-second share — after a slow tool round, or on the second ask when most of the share is spent — can carry a reasoning budget in the tens of tokens, which is below some providers' published minimum for the field and is a 400 rather than a short pass. The fix belongs in `internal/provider` (a floor in `thinkingRoom`, or `wallBudget` declining to send a budget it cannot honour, next to `reasoningBudgetRefused`), which this lane does not own. Filed here rather than worked around in `internal/session`.

## The bar's four questions

**The one abstraction, and who else could use it.** `callWindow` / `openCallWindow` / `toldItsWindow`: a bound and a statement of what the call is for, opened together, told to the model at the one door. Anything in this package that bounds a model call and would like the model to know it — the progress check that shares `newAuditAgent`, a standing item's firing, a repair round — opens one the same way and needs no second knob. The two properties it carries today (the deadline, and "this is the answer ask, not the investigation") are the two the ladder actually has.

**What was deleted.** `nudgeAudit` (replaced by `askForTheWord`, which is the same rung for both roads and takes its own share of the window); the bare `context.WithTimeout` in `auditOnce`; `nobody could check it in <window>` as a sentence; `checkerAskedTwice`, which after review turned out to be read by nothing but its own tests — `auditVerdict.twice` is the one composer of that sentence, and it gives the clause its subject.

**Which law tests guard it.** `callwindow_law_test.go` (`go/ast`, on `make test-laws`): every `Submit` in `task_audit.go` rides an `openCallWindow`, no `context.WithTimeout`/`WithDeadline` is opened there, `completeWithModel` calls `toldItsWindow`, and every `newAuditPace(` takes `auditWindowFor(…)` as its window. Beside it, `effortguard_test.go` admits `callwindow.go` as an effort-carrying file, and `TestTheClockLeadIsWrittenOnceAndReadBack` holds the invariant `taskCheckReason` depends on: `lookOutcome` is the only composer that writes the clock lead, and `takenAsItStands` — the other composer of a non-answer — lands the unattended run's `TaskDone` and never reaches that reader.

**What a reviewer would call a band-aid, and why it is not one.** The thirty-second share. It is not a new number and not a timeout added where a wait was measured: `auditPace` already cut the window into shares, and this change does not widen the window — a check with nothing to run still has nothing slow to do. What changed is that the share is TOLD, so the pass in front of the answer is sized to fit it rather than being cut by it, and that a cut keeps its evidence. The second candidate is reading the reason off the report's lead rather than adding a record field; it is the `taskHeldReason` pattern this package already reads gaps with, it keeps one sentence written once, and the alternative would have touched `TaskNode`, `TaskNotice`, the store, `TaskFacts` and two surfaces to carry a bit that is already in the prose.

**One trade, stated.** `lane.RoleJudge` makes a watched check route price-ordered like every other gate, where a leaf routes for a person's patience. That is the quality law's direction — the check is a gate reading an answer, not the conversation's own turn — and it is what makes the controller act on a silent machine inside a thirty-second share at all.

## Suite

Spark, at `e0d1c02b5`:

```
go build ./...                                          ok
go vet ./internal/session ./internal/manual ./internal/e2e   ok
make test-laws                                          ok   (26 packages)
go test ./internal/e2e/            (untagged word gate)  ok   0.521s
go test ./internal/manual/...                            ok   1.955s
make test-focus PKGS=./internal/session RUN='Check|Audit|Window|Clock|TaskNote|Settle|Unattended'   ok  42.588s
go test -tags e2e -run 'TestTaskStatesE2E/a_check' ./internal/e2e/
    the cut call was told 2400 thinking tokens of the 3900 its share can hold
    HEAD · ✓ ◆ Wrote hello.txt with · done · 32s · 1 file · branch kept
    --- PASS: TestTaskStatesE2E (43.83s)
```

`make test-touched BASE=origin/dev` could not be run on this box: the per-box suite lock (`scripts/one-suite.sh`) refused **thirty** consecutive attempts over an hour, two minutes apart, each time naming a different live holder — the queue was continuous from 22:14Z to 23:13Z. What ran instead is the same target, at the same commit, on CI:

```
touched packages   SUCCESS   e0d1c02b5   22:15:44Z → 22:20:25Z
light gate         SUCCESS   e0d1c02b5
check              SUCCESS   e0d1c02b5
```

The local run's own derived package set at the last attempt was `./internal/e2e ./internal/manual ./internal/session` (+ packages `origin/dev` had moved under, which CI's run against this PR's base does not include).

title: tasks: a check that runs out of time is told its window, keeps what it read, and says it was the clock (#941)

body:
## What was true

A stopped turn is read for what remains, and on the attended road every reading
with a line in it re-opened the turn — the same line as last time included.

Measured 2026-09-11, `dev@333acc67d`, live drive of the chat surface: a reply
had reported that `zeta.txt` did not exist, and the end-of-turn reader raised
the same observation three times running, each one claiming the missing file had
not been reported. The model spent three visible turns explaining that the
observation was mistaken, and the person read all three sides of an argument
they had typed no part of. The per-turn ceiling stopped the fourth; it should
have stopped the second.

This is #468's family, and #468's own "Still open" note predicted it exactly:
`checkpointCarryOnCap` let repeated echoes through up to the cap instead of
stopping on the first identical one.

## What is true now

**The floor the unattended road has always had is the floor both roads have.**
A reading that says exactly what the reading before it said is a standstill, and
the turn ends on it rather than being re-opened.

- `standstillFloor` (`internal/session/standstill.go`) is the ONE mechanism both
  principals decide a standstill with. It was `Steward`'s two fields and its
  comparison, lifted out and given to `Person` too; `Steward` now holds one and
  behaves identically.
- `standstillReason` is the one sentence both roads stop on — the same line the
  manual already documented for unattended runs, now reached from a conversation.
  The person reads it through the register's existing `stopping here · ` lead:

  ```
  stopping here · nothing moved since the last look and what is left is the same — the missing zeta.txt has not been reported · saying it again would not change it
  ```
- The stretch it is about ends the way the Steward's does — a reading with
  nothing left in it, and work that is still moving — plus one more that belongs
  to this road alone: **the next thing the person types**. A conversation is
  never followed by a stop it did not ask for.
- The ceiling on carrying on stays at three and now bounds only what it was ever
  useful for: a reader that keeps finding NEW things. A reader that repeats
  itself never reaches it.

`internal/session/checkpoint.go` is **unchanged** — the echo is decided by the
principal and the `DecideStop` road it lands on was already there. So are
`loop.go` and `agent.go`: this PR touches neither file the other session owns.

## Against the bar

- **The one abstraction**: `standstillFloor`. Any future principal that can say
  carry on gets the law by holding one.
- **What was deleted**: `Steward.carriedUnmet` / `carriedBrief` and
  `stewardStandstillReason`, replaced rather than left beside the new thing.
  Also the lane's `aforge-triage.md`, a scratch file that should never have been
  committed.
- **What guards it**: `TestAReaderObservationThatWasAnsweredIsNotRaisedAgain`
  (the whole turn through `Agent.Submit`: one continuation, the standstill line,
  the reader spent twice not four times), `TestAStandstillIsForgottenWhenThePersonSaysSomethingNew`,
  and `TestCarryingOnAnAskHasACeilingOfItsOwn` rewritten so its reader says
  something new each time — which is now the only way to reach the cap. The
  unattended road's four standstill tests are untouched and still pass, which is
  the proof the lift changed nothing there.
- **Not a band-aid**: no new counter, no new note, no new number. The defect was
  one road missing a law the other road already had, and the fix is the law in
  one place.

## The half that is NOT landed, and why

#888 also asks that the carry-on exchange not be **drawn** as chat. That is not
here, and it should not be guessed at:

A continuation's reply cannot be told apart from a turn's genuine final answer
by anything the transcript carries. Dropping the reply after a continuation —
which is what the lane's commit did, and what the issue sketches — also hides a
turn's real answer: `TestReopenedConversationKeepsCarryOnOutOfTheExchange`'s own
fixture ends `[carry on] …` → `"The work is finished."`, and that sentence
disappears under the rule. Keeping only the reply's tool-call rows loses a
prose-only fix instead, which is a common shape on this road — the reader says
"the answer did not mention X" and the model writes X.

The only fact that separates the two is the reading that comes **after** the
reply, which is exactly what the standstill above now knows and the display
projection does not. Recording it is a journal change (`sessionfile.go`) and a
live-feed question, not a shaping one. Written up on #888, which stays open for it.

body:
## What was true

PR #885 gave each conversation's task graph an admission governor that reserves one
measured **footprint** of memory per running node. The measured half is
`visible / running`, where `visible` is `treeResidentMB(os.Getpid())` — this process and
every descendant it started — and `running` was **this graph's own count**.

/proc cannot say which conversation started which compiler. So a second conversation's
build, under way while this graph had two parts out, was divided by this graph's two and
became **this** conversation's per-node footprint. That figure only rises by design, so one
reading taken during a neighbour's build narrowed every later fan here for the rest of the
session. The same attribution gap ran the other way on the reservation itself: each graph
read the other's visible memory as covering part of its own, and started a part the machine
had no room for.

## What is true now

The count the governor divides by covers every lane the reading does. `session.TaskLanes`
is one mutex and one int, and **every `TaskGraph.running` mutation goes through one door**,
`takeLaneLocked` / `giveLaneLocked`, which moves both counts together: the graph's own,
which the person's `task.parallel` cap is measured against, and the shared one, which the
machine reading is divided by. The frontier's start, `handBackSlotLocked`, `park`, `unpark`
and a standing firing's own lane all take that door.

`observe` divides the visible memory by that count and `admits` reserves against it, so
both halves of `share = visible / running` and `running × footprint − visible` are read
over the same population — every lane the machine is running, and every byte the process
holds above rest. A neighbour's build is counted as exactly what it is, and no conversation
can move another's per-node weight. No clamp to a fraction of `MemTotal`, no timer decay,
no per-graph correction.

**Which graphs share one account is said, not assumed.** `cmd/aforge`'s `v3OpenSession` —
the one door every conversation is built through (launch, relaunch, `/new`, `/resume`) —
keeps one account for the life of the process and puts it on every `session.Config`;
`Agent.graph` and `standingWideWork` read it off the config. A graph handed none is **alone
in its process** and keeps an account of its own (`newTaskGraph`). A package-level variable
would have been the same claim made silently, and it is a claim a library cannot make for
its caller: a test binary is one process and a hundred unrelated machines, and the first
draft of this PR proved it — a lane one scene left running narrowed the next scene's fan on
a Linux runner.

- **The one abstraction:** `TaskLanes`, reached through one door. Two new exported names
  (the type and `NewTaskLanes`) and one `Config` row.
- **Deleted:** the five bare `g.running++` / `g.running--` / `graph.running = 1` sites.
- **The law:** `TestEveryLaneMovesThroughTheOneDoor` (`go/ast`, so it is on the
  pull-request gate) — nothing outside the door may move either count, and the door must
  move both. It fails with the exact name of the offending function.
- **Not a band-aid:** the count is never corrected, clamped or decayed; the divisor is
  simply drawn from the same population the reading is.

`task_pressure_account_test.go` is the acceptance the issue asks for: two graphs, one
stated machine, one process, no sleeps and no `/proc`. Both tests fail on the old per-graph
count with the exact wrong figures the issue names — a lane measured at 6144 MiB instead of
4096, and four parts running where the machine carries three.

`internal/manual/chat/how-tasks-run.md` gains the person-facing half (tasks in your other
conversations are set aside for here too); `docs/design/task-start/DESIGN.md`'s
"Boundaries, stated rather than hidden" no longer states the gap as owed.

## Tested

Lane T of the question-views wave (#830), owner pick `multi — A`.

Rebased onto `dev` `704e0cf4c` (past #910, #919, #933, #973 and #972), with the three conflicts against #972 resolved by hand.

## What changes for a person

- **Several questions from one step are one panel.** Two or more open questions sharing the engine's step token (`Question.Batch`, #910) draw as ONE panel: a tab per question across the top edge (`● package.json   ○ go.mod   ✓ review`), `←→` between questions, `↑↓` still choose. `enter` or a digit **holds** the answer and moves on; nothing reaches the engine until the review tab sends every held answer through `answerQuestions` — one command, one `doorLine`, in tab order (#919's list door). A question nobody answered stays open and says so. `esc` is later for the whole set and keeps what was held.
- **Permissions from one batch are one frame.** Two or more permissions with the same `Batch`, each with a plain grant and a safe answer: what each call wants (tool dim, target in the data hue, identical calls counted `×3`, long paths cut in the middle), then `allow all N · one by one · deny all`. **No lifetime row**: a consent's answer scope never reaches the gate (#933), so the frame offers only what it can honour (#953 grades the calls and brings the row back). The pointer is each question's own pointer (`questionPointerStart`) read over the set. `one by one` opens the same questions as tabs.
- **Never joins:** an irreversible or confirmation question, a question with a hole or a dial (`←→` are its own keys there), anything from another step. Keyed on properties, never on Kind or text.
- Tabs follow the transcript rows they are about, not the order their gates finished in, and are called by what tells them apart (shared lead cut at a word or path boundary).

## What is deleted

- `internal/tui3/questionsheet.go` + its test (the sheet, its `s`/`g` keys, `formsSheet`).
- The surface's stand-in for the step: `questionStep`, `questionStepEnded`, the 3 s gather (`questionGatherMsg`, `Gather`), `questionReach.pending/boundary/forget`, `questionBatch*`, `questionStepAt`. The engine's step token is the one key.

## What P's #933 changed here

#933 removed the `viewTabs` rung as dead (its `when` could only answer false and its comment described this lane), so this change adds the view, the rung and its `when` together. It also made `questionScopes` answer nothing for a permission, because `session.Answer.Scope` never reaches the consent gate — so **the grouped frame draws no lifetime row and offers no `t`**, and `TestAGroupedPermissionOffersNoLifetimeRow` fails the day #953 grades the calls and the row comes back.

## Review fixes (Opus review of the first push)

- **A tab part-way through the widening answer drew its answers, not the beat.** `questionTabRows` had copied `questionPanelRows` and dropped its `len(q.beat) > 0` branch, so the digits picked shapes and `esc` backed out of the beat while the panel still drew `1 allow once / 2 always / ▸ 3 deny`. New `app.questionPanelInside` is the ONE place that branch lives, and the panel of one and the tab both go through it. `TestATabPartWayThroughTheWideningAnswerDrawsTheBeat` fails on the reviewed commit.
- **A rebase had reverted #933's colour ruling** in `DESIGN.md`'s `room` bullet. Restored, and every file #933 touched that this branch also touches was swept for the same shape.
- **The four-reads screens predated the rebase** and still drew `▸ allow all 4` with a lifetime row. Both live subtests re-driven and all eight screens recommitted — twice, since #972's evidence pane changed the body again. New needle `questionGroupSafeWord` asserts the pointer on the raised frame; nothing in that suite read the pointer before.
- **`GTabHere`/`GTabOpen` are unminted.** They were byte-identical to `GStepDone`/`GStepPending` in every tier but one ASCII cell and forced a fifth exemption into `TestOneGlyphOneMeaning` — the only law test this branch had edited non-additively. `internal/tui2/tokens` is now byte-for-byte `dev`.
- The review tab wears `✓` only when every question is held; the empty review no longer prints a third sentence saying what its rows already say; `questionGrouped`'s comment says which of its clauses is load-bearing instead of denying the kind test in its own first line.

## A defect on dev this fixes as a side effect

`app.questionBeatRow`'s second argument is written straight into `app.questionSpanRow` — the screen row a press on the widening answer's shapes resolves against — and it was the literal `2`. That is right only while the question's head fits the frame's top edge; behind a head long enough to wrap, every press on the shapes landed one row off per wrapped line. Taking the beat through `questionPanelInside` made it measured (`above+1`) rather than assumed. `TestTheBeatsRowIsWhereTheBeatIsDrawnUnderAHeadThatWraps` is the guard, and it fails with the literal restored: *resolves against row 2, but they are drawn on row 5*. Found by lane R reading the parameter rather than the diff; it is in the report's defect ledger because it was on dev and neither PR in this wave caused it.

## Proof

- `internal/tui3/questionset_test.go` — 25 tests (tabs, hold, edit, review order, partial send, empty review, esc, irreversible, answers from elsewhere not held, dressed copy keeps the step, transcript order, labels, frame, pointer, one-by-one, lifetime fan-out, counted rows, middle cut, no-safe-answer → tabs).
- e2e (live `deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash`, tmux): `TestQuestionsE2E/TwoQuestionsInOneStepAreOnePanelWithTabs` and new `…/FourReadsInOneBatchAreOnePermissionFrame` — both pass; gallery screens regenerated, the sheet's deleted.
- Acceptance drives as a terminal user, screens under `~/af-qv-reports/T/`: `live-ask3` (3 asks in one step → tabs → hold, go back, change, review, send; the model replied with all three answers in order) and `live-reads4` (4 reads → one frame → one by one → allow/deny mixed → one send; the model read three and reported the denied one).
- Manual: `questions.md` (*Several questions at once — tabs, go back to the previous question, answer them all at once*) and `permissions.md` (*Several approvals at once — approve all of these, allow all, deny all, one by one*), 7 new probes. Needles in `tuiwords_test.go`. The tabs' marks are the step dots (`tokens.GStepDone` / `tokens.GStepPending`) through `a.icon`; no glyph was minted.

Closes #840.

A waiting question's chip displaced the task row's door hint, so the one key that reaches the row disappeared exactly when there was something to reach it for.

`hintFitBeside` is `hintFit`'s ladder for the one line that carries a note beside the hint. **The door first and the note behind it**, and the clauses between them are the ones that give way: the note is a fact about the row's work and the door is the row's own key, so neither may be dropped for a page clause — not the fold, not the verbs, not the filter, not even the way out. The giving-way starts at the clause *after* the door and works forward, so the way out is the last to leave, which is exactly how `hintFit` already behaves everywhere else.

Two cases it handles on purpose:

- **A note that already opens with the separator.** A question with no head leaves the rail's own ` · ` at the front, so the join strips a leading one rather than adding a second. `railSep` is the one joiner down this column and a doubled ` · · ` is a line lying about its own shape.
- **A frame too narrow for the door and the note alone.** That is `hintFit`'s own last resort and the pair is cut, because there is nothing left to drop that would help.

The note's clauses are never dropped one at a time, because a note that lost its `alt+a` would be a question with no way left to reach it.

## Where this came from

**An aforge lane wrote this** — `~/af-lane.sh 840`, `aforge do` on `z-ai/glm-5.3` through OpenRouter, unattended on the Spark. It reused `railSep` and `hintFit`'s last resort rather than spelling either again, and wrote the change entry, the manual page, the unit tests and a 178-line end-to-end subtest. I read the diff and rebased it. Nothing needed correcting, which is the first lane today I can say that about.

Closes #894.

The `tasks` tool listed another window's work **one row per part**, and took its search cap over those rows. A window running one quick task with three parts drew four rows and spent four of the cap, so it could push a different window's whole task out of the answer entirely.

It now folds the way the `<elsewhere>` block already did: one row per family, with its parts counted on the family's own row, and both the cap and the overflow line count families.

## The two readings could disagree

The model gets both in one turn. `<elsewhere>` said `3 quick parts running` while the tool said four unrelated jobs, and a model deciding whether to start the same work believed whichever it saw last.

Both now come from `foldElsewhere` — **the block's own fold, reused rather than restated**. One writer is the only way the two stay the same sentence, and a second implementation of the same reading is what made them disagree in the first place.

Closes #892.

`x` over the task roster needed `alt+t` first, always. The manual promised a one-key stop the surface did not give.

**With exactly one stoppable row visible, `x` now raises that row's card directly**, and the row's own line names the key so the affordance is not something you have to already know. Two or more stoppable rows keep today's behaviour and `x` still types `x`.

## Why the multi-row case is unchanged

The argument for making the roster's keyboard askable was that *while the roster does not hold the keyboard there is no cursor and nothing is being aimed at*. With three rows on screen that is exactly right: a bare `x` would have to guess which one, and guessing wrong ends an hour of work.

It does not cover the one-row case. There is nothing to choose between, so the keystroke cannot land on the wrong thing. And the law the argument serves — one bare keystroke over a list must not be able to end an hour of work — is kept by the card, which asks and defaults to *keep going*, not by the focus requirement itself.

body:
Part of #927. Still owed: the issue's fix #3 (the grounding, spine and fan-out prompts state the depth the question warrants). It is recorded in the change entry and in `docs/design/waiting/DESIGN.md` §M "Still owed", because it changes what every planning pass is told and has to be measured against the planning bench before it lands.

## What was true, and what is true now

- **The wall was a stopwatch the model never saw.** Every structuring completion (resident + `aforge do`) ran under `pool.DefaultCallWall` (4 min), and no planning call carried a reasoning setting, so GLM 5.3 at its default `max` thought through the whole wall. **Now** every walled completion carries its wall to the effort ladder (`provider.WithThinkingWall`). The ladder derives a thinking budget: `share(level the pass runs at) × lane belief's rate for the asked machine × the time the completion really has`. At 210 tok/s × 4 min at max that is 47,880; at 20 tok/s it is 4,560.
- **One deadline, one derivation** (review D1). The time the completion really has is `walled.allowance`: the slot's wall, or the completion's share of the caller's own deadline when that is shorter. The same figure cuts the completion and is told to the model. The first completion takes half of what the caller has left (`completionsPerCall = 2`), so the answer ask always keeps the other half. A late round of a nearly spent command rail is therefore cut by its wall and asked for its answer; the rail no longer cuts it first and loses the thought.
- **A cut kept nothing.** `walled` returned `nil, ErrCallWall`. **Now** the walled decorator keeps what streamed. When a completion reaches its wall with thought on the wire, the decorator asks **once** for the answer. The ask sends the same messages, plus the thought, any begun answer and any begun tool call (as words) as the assistant turn, plus an answer ask. Thinking is off (required), the request shape is unchanged, and the ask gets the time that is left. `ErrCallWall` comes back only if that ask fails too. A completion that wrote nothing is not asked again.
- **The command rail cut honest work.** Both #927 strikes were `resident.commandWall` (10 min). **Now** `commandWall = spliceRounds (5) × pool.LongestCall (completion + answer ask)` = 40 min.
- **The receipt lied.** It said "the model stopped answering twice". It now says `I couldn't get this planned — the model thought past its time twice. Say 'try again' to requeue it.` The stage note and the receipt share one phrase, and `ErrCallWall` says the same.

## Review fixes (send-back of 02551c873)

| # | finding | resolution |
| --- | --- | --- |
| D1 | model told `w.wall`, not the deadline it has | `walled.allowance(ctx, n)`: min(wall, caller's remaining ÷ completions still to come); one figure feeds both `WithTimeout` and `WithThinkingWall`. Tests: `TestTheBudgetFollowsTheTimeTheCallReallyHas` (real adapter; a 1-min caller gives the budget for 30 s, not 4 min); `TestACallerWithLessTimeThanTheWallStillHasItsAnswerAsked` (an 80 ms caller with a 1 h wall is still cut by the wall and answered: 2 calls, the first has ≤ 40 ms) |
| D2 | no proof through the real door | `cmd/aforge/do_wall_test.go`: `aforge do --json` against a compiler that streams reasoning and never stops. Asserts the first body's `reasoning.max_tokens` (0 < budget ≤ 0.95×210×1 s), a second body carrying the thought, `settled: true`, exit 0, and no `stopped answering` in stdout/stderr. Control: the same model that answers is asked once, with the budget on its body. It reaches the wall through a `callWall` seam on `doRequest`/`brainOptions` (zero = `pool.DefaultCallWall`). **Mutation-checked:** removing chat.go's two `WithCallWall` lines fails both tests (exit 3 unsettled; no budget), and disabling the answer ask fails the first test |
| D3 | entry and close disagree | "Part of #927"; entry and §M name fix #3 as owed, with the reason |
| D4 | forming tool call kept nothing | `kept` records `StreamToolCallForming` per index; the answer ask carries `I had begun calling <tool> with: <args>` as words; the surface gets `StreamReplaced`. Test: `TestAHalfSentCallTravelsAsWordsAndIsVoided` |
| D5 | derivation recomputed per knob read | **left**: caching it means threading a field through `callKnobs` (`client.go` knobsFrom), which is outside the free files. The cost is per call, not per token: a map lookup and a four-level pace chain, paid only by walled requests. It is a perf follow-up for the provider owner |
| D6 | 20 ms wall also covers the answer ask | **left, cannot flake**: the stub answers the answer ask synchronously before any clock is read, and `walled.completion` keeps a nil-error answer whatever its timer says. A comment on `thoughtWall` now says so |
| D7 | manual overstated the guarantee | both pages now say that no budget is sent for an unmeasured machine or by a provider that refused one, and that the call still runs under the same wall |
| D8 | 80 min to bad news | **left**: it needs a real observation of splice round counts, which is not something to argue into a figure. The stage note keeps the person informed meanwhile. D1 makes each late round cheaper than `LongestCall`, never dearer |
| D9 | plan law read one directory | it now walks the tree with `filepath.WalkDir` and skips `testdata` |

## The one mechanism, and why it lives in `pool.walled`

The brief expected to reuse a #786 cut salvage. None exists on any road. `client.go`'s decodeErr branch cannot carry a partial out either: every watched call is a race, and `hedgeRace.abandon` returns the caller's deadline and nothing else. The partial exists only as the stream, so it is kept at the one layer that both hears the stream and knows the wall fired. **client.go, dispatch.go, hedge.go and lane/* are untouched.**

## Seam for the provider owner (files outside the free list)

| file | lines | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `provider/hints.go` | `effortRequest.wall`, `.lane`; `effortFrom` folds the asked lane | the budget is the other half of the effort decision |
| `provider/wire.go` | `effortAsked`, `resolveEffort`, `resolveReasoningBudget` | the reasoning field's resolution; the smaller of the rung and the wall wins |
| `provider/calllog.go` | `recordedEffort`: a wall budget is named `max within 4m0s` | that string is the think-duration belief key |
| `cmd/aforge/{chat,do}.go` | `callWall` on `brainOptions`/`doRequest` (zero = shipped wall) | the e2e's seam, same shape as `residentWait` |

## The bar's four questions

1. **The one abstraction:** the call wall as a contract. `walled.completion` is the single place a walled completion is sent, told its binding wall (`allowance`), and heard.
2. **Deleted:** the `nil, ErrCallWall` drop of a cut completion; the "stopped answering" sentence (ErrCallWall, stage note, receipt); the ten-minute rail and its false comment; the design doc's "owed" claim for this wall.
3. **Law tests:** `pool.TestEveryCompletionThroughAWallIsToldItsWall` (go/ast); `plan.TestPlanningReachesAModelOnlyThroughTheClientItIsHanded` (go/ast, whole tree); and the door itself, `cmd/aforge.TestAPlanningModelThatThinksPastItsWallStillPlans`.
4. **What a reviewer might call a band-aid:** the answer ask looks like a retry. It is not. A retry re-sends the same bytes and belongs to the layer above. The answer ask is a different question that only the wall can ask, sent once through the same client door. `spliceRounds = 5` is a count of the pipeline, not a tuning.

## Not done, on purpose

- Fix #3 (see top).
- On effort-dialect endpoints, OpenRouter maps a budget onto a word by its own rule, so the budget is a soft signal there. On those endpoints the answer ask is the guarantee.
- v3 (`internal/session`) arms no call wall.

Closes #915.

The tasks place drew a titleless conversation as `de9ea39e6f4c18c3` — a machine's word in the one column whose whole job is matching names. Home already solved this for its own lists with one spelling of the word, and the tasks place draws the same row, so it reads the name from there rather than spelling a second one.

## Why the check is case-insensitive

A titleless row's `Title` is never empty. `tasksConversationRows` fills it through `homeName`, whose title case has already raised the id's first letter, so the composer sees `De9ea39e6f4c18c3` where the id is `de9ea39e6f4c18c3`. A byte-exact comparison never fires. `EqualFold` is the one comparison that does, and the lane found that by reading the path rather than by guessing.

## Only the name changes

The row keeps its place. Its age stays empty, because `lastUserAt` is the zero time and the emptiness law draws nothing. And `chatProjectWord` still sees the row, so a project that is not this name does not echo the word back as a project tag beside it.

## Where this came from

**An aforge lane wrote this** — `~/af-lane.sh 915`, `aforge do` on `z-ai/glm-5.3` through OpenRouter, unattended on the Spark. It reused the existing `unnamedConversationWord` rather than adding a second spelling, wrote the change entry, the manual page, the unit tests and the end-to-end words row. I read the diff and rebased it; nothing needed correcting.
